title: Poor accessibility for the elderly
text:
Visiting the Vatican Museums is an impressive experience and certainly worth it. However, accessibility and care for the elderly are very limited.

I went with my grandparents and the tour was physically demanding: there are a lot of stairs and, although there are elevators, on several occasions it was not possible to use them. There are some benches along the way, but they are very few for the number of people there are. Also, in the cafeteria there are no chairs, only tables, which does not give you the possibility to sit and rest, something you would expect at least in that space.

As for the staff, the experience was disappointing. I asked for support on several occasions explaining the situation of my grandparents, but we did not receive help. When buying tickets, we only found availability with tour in Italian, even though in our group no one spoke that language, and we were not offered alternatives.

We were also charged for the headphones, but we had to insist several times to get them delivered.

It is a place of enormous cultural value, but the lack of accessibility and unwillingness of staff significantly affect the experience, especially for those visiting with older people.

title: Visit
text:

As in any religious place, correct dress required that usually cover shoulders and knees. When checking tickets (which are nominal for online purchase), you are asked for your ID. 
If you have not thought about drinking, or snacking, there are places to eat and drink (dispensers). However, you cannot eat and drink anywhere. There is the Vatican Post Office in the basement of the museum. 
We started the tour with the Pinacoteca, where there is a rich collection of Italian paintings. Then we went through the courtyard of the pine cone to reach the Chiaramonti Gallery and the Pope Clement Museum. The suite took us to Raphael’s rooms and the famous Sistine Chapel (where there are the most people).

title: Not the best time
text: I'm sorry to say that this was the most unpleasant experience of our trip to Rome. We booked a "skip the line" tour late in the day when crowds are supposedly winding down just before closing. Even at the late admission of 5:30 p.m., the crowds were still very thick. Honestly, it was hard to appreciate anything because we were shoulder-to-shoulder with people and the tour guide rushed us near the end to make sure we had enough time in the Sistine Chapel. The museum is massive and of course, contains beautiful art and objects. Admittedly, our main interested was the Sistine Chapel which is the end of the tour. In order to get there, you are forced to go through the museum. We usually do not join tours because we want to take our time and not be herded around. However, many travelers and Youtube videos suggested this as a way of avoiding long lines. So just be aware of the trade off between joining a tour and avoiding the admission line or going on your own and being able to take your time. Whichever way you go, it will be very crowded.

title: Wear comfortable shoes and pre-book your tickets!
text:
First things first, pre-booking is an absolute must!! We'd booked tickets for 9am entry and the queue for that was still quite long. The queue for those without tickets snaked right down the street!
We took the Metro from Termini to Ottaviano which was about a 10 minute ride and then a q minute walk.
Took about 20 mins to get in and through the security scanners. 
We'd booked tickets with an audio guide; took a while to locate these and they were a bit odd - I'd expected a headset but we were given handheld devices to listen to, which had to be worn around the neck and were a bit cumbersome.
The museum is absolutely vast and, if you were to stop and look at everything, you'd be there for more than a full day. We just kept walking and occasionally stopping. There's so much to see and take in. Many of the areas had beautiful art and painted ceilings so, by the time we reached the Sistine Chapel it didn't blow us away as we'd expected it to as it was yet another painted ceiling! Stunning in itself but not more so than the other areas.
Plenty of food options. We went for the pizzeria which wasn't busy and wasn't too extortionately priced. 
Several gift shops. Toilet queue not too bad.
Extensive gardens which we didn't really have time to appreciate.
An interesting visit with lots of walking.

title: Remains of ancient roman civilization
text:
The visit to Roman forum is typically combined with a guided tour of colossuem, roman forum and palatine hills. This is one of the most under rated portion of the guided tour, but a very important one. It was once the epicentre of roman empire, hosting temples, grand ceremonies and bustling markets.

Some of the most important temple remains in the roman forum are: temple of saturn, temple of vesta, temple of roma and venus, temple of castor and pollux; and cremation site of Julius Ceaser. 

We found the ancient roman civilization very similar to the vedic Indian civilization. Would strongly recommend taking a guided tour. Take an early morning tour to avoid crowds. Typically the combined tour for all the three sites is around four hours.

title: St. Peter's Basilica
text:
Visiting St. Peter's Basilica is nothing short of breathtaking. The sheer scale, intricate architecture, and artistic brilliance make it one of the most unforgettable landmarks in the world. From Michelangelo's magnificent dome to the stunning Peita, every corner reflects centuries of history and devotion.

The atmosphere inside is both peaceful and powerful, whether you are there for holy reasons, or simply there to admire artistry. Do note that it can get very crowded so would highly recommend an early morning visit.

title: Best experience in The Vatican
text:
I won't repeat what many have shared about the magnificence of St. Peter's Basilica. What I do want to let you know about is the Necropolis or Scavi tour. It is the tomb of St. Peter beneath the Basilica. Know that you cannot access the scavi without a separate entrance ticket. It is not part of the admission to the Basilica and not part of the Vatican Museum and Sistine Chapel tour. It was undoubtedly the best experience of our visit to The Vatican.

At the time of our visit, only 250 visitors per day are admitted to the scavi. To get tickets you must go the scavi.va website and request a date and time. Then you have to wait for a reply confirming the date and time and then pay for advanced tickets. It took as four attempts to finally get tickets and I think only after we said that we are there from XXX date to XXX date and we will take any date and time within that range. We actually didn't make any other plans until we found out the date and time of our visit to the scavi so we could work around it for the rest of our time in Rome.

The tour was fascinating and for me, a moving experience. The end of the tour dumps you right into the Basilica, avoiding the long lines outside. I highly recommend it. If you get a ticket, make sure you arrive there in plenty of time to find the entrance. I am in a rush right now and don't have time to write details. Just get there early and do not proceed to the line for the Basilica. You have to go left of the columns and pass two security check points and walk across an open plaza before you get to the entrance.

Good luck.

title: Fantastic place to visit, terrible queues to get in
text:
Fantastic place to visit, terrible queues to get in

We booked a fixed time slot of 1pm through HEADOUT.  We were to pick the tickets up at 12.30 but the queue at the pickup venue was chaotic as they were handing out tickets in time slots but the queue contained people with different entry times. 

Once that was sorted we were taken over to St Peter's Square with a guide (who we realised later was just to keep us occupied / informed through the long queue until we accessed the Dome - they didn't guide us around the church) and we reached the back of the security queue around 1pm.  It wrapped around the whole square and there was no way to avoid it as everyone had to be scanned and there were no 'skip-the-line' shortcuts, whatever the various tour operators tell you !  There were more security stations available, but they just weren't is use - the queues would have been halved if they had been open. 

We reached security and 2.20pm (so 1hr 20min later) and that was apparently not too bad (so try to avoid peak dates / times ...) and went straight to the Dome where you could with walk the 520 stairs to the top or take the elevator up to around 350 to the internal viewing platform, leaving just 170 to climb for an extra 5 euros to access the outside viewing platform right at the top of the Dome.  Best 5 euros we spent all holiday as we passed several sweaty and tired looking people who were taking a rest after climbing from the bottom - even the 170 steps will get your heart pumping and lungs working !  

The Dome is spectacular and looking down on the church gives you a different perspective from being in it at ground level, and reaching the higher level outside gives you a 360 degree view of Rome from its highest point, well worth the effort of getting up there.

Inside the church is fantastic and there is so much to see.  It is quite busy so you might have to wait to see everything up close and there was a queue to access the crypt area.

We couldn't see everything as we had something else booked (Vatican tour) and the huge queue had taken all of our spare time, but we saw the important things and got a good feel for the building.

You need to budget on 3 hours to see the whole thing, including the queue.

title: Sistine Chapel or Slaughterhouse? Health and safety regulations ignored
text:
I should have read previous reviews before we went. We are a family of 5 adults who paid €495 to Viator for the Vatican Museum, Sistine Chapel and St. Peter's Basilica Tour. From the start, despite the very best efforts of our guide, we were rushed through, with only a glance at most things and little opportunity to take photos. The real drama came as we continued towards the Tapestry & Maps rooms. Several tour groups converged and there was hardly room to move. We were corralled into tight spaces with no way out. If someone took ill or there was a fire there definitely would be a problem. We were stuck in a 'holding area' and passed through two extra rooms until the crowds in the Sistine Chapel were reduced. This was very uncomfortable and frightening.

In frustration, many people jumped the queue and went in front of us, causing us to become separated from each other and our tour guide. Women with small children in buggies banged into our legs from behind. At one point a tour guide shouted in my ear 'Keep up with your Guide'. It was chaos. My daughter asked if we were going to the Sistine Chapel or the slaughterhouse. I have looked at Trip Advisor reviews for the last two years and the word 'slaughterhouse' is used continually as is the phrase 'herded like cattle'. This is obviously a regular issue. We had not just arrived on a bad day.

At the entrance to the Sistine Chapel, tour groups from two different directions converged. Our Guide said that she would stand in front of The Last Judgement. We had difficulty finding her and because of the crowds didn't really see anything. People talked loudly and took photos. It was not a holy place. It was a hugely disrespectful commercial tourist trap. We then passed through the tombs of deceased popes, which was calmer and nicer and on to the beautiful St. Peter's Basilica. In front of one of the tombs of the Pope's was a stand with candles which could be lit for special intentions - minimum donation 3 Euros. It also had two further slots for donations - one for 10 Euros and the other for 20!! Commercialism at its best. That was the story of the day.

In my view health and safety regulations were not in place. It is an accident waiting to happen and the only reason for it is greed.

title: Bucket List only - Better Use of Time
text:
I have mixed feelings about this experience.

Summary:
The Good:
- Timed Entrance Tickets are the way to go.  We didn’t wait at all to enter, just a few minutes clearing security.
- Vast amounts of art of all types.  
- Sheer size of the collections
- Knowledgable Tour Guide

The Bad:
- huge crowds even late in the day
- the pathway to the chapel requires a insufferable amount of stairs, corridors, and rooms before arriving
- no real quiet time in the chapel
- feeling rushed all the time
- after the chapel, a just as insufferable walk to exit.
- no pictures allowed.  Heavily patrolled 

Do if you must (if a bucket list thing for you) or go if you have a good amount of time to kill in Rome.  For me The Basilica  was more impactful and I’d pick that over this.  I would not come to Rome just for this.

Full Review:
 We did a later in the day guided tour and our guide was great.  She provided an excellent overview history of the Sistine Chapel at the beginning using a large, bright digital screen to highlight places on the ceiling and walls of the chapel.  After that, it was a mess.  The amount of walking and transitioning up and down stairs was tedious.  The guided tour is 2-hours and you transition through the museum along with hundreds of other people.  The issue was your always fighting with others for space while moving.  

We had a train to catch later and were pressed for time, so we left the tour and bee-lined it to the Chapel.  It was a 10 min hurried walk up/down stairs and through a lot of pre-chapel areas before we got there.  Once there, we were rushed in, but only had a few minutes in the chapel along with hundreds people before moved towards the exit.  If you wanted to spend some time there, you had try find an approved seat, which weren’t many.  We arrived early evening, so the natural light was gone and the chapel only dimly lit.  No pictures allowed.

After exiting the chapel, it again was a series of up/down stairs with long transitions with hundreds of others to the exit near the entrance that you came in.   Again, another 10 min of hurried chaos walking.

I thought that some of the artwork before and after the Chapel was more interesting.

text: One of the most frequent reactions of travelers who first saw the forum for the first time: Is that all? Yes, this is all that remained after the Goths in 410, the Vandals in 432, and most importantly after the Christian Romans in the next millennium and a half, who dismantled most of the forum into churches and houses.  For the first time, it probably makes sense to go see the forum on a single ticket and walk along Via Sacra, wandering among the few remaining columns and stones and stumbling on the pavement. 20 years ago, I did just that. Now, every time I visit Rome, I simply walk from the Piazza Campidoglio to the observation deck and look at what little remains of the political center of the Eternal City.  Although initially it was like it was in antiquity, and then in the Middle Ages it was just a market square. And before that, the swamp.  For a long time after the overthrow of the tsars and the establishment of the republic, the market and politics coexisted in this place, as well as brothels. If you are standing on the observation deck, there will be a well-preserved Arc de Triomphe closer to you.  The arch of Emperor Septimius Severus was erected in 203 AD.  in honor of the 10th anniversary of the emperor's reign and in honor of the victory over Parthia, which, by the way, Rome survived.  To the left of the arch stands a wonderfully preserved building. This is the curia, the seat of the Senate. The small size of the building raises the question, how did the entire Senate, which numbered 900 people at the time of Julius Caesar, fit here? Apparently, they were going to another place together, maybe on the street nearby. Although people's assemblies, committees, gathered next to the Senate. And the building itself is a mock-up made during the time of Mussolini, who unsuccessfully tried to breathe the spirit of ancient Rome into the life-loving and pampered Italians. There is an empty rectangle behind the curia. In antiquity, perhaps the most beautiful building of the Basilica Aemilia Forum stood here. In those days, "basilica" did not mean a church, but a place of transactions. He was favored by moneylenders, merchants, and tax collectors. There are traces of bronze on the ground. It is believed that these are coins that melted during the fire during the first sack of Rome by the Goths of Alaric in 410. Right in front of you are 8 columns with an entablature at the top. These are the remains of the temple of Saturn of the fifth century. Saturnalia, the festivities that later developed into the Christmas holidays, started here every December in Rome. The lone column behind it is that of Phokas, the Byzantine emperor, the last to leave a mark on the Forum. Next to the column were rostra stands from which speakers in antiquity - the Gracchi brothers, Cicero. After the Battle of Antium, the noses of enemy ships were hung on them. Rostral columns in St. Petersburg trace their history from here. To the right of the temple of Saturn was the Basilica of Julius, built by Julius Caesar, where the city court sat. The three Corinthian columns are all that remains of the temple of the Dioscuri, the brothers Castor and Polux, whose Greek cult was transferred to Rome and was greatly revered. The semicircular, dilapidated building is the temple of Vesta. The Vestal priestesses of this temple had one duty to maintain an unquenchable fire. It was believed that if it went out, Rome would perish. They were the most revered women of the Eternal City with a lot of privileges, but with one unpleasant duty - they had to keep their virginity for 30 years while they served as Vestals (from the age of 6-10). If the passion was stronger, the Vestals were buried alive in the ground. Further to the left is the only ancient building in the Forum and the second after the Pantheon, which has survived to this day in Rome almost entirely. This is the temple of Romulus, which in Christian times became part of the basilica of Santi Cosma e Damiano, which saved him. The three massive cylindrical vaults behind it are all that remains of the Basilica of Maxentius Constantine, once the largest structure in the Forum. The Forum ends (and for those who enter it, on the contrary, precedes) the arch of Titus, erected in honor of the capture of Jerusalem during the first Jewish War in 70. The arch was erected 13 years after that and a year after Titus' death by his brother Domitian.  This arch served as a model for numerous arches already in Modern times during the Napoleonic Wars.

title: VAST AND EXTRAORDINARY ARCHAEOLOGICAL AREA
text: Near the Colosseum, enclosed between the Palatine Hill, the Capitoline Hill and Via dei Fori Imperiali, there is the vast and extraordinary archaeological area of the Roman Forum, a wonderful symbol of Roman times. The history of the site begins between the 10th and 7th centuries BC, when the area, originally marshy, was used as a necropolis. Over the centuries the area evolved with the construction of several buildings, resulting in the remains of buildings from different eras, until the medieval age, creating a heterogeneous fabric. After the expropriation and use of the area as a quarry of building material in the Renaissance period, which later became a grazing area with the burial, the area was rediscovered thanks to the continuous excavations begun at the beginning of the nineteenth century to arrive to the present day at the wonder that we can see and visit. The area has several entrances, but we opted for the entrance in front of the Colosseum, so an extraordinary and fascinating path opened up before us, helped by the description of the buildings and monuments from the App that we downloaded to the phone. Here is a summary of the wonders: we begin with the Arch of Titus, in memory of the victories of Vespasian and Titus; the Basilica of Maxentius, a large building used as a courthouse; the Temple of Romulus and the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina; the House of the Vestals, residence of the priestesses; the Times of Vesta and the Beavers; the Arch of Augustus; the Forum Square, with the Column of Seals and with the nearby Basilica Giulia; the Arch of Seventh Severus; the Curia, where the Senate met. To these are added other Temples and buildings. Exciting and magnificent path, where the enchantment of extraordinary beauty blends with history and wonderful art, to be faced slowly to be amazed and ecstatic all the senses!!!!  The visit of the area is perfectly organized, since you can buy the entrance ticket, including the visit to the Colosseum and the Palatine Hill, also online, avoiding the long queue at the ticket offices. Price (€ 16,00), organization, friendly and helpful staff, make the visit truly magnificent!  The whole route, done very calmly, we tackled it in about 2 hours. Fantastic and spectacular experience of a unique and wonderful place and rich in history!!!! Must visit, super recommended!!!!

title: a beautiful ride
text: Wonderful museums not to be missed. They constitute an exceptional complex both for the richness and quality of the works and for the sumptuousness of the environments. It's huge, we were there 2 and a half hours. I had planned a suitable route (we skipped the Art Gallery). After crossing the entire museum complex we climb a large helical ramp and access the Corazze Courtyard, covered with a steel and glass structure and the starting point of all the different visiting itineraries. Before we start, let's go up to the terrace, it's really worth it. From here you can admire the wonderful Dome of St. Peter and the Vatican Gardens. We return and pass through the Courtyard of the Pinecone: it is a large open space of 300 square meters (we see the huge bronze pinecone and the Sphere with sphere, sculpture by Arnaldo Pomodoro). From some perspectives we see the sculpture with the dome of St. Peter's Basilica in the background. We climb the stairs to the Gregorian Egyptian Museum. So, out of the blue, you are catapulted into the midst of mummies, hieroglyphs and papyrus from ancient Egypt. Continue your journey along the Chiaramonti Museum. It is an area completely set up by Canova: here you can find about a thousand ancient sculptures of all kinds. Not to be missed is the wing of the New Arm: bright barrel vaulted gallery with ancient mosaics in the floor and we remember the colossal Nile Statue and the statue of Augustus of Prima Porta. We go back and climb for the Pio Clementino Museum. It preserves in the vast collection of Roman art some absolute masterpieces (see my review of the museum). We climb the stairs and follow a long succession of finely decorated corridors, including the Gallery of Candlesticks and Tapestries. You pass through the beautiful Gallery of Geographical Maps. We follow the signs to go towards Raphael's Rooms: they are one of the undisputed and unmissable masterpieces of the Vatican Museums. We then proceed to the Borgia apartment (beautiful Hall of Saints’ Life), we pass through the Collection of Contemporary Art and arrive at the Sistine Chapel. You're left with your mouth open! At the end, you arrive at the Courtyard of the Pinacoteca: from here you have a unique view of the green area of the Vatican and especially the Dome of St. Peter. Remember not to descend the spiral staircase immediately as it allows you to exit the Vatican Museums. Follow the signs for the Carriage Pavilion: it is in a detached section and is one of the halls that I think you should definitely see. We go out for the Helical Staircase is one of the most spectacular and well-known stairs in the world, a masterpiece of architecture that makes any photo taken from top to bottom magical and vice versa. We had booked a guided tour of the Vatican Museums in advance, walked from the bus past hundreds of people who did not yet have tickets. We would then be allowed into the entrance area on time, our two-hour tour started from there with a little delay. 
The first stop was at a video board, where the paintings in the Sistine Chapel were explained for 20 minutes. After about 45 minutes we were just outside the entrance to the actual Vatican Museums. We then returned the headphones to the lady who was supposed to show us around the museums, as nothing interesting had been heard from her until then. 
So we let ourselves be pushed further through the museum without a guide. You had to wait a little longer for interesting exhibits before you had a reasonably clear view. There is no way to specifically view certain exhibits and then specifically go to the Sistine Chapel. 
After a good 2.5 hours of pushing through the halls, we were then in the chapel, were welcomed here by a guard who drove one forward, and by several hundred visitors (there are some pictures on the internet). It was just uncomfortable and we went straight out of the chapel. After almost 3 hours, the museum haunted us again.

In short, so much ado about nothing: a joke that is not funny, hypocrisy at the highest level.
Subjects, like the employee I had the misfortune to meet, deserve to be reported and fired in the trunk. Shame on you!!!
Unfortunately, this unpleasant and reprehensible episode, in the days that followed, has affected my stay in Rome and the memory that I will cherish of the city: this is the thing that I regret most.

ALESSANDRA

title: Michelangelo's masterpiece
text: There is so much to see and admire in the Sistine Chapel but the No. 1 attraction is Michelangelo's Creation of Man. How can you describe this masterpiece of art? The Italian guide has had plenty of practice. God is breathing life into Adam whois in a reclining position and embodies perfection as described in the Old Testament of a man being an imitation of God himself. A magical enigma is that the hands between the two almost touch, but don't. The chapel derives its name from Pope Sixtus 1X della Rovere, who was pontiff from 1471 to 1484. The 15th century decoration of the walls includes the false drapes, the Stories of Man and of Christ and the portraits of the Popes. Work on the frescoes began in 1481 and was concluded in 1482. In 1508, Michelangelo was entrusted to paint the ceiling and altering the decorations. Finished in 1512, the work consists of nine central panels that show the Stories of Genesis from the Creation to the Fall of Man, to the Flood and the subsequent rebirth of mankind with the family of Noah. In 1536, Michelangelo was tasked to further alter the decorations of the Sistine Chapel by painting The Last Judgement on the altar wall, causing the loss of the 15th century frescoes. The work, 42 feet high by 39 feet wide, was completed in 1541. If you see nothing else in Rome, you have to visit the Sistine Chapel.

title: Most IMPORTANT Hall in Vatican City! Most Overcrowded too!
text:
Although the St. Peter's Basilica is the centrepiece of Vatican City, the Sisitine Chapel is the MOST IMPORTANT hall in the entire Vatican City because the conclave to elect the Pope, the Supreme Leader of the Catholic Church, takes place inside this Chapel!

My uncle & I visited Rome for the first time in May 2025 and we visited the Vatican Museums twice in 2 days, both times with guided tours. The first guided tour was a morning tour which commenced at 7.15am and included climbing the dome of St. Peter's Basilica, visiting the crypt of the basilica, walking through the Holy Door of the basilica, visiting the Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel. 

IMPORTANT NOTE: The Vatican Museums consist of 54 museums, it is ENORMOUS!!! You have to walk through 17km of corridors, hallways, passageways and staircases in order to see all the exhibits in the 54 museums! The Sistine Chapel is the VERY LAST hall in the Vatican Museums. If you are a first-time visitor, you will most probably lose your way inside this enormous maze of 1200 exhibition halls, rooms, courtyards, corridors and passageways! Do yourself a favor and pay for a guided tour! PHOTOGRAPHY & VIDEOGRAPHY ARE STRICTLY PROHIBITED INSIDE THE SISTINE CHAPEL!

Before we arrived at the Sistine Chapel, our guide gave us an explanation about the paintings on the ceiling and the walls by Michelangelo, while referring to some pictures displayed in the Pine cone courtyard. Tour guides are NOT ALLOWED to speak to their guests inside the Sistine Chapel because it is ALWAYS OVERCROWDED during the normal operating times. When we arrived at the Sistine Chapel, we were shocked to see approximately 10,000 people inside the Chapel!!!! We struggled to walk through the crowd to get to the exit, we were literally squashed like sardines in a can(even worse than this!). There are museum security guards standing around inside the Sistine Chapel to make sure that visitors don't hang around inside there for more than 10 minutes and that nobody takes photos & videos. There are seats along the side of the walls but needless to say, all the seats are taken and those who occupy the seats seem to want to be inside here FOR A YEAR OR MORE!!!  Michelangelo's paintings on the ceiling and walls of the Sistine Chapel are truly beautiful, especially the Last Judgement. If you are afraid of crowded spaces, PLEASE BE WARNED!

For our 2nd guided tour, we took an exclusive after-hours guided tour of the Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel, whereby our group consisted of only 20 guests and 1 tour guide plus 1 museum security guard, and this tour started at 6.30pm, AFTER the Vatican Museums are closed to the general public. This exclusive night time tour is very expensive but TOTALLY WORTH EVERY PENNY!!! We had the whole museum complex to ourselves and when we arrived in the Sistine Chapel, we had the freedom to walk around freely and our guide could explain each and every detail of Michelangelo's paintings to us on the spot! WE HAD THE ENTIRE SISTINE CHAPEL TO OURSELVES!!!!!! We spent 45 minutes in here before following our guide to the exit and the tour ended at around 8.45pm.

These exclusive after-hours tours aren't available every day, in fact they are available only a few times per month and they are completely booked out very quickly. I did it with a company called The Tour Guy. Another company called Walks also offers a similar after-hours tour, the call the tour, "Alone in the Sistine Chapel". If you are planning to visit the Sistine chapel only once in your lifetime, you should consider taking this exclusive after-hours tour.

title: Follow the Rules and Allow Yourself LOTS of Time to Observe
text: It's hard to find words that haven't already been spoken about the Sistine chapel. What can you say? It's a legendary icon and should be on your European Travels bucket-list. There are STRICT rules you must follow, which should not be a problem for any visitor to follow. It's basic etiquette and modesty in clothing (it's required). No photography and no talking. You are here to observe and witness. And what an spectacular place it is. I went with a tour guide, so I feel I had an advantage in my appreciation of the art because she prepped and explained things to me prior to us walking inside. That said, if you do not have a tour guide, do not worry, you can still appreciate what you're seeing. Michelangelo's frescoes are INCREDIBLE in person; a genuine masterpiece. Take your time, do not feel or think you are rushed. This sacred space should be enjoyed, and since you are not allowed to take photos or video, make sure you look, think, and consider. Really get that image in your mind. Yes, you can Google or buy books with photographs of the Chapel, but there is something very special about being there and creating a memory.

title: Pay a visit even if religion isn’t your thing.
text:
So first all I bought fast track tickets to enter the Vatican from get your guide but I had to wait ages for the rep to arrive with our tickets. Although the fast track tickets are quicker we went in this week (march) , it was cooler  and still queued for 45 minutes. The normal queue snaked right around the Vatican so I assume these were waiting at least 2 hours. This would be more in the peak summer months. All belongings are checked through airport style security and you walk through an airport style detector. There are a number of homeless beggars on the walk up . There are also a number of ticket tout scammers trying to sell none existent tickets so avoid these.

Anyway once inside St Peter’s you will see how stunningly beautiful it is. It’s vast and very ornate. If you buy a bottle of holy water from outside you can get it blessed by a priest inside for a small fee “ donation “.  You will easily spend a few hours here. You can also get a ticket to climb into the dome but we didn’t go . 

Looking out across the seating area down the high street is an amazing view. 

Even if religion is not your thing like us , still pay a visit.

title: Third time here and still miss
text:
The must’s (written in my previous review of 2023 and free to visit) and where the main stream go to look are the St. Peter’s baldachin; Michelangelo dolorous sculpture of Jesus and Mary, the Pietà, which is always crowded (in everytime I visited in the last 3 years); the monumental tomb of Pope Alexander VII; Swiss guard change and this time made it to do the dome’s tour, in reality a self walking tour.  Tickets can be purchased directly there(*) in the back part of the basilica then wait for the lifts to be taken up to the dome balcony.  Once finished the dome balcony roundwalk, take the small alley that lead to the front part of the basilica (there are no signs and look anonymous) because that way is where is located the front terrace of the basilica with the statues, that classic Vatican piazza view from high.  Important, wear very comfy shoes because there are lots of stairs and some kind of bend walking (for tall people) because of the dome shape.  Third time here and still missed the Vatican necropolis/grottoes which will try to do and review next time.
 
(*) I know there are sites and travel experts that suggest to buy the tickets in advance but the thing is, to enter the Vatican basilica area is necessary to pass through stressy security checks and can take an hour maybe more so can risk to miss the reserved time-slot or plan accordingly by allowing much more time before… read previous reviews that some even were in line before and lost the time-slot, I guess that is just a matter of luck... the best is to be there in the early morning.  One thing more, consider also the rain factor, that whole Vatican piazza view from above is located outdoors!

title: A wonder two thousand years in the making…
text:
Catholicism is nearly two thousand years old, it spans the world, taken every nationality, race, and socioeconomic group… but it has only one true home. 

St. Peter’s Basilica is nothing sort of a wonder… the size, the scale, the grandeur. There is nothing like it anywhere on earth. As a temple to worship it is unmatched. 

As I took in the scale and scope of it, it occurred to me that in no modern endeavour does humanity care enough about something to treat ninety the reverence needed to build this. In that respect this is a sobering experience to be reminded of a faith, a belief, a will to belong, that just doesn’t exist anymore. 

This is more than a sight. To wander about and take it in is to have an experience. 

We took in the hall and the dome and it was simply breathtakingly majestic. 

I recommend it to anyone, religious or not. It’s a marvel to be seen at least once in your lifetime. 

Take the trip.

title: Lots to see but very crowded
text:
An impressive building with lots to see however we haven’t been anywhere quite so crowded in a very long time. We visited in March and although we were expecting crowds, there were way more people than we imagined there would be at this time of year, I dread to think what it is like in the summer, I am not sure how you could possibly fit anymore people in the building. One of the main issues is the amount of tour groups walking around. People stopping in random places while the tour guide talks about something which then holds up the crowds behind them. Chaos. 

The museum itself has lots of interesting artifacts and the audio tour is helpful as there is so much to look at. The Sistine chapel was a disappointment as there is scaffolding up so it just feels like any other room, expect for the ceiling which is impressive. As with everywhere else, it is way too busy in there and there are very few places to sit. 

The staff in the museum were helpful as I have a disability and use a walking aid so they helped me to get around and were friendly. 

The staff in the café in the middle of the square were miserable though. 

Overall it is a very impressive place and there are lots of wonderful things to see but there are way, way too many people in there.

title: Useful tips for families with small children. Skip the queue.
text:
If you would like to spend hours admiring beautiful and impressive artworks, then here is the right place. You can access the Sistine chapel and the Dome via the Museum. The tickets of 20 Eur are worth it. If you want to access the Dome, you need to pay extra for the Dome. The museum has lots to offer of paintings, sculptures and exhibitions from other continents as well, which I didn’t expect. If you’re traveling with small children, then I have some useful tips. With small children, you can skip the queue. Walk right to the entrance of the museum. It went smoothly for us until we discovered the lack of lifts (more correctly, the willingness to let us use them), as the guards had to leave their posts to accompany us up and down the lifts. To access several areas, we had to carry the pram through crowded stairs. It was tiring. I would recommend light and small prams or no pram at all. 

It was nice to travel during low season, with no one rushing us out of the room. We spent too much time in each room,  ended up with limited of time to admire the most important paintings, the Michelangelo’s paintings in the Sistine chapel and we missed the Dome. By the way, this famous painting of creation of Adam («E-T phone home» with God) is right in the middle of the ceiling. It was so difficult to spot, because there’re so many paintings to look at and that room was the most crowded. I simply had to google it up afterwards. 😅

My total review, the service could be better for people with disabilities and prams with access to the lifts, and more signs to guide us. It was hard to know where to begin and were to end up. Otherwise I would have given five star.

title: Beautiful chapel
text:
I concur with most of the reviews that this place is overly crowded. But this is normal for all important places of worship that I’ve been to such as  Mecca, Hindu temples etc.

title: Breathtaking. The Final Stop and Highlight of a Visit to the Vatican Museums
text: The final stop on your tour of the Vatican Museums and the highlight of the museum. They definitely save the best for last. Many art historians consider the Sistine Chapel to be the greatest work of art by a single individual. It is a breathtaking experience. Michelangelo painted the frescos on the ceiling between 1508-1512, while lying on his back and completed The Last Judgement in 1541. Having a rented audioguide with you adds to the appreciation of what you are seeing. This is also the room where Cardinals gather when electing a new Pope. The small stove that sends out black or white smoke announcing whether a new Pope has been elected can be seen.  It can get very crowded in the room but take your time, find a seat along the side of the room for a bit, ignore the chaos around you and enjoy the experience of what you are seeing as you gaze upward. Note that no photography is allowed in the Sistine Chapel although some of us are compulsive and shameful rule breakers.

title: Symbol of Christianity
text: They came to the Cathedral around 9am on Monday morning - it was raining outside and the queue was small - only stood for 15 minutes. Admission is free - in the autumn I was already in Rome and the queue was huge at midday and everyone showed some tickets. I understand who wants to speed up the passage. But we're lucky enough this time. By the time they left 40 minutes later, the line was already across the square. We first went down to the ground floor - you can see the gravestones of some popes and even the front top of St. Peter's burial ground. And already directly from the crypt went up to the Cathedral. By the way, there are toilets in the basement. What a great Cathedral! I'd forgotten, even though I'd visited it twice before, along with the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel. But after many hours of trekking through museums, the Cathedral no longer evoked much emotion. But this time, from this morning on, it hit more than before. Sister was a first and she was speechless. So we went in circles a few times, trying to get a peek inside the chapels, where visitors are usually not allowed. We were even allowed into one with a group of nuns. As always, Michelangelo's work was impressive. But later, in a completely different church, I saw a very similar Pieta and that became the main mystery of this visit to Rome - later I read that it was a copy of the artist Lorenzo Lotti. But it's incomparable to the original. Although Michelangelo was only 24 (according to other sources, 23 at all) when he created this masterpiece. But the cathedral contains many other striking creations. So it's worth coming to the Cathedral, but if it's your turn and you only have one day, you should come as early as possible. Or if you have a few days in the Eternal City, then the Vatican should devote the whole day - take tickets to museums in advance, sit in the unique Sistine Chapel, consider the amazing uniform of the Swiss Guards and admire the power of St. Peter's Cathedral - it really is a symbol of Christianity and it doesn't matter if you are Catholic or not.

title: Don’t use Rome City Tours
text:
I went without a guide and booked with Rome City Tour on trip advisor.  My ticket was for 12:00 and Rome City Tour’s instructions said you would receive the ticket via email 2 hours in advance.  I tried calling them on whatsapp at 10:15 when I had not received my ticket.  I didn’t get an answer but they did respond to a whatsapp message.  They said I should receive it by 11:00 due to the servers being slow.  

I had an hour walk so I set out on my way and arrived a little before 12:00.  Still no ticket.  There was no one onsite to help me.  The address they gave was just the entrance to the museum.  I messaged again. They asked me if it would work for tomorrow or after 2:00 today.  It was starting to rain pretty hard at this point.  

I said no, today at 12:00 was my time and I need my ticket.  I told them the latest I was willing to go in was 1:00.  I heard back from them 16 minutes later and they said they needed 10 minutes and they would get the tickets for 1:00.

Seventeen minutes later I had a ticket for 1:30.  It was attached to a group ticket so it looked like I paid more for it than I did.  I will be watching my bank account.  I do not trust these people.  

They gave me instructions to use passenger way 2 or 3 and they would let me in at 1:15.  This was incorrect.  When I asked the staff at the entrance they told me to get in a long line that was away from the passenger way entrance until it was 1:30.  I was also supposed to use passenger way 1.  The long line moved up to the entrance at 1:30.  

Do not use Rome City Tour unless you want a horrific start to the museum and Sistine Chapel.

Once you actually get in, there is a set path you have to take.  I just wanted to see the Sistine Chapel but you have to go through the maze to get there.  It is just like an ikea maze without shortcuts and tons more people.  It took me 1.5 hours and I didn’t look at anything else in the museum.  You will go up and down tons of stairs and if you ask how to just get to the Sistine Chapel it is always just ahead, turn left.  Once you are ready to leave, it is not clearly marked how to leave.  You are stuck in there with so many people and unable to find your way out.  If you are not into seeing everything, I don’t think it is worth it.  Especially on a rainy day.

I went on a random Wednesday in October so I think it is just always crowded.

title: 551 steps but only 321 if you purchase the lift ticket
text:
We recently went to St. Peter's Basilica as part of our Jubilee visit to Rome and spent some time visiting the dome as part of our experience. Entry tickets were reserved online prior to our visit, there are scheduled visitation times, it is recommended that you visit the basilica 45-60 minutes prior to your scheduled entrance (stairs and lift) up to the inner dome. 

We did the lift visit (saving around 231 steps of climbing), taking you up to the roof terrace of the basilica where you can walk around the contoured rooftop. There are public toilets, gift shop and cafe here. You then enter the steps only section which is a two part experience. 

First you enter the inner cuppola area where you can see the mosaics up close and peer back down to the basilica main floor around the baldachin. This is a really neat opportunity. The amount of steps climbed to this level is fairly minimal, making the visitation comfortable for most. 

You then climb a narrow and curved single-file staircase up to the top of the dome where you have outside access and 360 degree views of Vatican City, Trastevere, the Historic Centre and Roman countryside. We very much enjoyed the views, particularly immediately east where you see the iconic Piazza di San Pietro from the dome's elevated position. This second part requires quite a bit of climbing which might be challenging for some. 

On the whole, this was a rewarding experience. Just be ready for some climbing on the day. Even with the lift ticket, you will still need to climb around 320 steps, much of which is in single file, confined stairwell that curves its way up and down the upper dome. As generally healthy people, this wasn't bad for us but we did note some people struggling with their climbs on the day.

title: Never imagined that Michelangelo would be a source of such displeasure and angst
text:
Awful experience. We were, like everyone else, forced to visit of every nook and cranny of its massive buildings through harrowing narrow corridors, many with art works -- modern, Egyptian and African art and artifacts -- that have nothing to do with the Vatican’s real history and raison d'etre.  

It was overcrowded, suffocating, tiring and wearing.  Just way too many people, many with bulky backpacks, parents with large strollers, large groups blocking access into narrow entrances, people standing still holding up their phones to take pictures of everything but mostly of themselves.  - unaware that they were blocking millions of people behind them -- or looking down at them to see the pictures they just took (or to check messages).  

We finally made it to the Sistine Chapel, completely exhausted and out-of-sorts, only to find a standing-room-only mob of zombie-like visitors all taking everything through their phones or posing for pictures, and the Last Judgement completely hidden behind the temporary renovation façade that was not disclosed to us by the “Loving Rome” vendor through which we purchased our tickets. 

In sum, this was the most unpleasant travel experience we ever had, spanning some 50 years across some 30+ countries around the globe. 

We never imagined that Michelangelo would be a source of such displeasure and angst.

title: What should have been a fantastic museum visit is marred by woeful incompetence
text:
The Vatican museums house some of the world’s most beloved masterpieces. It is a collection revered the world over - anyone interested in history would want to see at least some of it. We certainly did. 

We arrived early to cater for the long lines. This is when the fun began. The queuing area is staffed by what I can only assume to be the Italian version of the Keystone Cops. There were many queues and according to staff, their purpose and applicability changed from moment to moment, depending on which Keystone Cop was doing the talking, These queues were dependent on the time of people’s tickets. However there were no signs, no meaningful guidance from the inepts at the gate, it was a free-for-all. It was ugly, it was messy - for families it was unforgivably awful. 

My thought on the way in that at the home of Catholicism, with nearly two thousand years to plan - it’s depressing this is the state of things. 

Inside the museum, what should have been  a beautiful experience is made just awful by the fact the place is grossly, enormously, irrationally stuffed with people. It is simply too busy. 

The things put in place to help manage the heaving masses made the experience more confined, more rushed, more miserable. Every time I went to stop for a moment to look at something, or to talk to one of my kids, there was yet another person wanting to get by, or wanting to see the thing next, or wanting to just look, or just cross… it was just dreadfully woefully dreadful. 

For reasons that defy explanation, the museum operates some asinine one way system around the exhibits. It feel like being cattle. The net effect is that you can’t go from the things you want to see to the next, then the next. You have to follow the stupid system. 

I’ve recently visited the Louvre, which was less busy, less regimented, less controlling, and as a consequence much more enjoyable. 

Don’t get me wrong there are wonders to see at the Vatican Museum - but seeing them is just painful. You do it because this is the price - not because it’s agreed experience. 

The whole thing is just marred by an idiotic incompetence in organisation and it’s a terrible shame.

Take Walks Vatican tour review – The Travel Temple
The Vatican receives overwhelming acclaim as an unmissable, awe-inspiring, and historic destination, often described as a "once in a lifetime" experience for its art and architecture, particularly the Sistine Chapel and St. Peter's Basilica. However, reviewers strongly emphasize that it is overcrowded, with long, often hot, queues and high-pressure, rushed, or "herded" experiences in popular areas. 
Key Reviews and Tips:
Essential Advice: Book tickets well in advance online to skip the massive, slow-moving queues, or consider a guided tour to navigate the overwhelming crowds.
Pros: Incredible, world-class, and unparalleled collections of art, sculptures, and history.
Cons: Extremely packed, especially during summer; some report rude staff and limited time to appreciate the art, specifically in the Sistine Chapel, where visitors are moved along quickly.
Best Time to Visit: Early morning or later in the day to avoid the worst of the crowds.
Alternative: The Vatican Gardens are noted as a more peaceful alternative, though they require a separate, pre-booked guided tour. 
Most reviewers agree that despite the chaos, the cultural significance makes it worth the effort.

title: The most horrible experience in Rome

The visit to the Vatican Museums was, without exaggeration, one of the most horrific experiences of my trip to Rome. We had purchased tickets on GetYourGuide with skip-the-line option, for a total of 112€ in two. Even the fact that we had to go to the meeting point first to have the actual tickets printed was uncomfortable and unclear.

We had the entrance scheduled for 11:00, but due to the endless waits at the metal detectors we only entered at 12:40, after a good 1 hour and 40 minutes of queueing. Of course, this is not directly the fault of the ticket provider, but in fact paying extra for the “skip the line” turned out to be just a waste of money, almost a mockery.

Once inside, the situation was even worse: an impressive amount of people, to the point of being literally dragged by the crowd without being able to stop and look at anything calmly. Environments with microscopic doors where dozens and dozens of people had to pass at once, creating continuous traffic jams and a suffocating experience.

Undoubtedly wasted money and one of the most disappointing experiences of the entire trip. I wouldn't do it again.

If I could, I'd put 0 stars out of 5.

title: To visit? Definitely, but NOT when the Last Judgment is covered for work that will last three months!!
text:
Positive experience but unfortunately handled in a very superficial and rough way. The approximation of the work of the office in charge for communication and relationship with the public begins already at the time of purchase of the ticket where there was no trace of the start of work in the Sistine Chapel. Basically the Last Judgment was covered by a cloth that had to reproduce the underlying work in high definition ... a cloth so transparent that you can see very well ... the scaffolding mounted!! Fortunately, the SONIA guide was very good at explaining, and this gave meaning to the visit that ended not admiring Michelangelo's masterpiece ... but trying to imagine him on the scaffolding ... and trying to forget the sentence formulated by the office of communication and public relations that to our complaint - when we learned of the start of the scheduled and not urgent works - replied verbatim: "during the restoration work for the extraordinary maintenance of the Last Judgment, which began last February 1, the Sistine Chapel will remain open to the public, continuing to welcome faithful and visitors, while, behind a high-definition cloth reproducing the image of the same Judgment, the restorers will carry out the cleaning operations. Scheduled visits will be held regularly and therefore there is no partial or full refund of the amount spent" .. One is obviously left with a bitter taste in the mouth for not having been made aware, during the purchase, of the impossibility of seeing the Last Judgment. Serious lack of due notice, especially in view of the fact that the ticket cannot be refunded or changed date.
N.B. Try to arrive at least 45 minutes before the start of the visit because the entrance to the museum is a real mess, especially at the weekend. All visitors, with or without a purchased guide, and groups, converge at the same point and there are no dedicated corridors for each type of visitor. In this way, the 30 minutes suggested in the ticket are absolutely not enough to reach the ticket office (where you need to queue up to hand in the voucher arrived by email and take the real ticket) and then report to the internal meeting point for the guided tour.

title: I hope this review gives interest.
text:
My tour was canceled because the tour guide came upon illness. 

St. Peter’s Basilica 

It is the largest church on Earth. The Christians, who at the time seemed like a radical cult to some, were the best scapegoat for an emperor with no conscience. Thus, Nero initiated the persecution of Christians. According to tradition, St. Peter, St. Paul, and countless other Christians were martyred during this time.
The Stadium of Nero was located on the very spot where the Vatican exists today. According to tradition, after St. Peter was taken from the cross, he was buried in a nearby necropolis along with pagans.
Constantine legalized Christianity. He then took it upon himself to build a church on top of St. Peter’s tomb. 
The most fascinating fact I discovered through research was that over 10,000 unpaid workers were involved in the construction of the new Basilica. The old Basilica had experienced many tumultuous periods, first between 330 and 800, and again from 1250 to 1400. Overall, the book met my needs, and I would recommend it.
The construction of the new Basilica, which was funded by donations in exchange for forgiveness from the Catholic Church (or "indulgences"), ultimately led to the Protestant Reformation.

Having a guide leading the group through the labyrinthine complex and offering excellent commentary about the history and architecture of the church was well worth the cost. 

After the tour, I attended the daily mass at the altar of the Chair of St. Peter. Wanting to check out the Vatican Grottoes, I returned a couple days later, but had a hard time finding the entrance. Currently, you have to exit through the front, turn left (north), go down the stairs outside, and turn left again. Overall, it was a wonderful experience making a pilgrimage to the greatest church in Christendom.

title: THE WONDER OF A MASTERPIECE
text: In the Vatican City State, in St. Peter's Square, where according to tradition the burial of the Apostle Peter took place, stands this wonder, a true masterpiece of Italian art. It is the largest of the four papal basilicas in Rome and probably the largest in the world. Construction began at the beginning of the 16th century, on the site where the ancient Constantinian basilica once stood; during the work, various projects and architects followed, until the consecration of 1626. The majestic and magnificent facade, which overlooks the spectacular St. Peter's Square and is preceded by a staircase, is composed of giant order columns, framing the entrances and the Loggia delle Benedizioni. On the top there are 13 large statues (Jesus, John the Baptist and the Apostles), while on their respective sides there are two clocks and under the left one there is the bell cell. A splendid and majestic portico, closed by a gate, runs along the entire facade; inside there are the beautiful five portals with bronze doors to enter the Basilica. The wonderful and enchanting interior is a huge space divided into three naves; the huge central nave, with barrel roof and splendid marble floor, features numerous and splendid marble statues in the niches of the pillars, as well as two beautiful and monumental holy water fonts and the bronze statue of St. Peter. The right aisle is an inexhaustible source of magnificent masterpieces: it begins with Michelangelo's wonderful Pietà, continues with several marble monuments, ending with the large and splendid Chapel of SS. Sacramento, rich in gilded stucco and with gilded bronze ciborium by Bernini. The left aisle is also full of magnificent masterpieces: it begins with the beautiful Chapel of Baptism, rich in mosaics and with a magnificent and monumental baptismal font, continues with several marble monuments, ending with the large and splendid Chapel of the Choir, rich in gilded stucco and with mosaic in the altar. The transept is enchanting, where there are 3 magnificent altars on each side and, in the niches of the pillars, several statues of Saints. At the crossroads of the transept with the nave, the majestic and wonderful dome, large and with a height of over 130 meters from the ground and decorated with the mosaic technique, is revealed. The space below is occupied by Bernini's grandiose and wonderful bronze canopy with twisted columns, which houses the Papal altar, below which there is the sacred Sepulchre of St. Peter. On the apse wall there is the choir, with the beautiful and monumental Chair of St. Peter in the center of the wall, another great work by Bernini. A unique, wonderful and majestic place, where large numbers mark different masterpieces of inestimable historical and artistic value distributed in the immense interior area! A unique Basilica in the world, indescribable for its beauty and wonder, as well as an exceptional place of prayer and spirituality for world Christianity! You remain speechless and without adjectives, impossible not to come out ecstatic!!!! Definitely not to be missed, to visit absolutely!!!!!

title: ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ A Truly Inspiring Experience at the Vatican – Book Ahead!
text:
I visited the Vatican for a 9:00 AM entry in November and it was absolutely flawless. There was no queue at all — I walked straight in with zero waiting. The whole process was incredibly organised, and I can’t stress this enough: you MUST book your tickets in advance to enjoy the same smooth experience. If you turn up on the day, the queue is super long and you stand for hours and have to wait. 

Inside, the Vatican is every bit as breathtaking as people say. The art, the atmosphere, the history — it completely surrounds you. I also climbed to the top of St. Peter’s Basilica, and that was an adventure in itself! There are 320 steps to the very top (the lift only takes you part of the way), and it’s definitely challenging. The climb is exhausting, but the moment you reach the top, it all becomes worth it. The view over Rome is phenomenal, and there’s a quiet, spiritual feeling up there that’s hard to describe. The steps are super tight and is shared in both directions. There are some int small resting pints every so often but not many and there are usually many people waiting behind you as well as it front. It’s a small viewing platform and once you’re up, you’re stuck. It has amazing views. 

The entire visit felt very moving and deeply rewarding. Everything was well organised, the staff were helpful, and being able to walk straight in at opening time made the experience even better.

If you’re visiting Rome, the Vatican isn’t just a highlight — it’s an unforgettable, spiritual, once-in-a-lifetime experience. Book early, go for a morning entry, and take your time to appreciate every moment.

title: Not what I was expecting 💁🏼‍♀️
text:
The Sistine Chapel.. first of all, it is not a proper Chapel, it's more like a long hall and it is very, very crowded. Let me split the review into two parts: the art and the atmosphere/organisation. 
The art 🖼 
We all know that the Sistine Chapel is a place to be seen, mostly for Michelangelo's paintings (the ceiling and the Apocalypse). The paintings are indeed very beautiful and it's worth going through the visiting experience to see them. I can see why it was a struggle to paint it and why Michelangelo was seen as a genius at the end of it. It is indeed a masterpiece. 
The atmosphere 🫣
You reach the Sistine Chapel after you've already been through a good part of the Vatican Museums. 🇻🇦 You can feel that you've arrived because everything begins to feel incredibly crowded and there are warnings: silence and no photos. Inside, there are a bunch of men in suits that hurry you since there are so many people, you cannot stop to enjoy the view. Your only chance is to find a place in the crowded middle or   a sit at the sides. I would say it's like being in a very crowded train station where everyone is rushing not to miss the train. 
All in all, I would say it is worth the visit but the experience is underwhelming.

title: Beautiful Chaos
text:
I enter the chapel. 

An Italian man in a black suit frantically waves me to the side 
"Go! Go! Go!", funneling me to the next man, also dressed like a body guard. A chain of tuxedoed men hurries me round the edge of the Sistine chapel.

Before they can stop me, I duck out of the stream they are channeling, i to the throng at the centre of the chapel. The guard shouts "quick! Go more to centre!"

It's loud, people are chattering, the odd smartphone reaching up to the ceiling to capture Adam.

Three quick notes, then an automated announcement "PLEASE BE SILENT, THIS IS A PLACE OF WORSHIP. REMEMBER THAT PHOTOGRAPHS ARE NOT PERMITTED"

The crowd pays no heed. I sit near to Karen. She loudly shushes the unfortunate next to her, "silencio!", then returns to her phone call - truly an appreciator of fine the arts.

One of the body guards shouts"SILENCE! THIS IS A HOLY PLA-" only to be cut off by the announcement  "PLEASE BE SILENT, THIS IS A PLACE OF WORSHIP. REMEMBER THAT PHOTOGRAPHS ARE NOT PERMITTED"

I do not know what Michaelangelo would have thought of the sheer chaos of the Sistine chapel, for serene it is not.

title: It could have been much better
text:
Well, the place is just amazing and the art….crazy I can tell you that. The level of art that you can find inside can’t be described. From the paintings collection to the sculptures, Egyptian section, etc and of course: the Sistine chapel in the Vatican museum. However not everything that shines is gold. The price? They tried to scam us 100 times. We went with a small baby and guess what…. You can skip the line (5 hours of line!!!) and it’s 20 euros ticket… the people outside are trying to scam you they asked us for 125-150 euros per person! And it’s 20…. (With a baby you don’t do the line, confirmed, plus it’s 20 euros. General admission is 20 euros but you need to do the line…so in this case better be up early) Be careful. The bad thing is that these scammers are around all Vatican offering you tours for 100 euros, 150…. Guided ones… My friends I don’t need a guided tour, a SIM card is 30 euros and I get access to infinite information. In any case, going with a stroller and a small baby? Don’t go I wouldn’t recommend the opposite seriously we almost got crazy. Another point: ladies and gentlemen from the Vatican Museum Management, I get you need to make money but you can not over sell tickets and allow thousands of people or some day someone will die of anxiety there I swear to God. 
In any case, the art: amazing, incredible I was wowed and I’m as I love art and story but the whole experience? No. Paying 20 euros for this? I would say “ok” but paying 50 or 150 as they ask you outside to “skip the line”? No, thanks. 
One last note: why cannot someone take pictures there? What’s the problem? There are millions of pictures online….  It’s a pity that internet is killing everything seeing this overcrowded as this is something to admire… in any case, worth the visit if you come in a day where you don’t have 1 million of people around and you can do things as breathe or walk.

title: So much beauty and so many people
text: Evoking the sacredness and artistic beauty of a place like the Sistine Chapel would be almost superfluous and therefore in this review I will limit myself to providing some practical information regarding the visit. The Chapel is located halfway along the tour of the Vatican museums and is the place where the largest public gatherings inevitably take place. Visitors are admitted inside very slowly but once inside they are invited to immediately reach the center of the room and only from that point is it possible to observe the splendid frescoes that cover it. In theory there would be an invitation to remain silent and not take photographs, in practice a bit of everything happens and in the presence of so many people it is not really possible to fully enjoy the visit. The advice is to try to visit half an hour before the museums closing time, at that time there should be a little less crowd but then you will have to hurry to reach the exit in time as it is not really close. Beyond the difficulties linked to the large influx of visitors, it remains one of those places that must be seen at least once in a lifetime.

title: Crowds, crowds, queues, queues, pickpockets, beggars- an embarrassment for the church.
text:
First of all, we paid for skip the line which was entirely pointless as im not entirely sure if this queue was longer than the other queue.
Then after reading reviews that it wasn't worth buying advance tickets to climb into the dome we stood in another queue for a hour and a half to buy tickets to climb the dome.
My mum went up in the lift and then queued a further 30mins to get in the lift.
There is no help or assistance at the top. On the stairs to the cupola you queue all the way up and all the way down.
My mum stood for so long waiting to get the lift down, she gave up and had to come down the stairs.
The exit from the square was surrounded by beggars which upset my daughter. It's a disgrace really that those who live in Vatican city pay no tax, and just the proceeds from paying for Vatican access raises over £2000 per Vatican resident per day, but they can't sort out the homeless people begging in the streets.
Pickpocketing is rife in the area, someone tried to grab my mums handbag but it was wrapped round her body.
Honestly- what a miserable experience. Very simply- having a police presence, having number limits on tourists and insisting on advance bookings for dome access, and maybe investing more in supporting the thousands of people living in poverty would improve the experience and reflect the church values better.

text:
I have never experienced such inept organisation as I did here. We had bought prebooked tickets for 1.00pm entrance but were met with a huge crowd of people, both prebooked and people who just turned up on spec, all mixed together. The police who were supposedly in charge of directing everyone didn’t have a clue what to do. It took well over an hour to get in only to be faced with another security check, more queues and disorganisation. 
On entering St Peter’s the first thing we saw was hundreds of perspex chairs filling the whole area which looked totally out of place and actually cordoned off so you couldn’t sit down anywhere if you wanted to.We joined another shuffling line to view Michelangelo’s Pieta which I had wanted to see since my teens (I am now 71 so it’s been quite a wait).The Pieta is placed some distance behind a barrier and behind a huge glass screen which spoils the effect. It was a huge disappointment. There is no way to stop and examine the statue or to have a moment of quiet contemplation and appreciate its beauty. It’s just another tick list item to be viewed through a mass of mobile phones held aloft for the obligatory photo. There was nowhere to sit for a few moments peace and quiet  and reflection -  it’s a church for God’s sake!!
I felt very sad by the fact that no thought or consideration is given to anyone; it’s just cram in as many people as possible. 
Give this a miss but do visit the Vatican Museum and Sistine Chapel which was well organised, fascinating, and far less crowded.

title: Superb
text:
The Roman Forum in Rome is an absolutely fascinating archaeological site that plunges the visitor into the heart of the ancient history of the eternal city! This vast collection of majestic ruins testifies to the greatness of Imperial Rome, with its temples, basilicas, triumphal arches and vestiges of daily life. Walking among these thousand-year-old stones allows you to feel the atmosphere of a glorious past.

The remains of the Temple of Saturn, the Basilica of Maxentius, the Arch of Titus and the Curia are particularly impressive. The place is rich in history and every detail seems to tell part of the story of ancient Rome.

However, like many of Rome’s sights, the Roman Forum can be very crowded, especially in high season. It is advisable to visit early in the morning or late in the day to avoid large crowds and fully enjoy the Mood of the place.

A must-see place for lovers of history, archaeology and ancient culture. A visit that leaves a lasting mark and inspires deep respect for past civilizations. Really not to be missed during a stay in Rome!

title: One of the most spectacular heritage sites in Europe!
text:
The Roman Forum is one of the most iconic heritage sites in Italy. For centuries it was the centre of daily Roman life where public speeches took place, statues were erected to honour Rome's leaders, and elections were conducted. Many of the most important buildings of the Roman monarchy, the Republic and the succeeding Empire can be found here, including the Temple of Vesta and the Temple of Saturn. Some of the other buildings worth noting here are the triumphal arches of Emperors Titus and  Septimius Severus, the Senate house Curia Julia, and the colossal Basilica of Maxentius, which was the largest building in the whole forum.

The Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill are considered a single archaeological site, so you can access them with one ticket. If you're interested in history, it will take you at least 2-3 hours to explore the Forum and the Hill, though you might want to give yourself 4 hours if you want to explore everything. I visited the Forum in the late afternoon and I was unable to enter some parts of it and the Palatine Hill as they had closed early. title: Roman forum experience
text:
Note: the roman forum and palatine hills are combined together in the same archaeological park, with one combined ticket.

I love historical stuff, and the historical/archaeological stuff here is super interesting worthy of 10 stars! It's very big and if you like this stuff you could easily spend a whole day here. Standing here makes me feel connected with the past and words like impressive / grandiose fall short of describing this place.

However, the overall experience has a lot of room for improvement. This place is verryyy big. There was no official map on paper or online that I could find. Staff at ticket booth said to scan QR code inside. Once inside, there was nothing to scan, and close to zero staff members to ask for things like information/direction etc. I did ok with Rick Steves audio tour, but overall the signage inside is extremely poor. I ended up turning back at dead ends, turning around in circles trying to find the entrance to something, and walking back and forth down the 2 main roads of the forum to find what I wanted to see. That adds up to a lot of walking, fyi. And most of the roads are uneven stones or dirt roads. frequent stairs too. This especially pertains to the "super sites". Once I found them, they were truly amazing archaeological sites to see, but the process of finding their individual entrances was painstaking. Again, like I said, unhelpful or nonexistent signage, and no staff to ask. I had to rely on Google maps, which was only half reliable.

The few staff that were present near the entrances all seemed pretty genuinely disinterested in being there. I get it, it's sweaty and hot in Rome, but still, genuinely disinterested staff in such a magnificent museum is really demoralizing.
Also, the staff will often close things slightly ahead of the stated closing time / last entrance time. That was annoying, and I don't think it's right.

Despite all of that, the experience of being able to see / feel / learn about this amazing historical site is still worthwhile. The awesome view from the palatine hill Belvedere was also unbeatable (but which also took forever to find lol). If you don't like history though, it's just a bunch of brick/stone/marble ruins. Whether or not it's worth it depends on preference. I def think worth it even after all the little hiccups.

title: A showcase of Michelangelo’s greatest masterpieces
text: Undoubtedly one of the greatest treasures of the Vatican City, the Sistine Chapel is one of those attractions that you must see at least once in your lifetime to truly appreciate the genius of Michelangelo. Already popularly known as the archetypal Renaissance man, Michelangelo's creative mastery has veritably reached the pinnacle with his jaw-dropping masterpiece on the ceiling and altar wall of this 15th-century chapel. He's solely responsible for all the frescoes on its ceiling, spending 4 years between 1508 and 1512 to leave his lasting legacy. Occupying the ceiling frescoes are the 9 Biblical depictions from Genesis, with the Creation of Adam taking centerstage as Sistine Chapel's most iconic image. Another of Michelangelo's celebrated masterpieces, the Last Judgement, adorns the entire altar wall. Its religious importance goes beyond these frescoes; it is also the place where new popes are crowned. The Sistine Chapel is part of the enormous Vatican Museums, and entry to the museum includes this chapel, though this is the last stop of the visitors route through the museum. Expect the chapel to be super-crowded, and you'll be lucky to get a seat around its perimeter from where you can look up to gawk at the majestic frescoes. Beware that no photos or videos are allowed in the chapel though binoculars are permitted, and there will be museum officers walking around and balking at those who disobey this directive. You will be literally awestruck just admiring the unparalleled beauty of the frescoes. Truly a swoon-worthy grand finale to your Vatican Museums exploit!

text: The Sistine Chapel stands as an unparalleled masterpiece of Renaissance artistry and spiritual significance. Its awe-inspiring ceiling, adorned with Michelangelo's iconic frescoes, captivates visitors with its intricate detail and profound narrative. From the creation of Adam to the Last Judgment, each panel is a testament to the genius of its creator and the enduring power of human creativity. title: Virtual tour to an old art venue
text:
The Sistine Chapel was built between 1473 and 1481 during the papacy of Sixtus IV, being a prominent example of Renaissance art. What catches your eye as soon as you enter is the mural painting found in every corner of the Chapel. This type of painting is known as fresco, in which pigments are applied on a layer of wet plaster. This allows the colors to penetrate the plaster as it dries, resulting in a durable and resistant painting. These frescoes were painted by renowned artists of the Renaissance, such as Michelangelo, Botticelli, and Perugino.

The importance of the Sistine Chapel lies in its historical and artistic value. It is a sacred place for the Catholic Church and has been the setting for important events throughout history, including papal conclaves, where a new Pope is elected.

As someone who took a virtual tour, I can say that each stroke is impressive. Every piece of art found there makes you want to appreciate it for a long time, and the truth is that it's worth it, as it is something wonderful.

During the Renaissance, the Sistine Chapel was a place frequented by the cultural and religious elite of the time. Artists, intellectuals, and religious leaders, as for those who lived near the Sistine Chapel at that time, were mainly the clergy and employees of the Vatican.

In conclusion, what I want to say is that the Sistine Chapel was a place made to be appreciated and admired. It is a jewel of art, and each fresco seems to be telling a different story. I personally loved it, and I would really like to be able to visit it myself someday.

St. Peter’s Basilica is without doubt one of the most breathtaking and unmissable sites in the world. Even before you step inside, the grandeur of St. Peter’s Square sets the tone—a vast, magnificent space framed by Bernini’s colonnades that welcomes millions of pilgrims and visitors each year.

The moment you enter the basilica, you are overwhelmed by its scale, beauty, and serenity. The soaring dome designed by Michelangelo, the ornate chapels, and the masterpieces by Bernini and other Renaissance greats make this far more than just a church—it is a living museum of faith and art. Highlights include Michelangelo’s Pietà, Bernini’s Baldachin over the Papal Altar, and the dazzling mosaics that decorate the walls and ceilings.

Climbing to the top of the dome is highly recommended. The views over St. Peter’s Square and across Rome are simply spectacular and worth every step. Entry to the basilica itself is free, though lines can be long, so arriving early is best.

Whether you are religious or not, the basilica offers a powerful experience of history, spirituality, and human achievement. Truly one of the greatest architectural and cultural wonders of the world—an unforgettable highlight of any trip to Rome.
