title: Half-forgotten pages of the Vatican!
text: The wanderer who has made the journey from Pinturicco to Dali is finally rewarded with access to the Sistine Chapel (Cappella Sistina), where since 1484 cardinals have gathered for a conclave to elect a new pope. Our guide Elena told an interesting thing: no one initially intended to make this place the main center of attraction in the entire palace. Michelangelo was invited to paint the ceiling only because Bramante and Raphael recommended him to the pope, hoping that the Florentine would finally fail in painting and they could again become the main geniuses at court. Their hopes were not justified, and the artist spent 4 years lying with a brush in his hand on his back under the ceiling of the chapel, and when he got down from there in 1512, it turned out that nothing more powerful than these Old Testament scenes had ever been seen in Renaissance Rome. On the ceiling he depicted “The Separation of Light from Darkness”, “The Creation of the Sun, Moon and Earth”, “The Separation of Land from Water”, “The Creation of Adam”, “The Creation of Eve”, “The Fall and Expulsion”, “The Sacrifices of Noah”, “The Flood” " and "The Intoxication of Noah" and the Sibyls and Prophets seated between them. Nevertheless, under Michelangelo's arches, the first artists were engaged in the interpretation of biblical subjects: Perugino, Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Luca Signorelli. The wall to the left of the altar is dedicated to the Old Testament, there they follow one after another " The Journey of Moses into Egypt” - a joint creation of Perugino and Pinturicchio, “The Trial of Moses” and “The Punishment of Korah, Dathan and Abiron” by Botticelli, “The Passage of the Red Sea” by Biagio d’Antonio, “Moses on Mount Sinai” by Cosimo Rosselli and “The Death of Moses” "Luke Signorelli. To the right of the altar is the New Testament - “The Baptism of Christ” and “The Presentation of the Keys to the Apostle Peter” by Perugino, “The Temptation of Christ” by Botticelli, “The Calling of the First Apostles” by Ghirlandaio, “The Last Supper” and “The Sermon on the Mount” by Cosimo Rosselli. Opposite the altar walls - “The Ascension of Christ” by Hendrik van den Broek and “The Dispute about the Body of Moses” by Matteo da Lecce, replacing the frescoes of Ghirlandaio and Signorelli on the same themes lost as a result of the collapse of the walls. Be that as it may, having completed work on the ceiling, Michelangelo decided that he said goodbye to painting. But it was not to be, Pope Clement VII persuaded the artist to take up the Sistine Chapel again. He tried to resist, he was much more interested in the tombstone of Julius II, for whom he began to make Moses, but Clement was stubborn, and as a result, in 1541, on the altar wall of the chapel, where two windows had to be covered up, a number of frescoes, including Perugino and Michelangelo himself, and to give the surface a slight slope so that dust would not settle on it, the grandiose “Last Judgment” appeared. The artist gave his own features to the face of St. Bartholomew, who presents his own freshly flayed skin to the audience and the Creator for consideration - this is one of the darkest self-portraits in the history of painting. Several hundred naked figures scattered along the wall of the chapel were such an enchanting success that people began to come to Rome specifically for them. True, Pope Pius IV, an incredible hypocrite, ordered Michelangelo's student Daniele da Volterra to paint loincloths for all the characters. Under the “Last Judgment” there are two narrow doors, the right one leads to the so-called “weeping room” (camera lacrimatoria), where at the end of the conclave the cardinal elected head of the Roman Catholic Church retires. There, the future pope chooses the name under which he is going to rule and puts on his vestments, which are stocked in three sizes just in case (they say, however, that not a single suit suited the short and stocky Cardinal Ratzinger🤣). Mere mortals are not allowed into any of the doors; they can go either to the left, to the exit from the museums, or, if there is time and energy, then to the right, from the Sistine Chapel, you can, bypassing all the queues, go straight to St. Peter's Cathedral.

title: One of the wonders of Renaissance architecture!
text:
St. Peter's Basilica is one of the most famous churches in the world as well as the largest church in the world by internal capacity. A church has existed on this location since the 4th century, but the Old St. Peter's Basilica fell into disrepair by the 15th century. Construction of the new church began in 1506, but it wasn't completed until 1626. Many great architects and artists of the Renaissance took part in the construction and decoration of the church and some of the most famous ones among them are Raphael, Donato Bramante, Michelangelo, and Bernini.

Some of the highlights of the basilica are the spectacular dome, designed by Michelangelo, St. Peter's Baldachin, which is a bronze canopy by Bernini, and the gilt bronze casing for the Chair of St. Peter also designed by Bernini. Other interesting parts are the Vatican Grottoes where over 90 Popes are buried, and the Vatican Necropolis, which contains archaeological remains dating all the way back to the Romans. It's possible to enter the grottoes on a regular visit to the basilica, but you'd have to pay for a guided tour to explore the necropolis.

St. Peter's contains many magnificent sculptures, including the statues of St. Longinus by Bernini and Saint Andrew by François Duquesnoy. However, without a doubt the highlight is Madonna della Pietà (also known as Pietà), Michelangelo's masterpiece depicting the Virgin Mary grieving over Jesus who has just been taken down from the cross. This work is renowned for its emotional depth, as well as the beauty of the depicted figures.

The basilica offers several different tickets. The cheapest option is the basic €7 ticket, which entitles you to a self-guided visit with a digital audio guide. Alternatively, you can book the much more expensive €17 (stairs) or €22 (lift) ticket for the basilica and dome, which will allow you to also explore the magnificent dome and enjoy spectacular views of the Vatican grounds. Last, but not least, if you are keen to get the full experience and see the necropolis too, you can reserve a separate guided tour for €20.

St. Peter's is one of the most beautiful churches I've ever visited and I would say that if you go to the Vatican on your trip to Rome, you should definitely explore this site too, especially as the basic entry ticket is fairly cheap and you can easily spend over an hour enjoying the splendid interior of the basilica.

title: The Mess of Rome
text:
Rome is truly a spectacular city, rich with history, culture, and breathtaking architecture. The Basilica, in particular, is a stunning testament to the grandeur of ancient and religious art. However, unfortunately, what should have been a highlight turned out to be the most frustrating experience of our trip.

Despite purchasing fast-access tickets in advance, we were not allowed to enter during certain hours. Instead, we were left waiting in a massive, disorganized crowd for over two hours under the hot sun without any communication, guidance, or shade. To make matters worse, no refunds were offered, as entry was technically “free,” provided you endured the conditions. The “fast-track” option felt misleading at best, and outright exploitative at worst.

This chaotic experience soured what should have been a memorable visit. I would advise others to research the most up-to-date access rules carefully or consider visiting at off-peak hours. Some have mentioned entering through the rear entrance as a smoother option, something we wish we had known.

Additionally, a word of caution for parents: our children had a distressing encounter with local kids that appeared to be racially motivated. While this may not reflect broader attitudes, it’s important to stay aware and be cautious, especially in crowded tourist areas.

In summary, while Rome is full of wonder, this particular experience felt unnecessarily stressful and poorly managed. I hope improvements are made to match the beauty of the place with the dignity of the experience.

title: Walk Through the Heart of Ancient Rome – Bring Water and Imagination!
text:
Exploring the Roman Forum felt like stepping into a living museum. You’re literally walking in the footsteps of Julius Caesar, senators, and everyday Romans. The ruins are extensive—temples, arches, basilicas, and even what’s left of the ancient government buildings that once ruled an empire.

We spent about 1-1.5 hours wandering through. It’s not super well-marked, so a guided tour or audio app would be helpful if you want deeper context. Even without one, it’s a surreal experience to be in such a historic and iconic location.

💡 TIP: There are fountains throughout the site where you can refill your water bottle—a lifesaver on a hot Roman day!

👟 Wear good shoes, as the ground is uneven and dusty in places.

☀️ Little shade in most areas—bring a hat and sunscreen!

📸 Great photo ops from Palatine Hill looking down into the Forum.

This is a must-see for history buffs, and it's included in your Colosseum ticket. Very busy, but absolutely worth it.

Would recommend visiting early in the day or later in the afternoon to avoid peak heat and crowds.

title: Visit to the Roman Forum: instructions for use
text:
After the National Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art and the Colosseum here we are at the third free visit of the initiative "Sunday at the museum" which provides free admission on the first Sunday of the month to the museums indicated on the official website.
Small suggestion: avoid showing up at the opening (go instead to the Gallery that provides the online ticket with time) and show up around 1pm. In just 20 minutes I was in.
As for the forum, clarification is needed. The lower part that goes roughly from the Arch of Titus to the Arch of Septimius Severus is the Roman Forum proper, the upper part, on the hill that bears the same name, is the Palatine.
Both are accessed with the same ticket that also includes the Colosseum. 3 in 1 in short.
It's a unique place in the world, if only for the story it tells. Visit it with due calm wearing comfortable shoes because there is so much walking and often on pebbles.
There are no refreshments, arm yourself with water and snacks if necessary.
For an accurate visit, if you want to save the money of a professional guide who will inevitably follow a predetermined path, I strongly suggest buying an illustrated guide. There are various types and for all budgets. In any case, most of the buildings have a very useful information plate.
There is also a third way: audio guide rental.
Since it is mostly remains an impromptu visit without any support could be unsatisfactory.
Last word of advice. On the Palatine Hill there are panoramic terraces with a wonderful view of the forum: take all the time you need and be enchanted by this magical place.

title: Stunning outdoor museum
text:
The Roman Forum was the second part of my combined Colosseum and Forum ticket that cost €18. This also includes Palatine Hill and some other small areas. The information is all readily available on the tickets that I booked online. As far as I understood the tickets allowed for entry to the Colosseum once and then the Forum within the next 24 hours. Don't quote me on that though.

The attraction is a mix of a large open air museum  and gardens. There are some buildings to enter but it is mostly outside. Take a hat and some food. There are water fountains for hydration, if you have a bottle to fill.

The prettiest areas are up on the highest levels. You climb a ramp through a large building and come out in a very pretty area of gardens and an orangery. I'd never seen an orange tree before, and you could smell the citrus in the air.

The views from up top were wonderful, offering some great views of Rome. It was a very tranquil place, despite there being quite a few people about. I found I was still able to find some areas away from quite so many people.

On the way back to the exit you can see Circus Maximus from above and there were parakeets flying about in the trees in the SE of the forum.

Sadly, I thought the queues for the forum were worse than those for the Colosseum. I entered near the Colosseum and was queueing for what felt like an hour. There are other entry points though so perhaps you don't have to queue that long.

Once we got inside, we were forced to walk around this wack building for what felt like forever, never knowing when we would make it to the chapel. We passed by tons of old clay crap that nobody cares about, and were squeezed in with about 300 other people in each room. It smelled like nobody in there knew what deodorant was. I almost threw up because of how hot and crowded it was. We finally get to the chapel, and it’s a nightmare. Hundreds of people are being herded through the room, and you don’t get any time to enjoy it. It’s loud and annoying, and all we wanted to do was leave. Trying to leave the building was like trying to find our way out of a black room with no windows or doors. The exit signs seemingly led to nowhere. We passed tons of gift shops, but none of them sold water. 

I’d always had a hard time imagining what my personal hell would be, but now I know. It’s the Sistine Chapel.

title: Walking Through History
text: Visiting the Roman Forum is a remarkable experience. You are walking through history. This was the political, religious and commercial center of ancient Rome. Today the ruins of great temples, government building and palaces remain and with some imagination you can sense what an impressive place this must have been. You can buy a combo ticket that includes entrance to the Colosseum and to the Roman Forum/Palatine Hill, but this should be purchased well in advance as the timed entry slots for the Colosseum sell out quickly. Alternatively, you can sign up for a guided tour of all the sites although this will be significantly more expensive. Avoid visiting on the free days as it will be jammed with locals. This is the first Sunday of the month in the off season but varies during the summer. For a tremendous bird's eye view of the Forum, climb up Palatine Hill to the terrace in the Farnese Gardens. You can also get a nice view of the western end of the Forum from the terrace at the Piazza del Campidoglio and an even better up-close view from the underground passageway to the Tabularian in the Capitoline Museum.

title: So much history
text:
How lucky are we, that we have access to these incredible places in 2024? How fortunate that there are teams dedicated to preserving the structures, the histories, the meanings? 

And there is so much - SO much - history, meaning and story here. We opted for a guided tour because we wanted to take advantage of their advertised ability to get access to all the places we wanted to get access to (this was a combo tour, the Colosseum and the Forum, and they lied about what they'd be able to do for the tour group.) 

We were there in mid-August, so it was hot. And crowded. The Forum was much easier to maneuver because of the sheer amount of space available for tourists, but it was still crowded. Our guide pointed out some of the interesting structures, told us some of the history and meaning behind what we were looking at and kept us moving at a decent pace.

I do admit that after a while, my mind kind of turned off. Like, I wanted - I so badly wanted - to hear it all and absorb all the history - but the heat, the standing in the sun, my own exhaustion...it all conspired to beat me. After a while, I wandered off a bit, taking pictures of things in the opposite direction of where our tour guide was pointing, zoning out on the things I was seeing. 

And I'd like to end this post with appreciation for the many water fountains sprinkled around the grounds of the Forum. We definitely took advantage of them, refilling our water bottles every time I saw a fountain, even if it meant breaking from the group to do so. The hydration helped, for sure.

title: Roman Forum: Crowds, Noise, and an Amazing Experience
text:
This was a difficult review to write. I visited Rome (in July) years ago and being surrounded by the ruins of the Roman Forum was an experience that is forever etched in my memory. I wandered freely through ruins, multiple times throughout the day and evening, taking in the history in a peaceful almost reverent environment.

Fast forward….. The Forum is now an area surround by a fence and a ticket is needed. As a museum professional I understand and applaud the need to protect the ruins, reduce the crowds, and have a revenue stream for the upkeep. Because everyone is now forced into a restricted area during set open hours the crowds are condensed and all streaming along the designated paths. It also seemed like most people were there as a part of an organized group, moving as one, so you had to try and navigate around or through them. Lots of selfies taking place which means people are not aware of what is going on around them which added to the difficulty of walking around the Forum.

I did find that the ruins on the edges of the Forum were less visited, especially by the large groups. The groups are on a schedule so they are hitting the “highlights” not the entire area.

There are very few labels describing what you are seeing so before you go familiarize yourself to what you are looking at, especially if you are not on a tour. There are some good websites that have descriptions and sketches of when it was built and current photos so you can identify the ruins. Unfortunately, I was not able to paste any links here.

Purchase the first available ticket in the morning, fewer crowds. You can purchase tickets onsite but the line was long so save yourself the hassle and book online. If you are going on your own, not taking a tour, buy your ticket from the official site, Parco archeologico del Colosseo. There are a lot of sites charging you more, beware. The ticket gives you access to the Forum, Colosseum, and Palatine Hill. But be sure you know what you can and can’t see with the ticket to avoid disappointment. You must show an ID along with your ticket to enter, and not a photocopy.

There are companies that offer tours that will give you information as you walk along the path as well as special access. In addition to going on my own I did join a tour that gave an underground Colosseum experience that included the Forum and Palatine Hill (I will review that tour) and it was absolutely worth the cost.

I did give the Forum only 4 stars, which hurt my heart. If the review was only about the ruins (or from my first visit) the stars would be off of the chart but this review was about the entire current experience. The crowds, noise, and rude selfie-takers slightly marred the overall experience. But, how can you visit Roman and not go to the Roman Forum.

Imagine yourself walking the cobble stone path, conducting day to day business, and walking by the temples devoted to gods/goddess. Try and let everything else melt away because walking among the ruins, immersing yourself in the history that surrounds you is priceless.

First grand structure is Constantine’s Arch which represents a landmark in history, when a military battle made Christianity the mainstream religion in Rome and the entire Western World. title: Despite its size, the museum is fundamentally foreseeable.
text: Despite its size, the Vatican Museums are still, unlike the Louvre and the Hermitage, fundamentally foreseeable. But you wait in line for longer because tourists in Rome are definitely no less than in Paris and St. Petersburg. This time it was 3 hours. Of course, the collection is not as versatile as in the Louvre, the Hermitage and the New York Metropolitan, but it best represents Italian art and above all its pinnacle - the High Renaissance. And the main credit for this goes to the initiator of the collection - Pope Julius II, in a saddle and with a sword, who felt better than at Mass. He brought in Raphael, who created the famous frescoes in the so-called "Raphael Dances", and Michelangelo to create the famous Sistine Chapel. But Leonardo da Vinci is represented in the museum, and in general, in Rome only one painting, and that one unfinished due to his departure to Milan - "St. Jerome". The two-piece painting was long considered lost: one was covered with a chest in an antiques workshop, the other served as a seat in a cobbler's shop. This painting is located in the Vatican's Pinacoteca, where the remaining masterpieces of Renaissance painting are located: "Stefanevski's Triptych" by Renaissance ancestor Giotto, "Pietà" by Bellini, another "Pietà" by Lucas Cranach, paintings by Raphael "Transfiguration", "Madonna Foligno", his altarpiece Oddi ("Coronation of the Virgin Mary"), 2 paintings each by the Venetians Titian and Veronese. At the end, Caravaggio's "Removal from the Cross" is in Hall 12.  There's also the lesser-known Dominicinos, Guercino, Guido Reni.  In general, decent, but the Pinacoteca alone is weaker than the Uffizi Gallery and Pitti in Florence. Ancient sculpture is displayed in the Pio Clementino Museum. Absolute hits here are "Apollo of Belvedere," Michelangelo's favorite "The Belvedere Torse" and "Laocon and Sons," found at the Colosseum just in 1506, when Pope Julius founded the collection. In addition to the above, there are separate Etruscan, Egyptian and Christian museums. But of course, the main attraction points for tourists are the Raphael Dances and the Sistine Chapel. Of the four stanzas, Raphael himself painted two in full. The absolute masterpieces are, of course, the School of Athens and the Mass in Bolsen. Anyone with higher education must have seen the images from the "School of Athens" in books and textbooks, so much so that they have entered the blood and flesh of modern culture. Raphael wrote off many philosophers as contemporaries - Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Bramante. Well, and the apotheosis will be "The Sistine Chapel," a great work by the great Michelangelo, which he created in two approaches a quarter of a century apart.  And the first part of the ceiling of the chapel on the themes of creation of the world and sin are the pinnacle of the Renaissance - a true hymn to man, and the fresco "The Last Judgment" on the altar wall - its end. The fresco depicts the souls of the dead rising up to meet God's wrath.  It's simple – in between is the beginning of the Reformation and the Counter-Reformation, hence the pessimism. By the way, when you're making slow progress waiting in line for the Sistine Chapel, go into the next room, which they do, maybe one in 10. There awaits a collection of contemporary art worthy of any museum: three paintings by Salvador Dali, Max Ernst, Kandinsky, Chagall, Otto Dix, Kirchner, Bacon and even the ideologically distant Mexican Trotskyist painters Siqueiros and Diego Rivera. Of course, in addition to outstanding sculptures and paintings, the interiors of the Vatican Palace themselves are interesting. Especially the famous Motto staircase, made from a Bramante sketch, where unintersecting spirals allow you to separate the ascendants and descendants.

title: The political and religious centre of Ancient Rome
text:
The Roman Forum is where you find the heart of Ancient Rome in a scattering of building foundations, standing columns and nearly 2000 year old remains. The grounds are sandwiched between the Colosseum, Palatine Hill and Capitoline Hill and can be viewed fairly well from vantage points along and on both sides of Via dei Fori Imperiali as well as upon vantage points at Capitoline Hill at no cost. You can also view from Palatine Hill and up close by walking the actual grounds with purchase of entry ticket. 

Opening hours are 8.30am to 4.30pm daily and ticket prices vary depending on which combination. They can be booked online or at one of the ticket offices near the Colosseum and Arch of Titus at the foot of Capitoline Hill. 

Within the Forum grounds you can walk along the ancient Via Sacra and other various roped in walking paths getting up close to the ruins. At times it can be difficult to know what you are looking at so a good guidebook pointing the various basilicas, market buildings, administration palaces, temples and other monument ruins present. 

Allow yourself some time to investigate the forum and learn about the various building ruins that you are seeing. While there isn't much to see much of the time, they have interesting history and stories that mean you can easily end up spending an hour or so exploring these grounds while sightseeing in the area.

title: We ran out of sight of the Sistine Chapel without warning
text:
The guided tour of the Vatican Museums was a very positive experience, mainly thanks to our guide, Valentina, whose work was excellent. He was able to make the visit very entertaining, focusing on curiosities and details that are difficult to perceive on his own or through an audio guide.

It was clearly evident that she was very well trained and that she knew how to keep the group’s attention, explaining nuances, symbology and little-known aspects of the works: from moods of the painters to autobiographical elements in artists who could not sign their works but self-portraiture within them. Such explanations add enormous value to the visit.

In addition, Valentina always showed a very professional and human attitude, even trying to check if there was any possibility of access to the Sistine Chapel at the end of the visit, and she felt sincerely affected by not being able to offer us that important part of the experience.

That said, we consider it unacceptable not to have been informed in advance of the unavailability of the Sistine Chapel, especially given that the visit cost €40 per person. When booking we provide contact details (email and telephone), so we believe that at least this should have been communicated in advance.

The reservation was made one week in advance and at no time was it indicated that the Sistine Chapel was not accessible. We understand that the Pope’s agenda is not organized overnight, so this lack of information represents a clear deficiency in the management by the organization.

In short, an exceptional guide that did everything possible to offer us the best experience, in front of an organization that should improve communication and management of extraordinary situations like this.

title: Paid forced march
text:
We had bought skip-the-line tickets for a tour start at 4:30 pm. The first thing we had to do was figure out where to queue, it was complete anarchy. We managed to crack the crowd to get closer to a neon vest... which told us "go see my colleague there." New sequence to try to split the crowd and 15min later, the colleague tells us "the tail of 4:30 is there" vaguely pointing us in a direction. We were bothering him, he was overwhelmed. We finally put ourselves in a queue, people were reassuring as they could by asking the neighbor's schedule... We finally moved forward and after about 45 minutes of queuing, we entered. 
We targeted three rooms and nothing else. What we never imagined was that the museum took up the Ikea idea: if you want to buy a wooden spoon, you have to go through all the shelves before you can go out. Unless it was Ikea who stole the idea from the Vatican Museum, I don't know. So we stalled, the crowds were such that it was difficult to stop and watch this or that work. When we finally thought we'd get to one of the rooms we wanted to see, the passage was closed and we were diverted to the museum entrance... to restart part of the journey. "A deviation is underway," I explained. Unable to leave the stream most of the time, we had to cross a few hundred rooms. So we can summarize it as follows: we move under pressure, we see nothing. 
The final bouquet is the Sistine Chapel. There, you get yelled at if you are not in the right place ("Mr. push yourself towards the center"), you get pushed by the "vigilantes" towards the exit. 
The only good time is when you feel that you are going to escape the river and leave the museum.
It's a marathon version of a paid hike from New York on the attendance side, not a museum tour. You might as well donate to the museum and not go.

title: An amazing tour of art masterpieces and the iconic Sistine Chapel
text:
The Vatican Museums hold a vast and amazing collection of Christian and ancient art, including some of the world's great masterpieces. Because of its size and popularity, it's best to take a guided tour, preferably early in the morning when the crowds are lighter.

I took one of the key master tours, which is offered through a few different companies. It's quite expensive, but getting to see the galleries without other groups and gazing at the glorious frescoes of the Sistine Chapel in near-silence was a once in a lifetime experience and well worth the price.

The key master and guard who accompanied us were wonderful hosts, and the guide provided excellent commentary on artwork like "Laocoön and His Sons," "Sarcophagus of Helena," and the Gallery of Maps. The tour ended with a generous breakfast at the Bistrot La Pigna.

Afterward, I continued exploring the exquisite Raphael Rooms, home of the famous "School of Athens" fresco, as well as the fantastic Modern Religious Art galleries, with works by Matisse, Picasso, Van Gogh, and Dali. A final highlight was the beautiful Bramante staircase.

Overall, the Vatican Museums are a must-visit experience in Rome for all lovers of art.

text: Finally seeing the Vatican Museums after a lifetime of faith was truly a moment of grace for our entire family from Cebu. Standing under Michelangelo’s ceiling, especially that famous Creation scene, was a profoundly humbling moment that connected us deeply to our Catholic roots. You realize how much sacrifice and devotion went into preserving this heritage for the world. We spent the whole day inside, but honestly, it still felt too short. We were so impressed by the curation and the respect shown to all the relics and masterpieces. title: Bad experience  and Priority ticket scam
text:
I have visited the Vatican museums last week, with my wife and 2 children. I went there, on saturday, the 8th of november. Arrived there at 9:00, hoping to spend a good day with  my family. I looked for the place to buy tickets. Many "guides" tried to help, selling "priority tickets", so that I would not have to wait in line to buy a normal entrance. Some even said that, If I did not have a priority ticket, it would not be possible to visit that day. 
Anyway, I finnaly found the line to buy "normal" tickets and went there. Less than 200 people were waiting in front of us. Nevertheless, we had to wait more than 4 hours to finnaly enter. What I confirmed was that "normal ticket" line has no attention at all. What you see is that, for around 15 minutes, all others with "priority tickets" (that cost 3 or 4 times the regular price), enter. Then, each 15 minutes, around 10 people from the "normal" line, are allowed to enter. This would give a relation to 10 "normal" to around 2 or 300 "priority". This is not decent. Many people are surely making money from this.  Finnally, when I started asking the guard that was coordinating the lines what was the criteria, he finnally starting calling 15 persons, instead of 10. This scheme is a trap, because, the longer the "normal" users wait, the higher the incentive to buy "priority" tickets will be. 
Finnally, as feedback, after waiting more than 4 hours (that could have been much less, if this "priority ticket" scheme was not happening), when we finnally entered, we were so tired that we did not appreciate the visit and just wanted to finish it and go home. The museums and collections are great, but the overall experience is terrible.

title: 2000 years of history
text: The Vatican museums are a must for anyone visiting Rome. They contain a staggering amount of Roman, Italian and indeed Christian history going back millennia and are the largest museum in the world after the Louvre. The museums are very well structured, with two paths once access is gained - the one through the more salient galleries, including the Pio Clementino museum with Greek and Roman statues, the Gallery of Maps (a personal favourite), the Borgia apartments and of course the stunning Sistine Chapel with frescoes by Michaelangelo. The second path takes one through the Christian and Jewish Lapidariums and the Pinatcotecca which is often overlooked but highly recommended. Overall a great visit even if the number of people is mind boggling. Definitely book tickets online from the Vatican website. Prepare for some waiting and security checks.

We are Catholic so we love a lot of the Vatican experience, especially St. Peter’s Basilica but the Vatican should be ashamed of the way they run the museum. It is a very dehumanizing experience where incredibly Rude men in suits (don’t think they are docents…they know nothing) usher you in one direction through the halls like cattle. It seems the sole purpose of the museum is to make it to the end to see the Sistine Chapel where you are corralled in a bullpen in the center. Because the museum is mostly hallways you will find it difficult to stop and marvel at the treasures on the way due to the hordes of people being ushered along the halls and large tour groups who won’t move to the side. This is not a peaceful museum experience and it was a complete nightmare for us. The Vatican should separate out the Sistine chapel with another entrance and allow people to view the museum in the manner in which a museum should be viewed. We also visited the Louvre on our trip. It was equally crowded but once inside we were able to amble through and visit many beautiful exhibits without feeling like cattle. We could sit and appreciate an art piece in peace. The Vatican has many treasures but they don’t know how to run a museum.

title: The world’s best open-air museum?
text:
The Roman Forum is, along with the Colosseum, the greatest demonstration of the splendor of the Roman Empire that is still evident today. Located at the foot of Palatine Hill, the Forum is dotted with ruins of ancient Rome's most important government buildings, which makes it one of the most fascinating and probably the world's best open-air museum.

For centuries, the Forum was the hub of political and social activities for the Roman citizens - site of triumphal processions, venue for public speeches, and the nucleus of commercial affairs. Today, it is a sprawling ruin of architectural fragments and ongoing archaeological excavations. With the combined ticket to access the trio of ancient sites including the Colosseum and the adjacent Palatine Hill, you would need a full day to take in all the points of interest and truly appreciate the significance of these ruins. Not to be missed are The Curia, Arch of Titus, Temple of Antoninus and Faustina and the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine. A breathtaking vista of the Forum can be viewed from the top of Palatine Hill. As you walk down Via Sacra, close your eyes and time-travel back 20 centuries and visualize what Julius Caesar would see as he walked down the same street during its heyday. Only then, can you truly say: "I came, I saw and I conquered."

title: Another must-see spot in Rome
text:
There are multiple gates where you can enter the Forum.  The one closest to the Colosseum is the busiest.  If you enter there and have a pre-booked ticket (very advisable), walk nest to the big line but on its right side. This line is for those who do not have tickets. When you reach the head of the line, you'll see a mostly empty checkpoint for those with tickets. If you view the Colosseum entrance as 6 p.m. on a clock face, we exited at 3 p.m. and saw no lines there. You may want to check that out (or one of the other entry points) to shorten your wait if you lack tickets. 

Doing a little reading in advance will definitely enhance your enjoyment of this site. What you'll see is largely a set of monuments and ruins.  However, with a little context, it is easier to appreciate why this is an important place. Basically, this was the nexus of important historical events in Rome for over 500 years. Every major figure in Roman history from ~ 300 BC to 300 AD spent time here, rallied supporters here, and in some cases was killed nearby. The site of Julius Caesar's cremation is preserved here. There are triumphal arches, the ruins of early temples, the ruins of great public buildings, etc. 

Just wander through and read the signs explaining the significance of each plot within the site. The flow of historical figures and events is staggering. This was an amazing place.

title: A Timeless Journey through Ancient Rome - Roman Forum
text:
My recent visit to the Roman Forum left me in awe of the rich historical tapestry that unfolded before my eyes. This sprawling archaeological site in the heart of Rome is a captivating window into Ancient Rome's political, social, and cultural heritage. Stepping foot in the Roman Forum is like stepping back in time, where the layers of history come alive and tell a mesmerizing story.

Walking through the ancient ruins, I couldn't help but be overwhelmed by the grandeur and significance that this site once held. The Roman Forum was the bustling center of public life in Ancient Rome, where important political, religious, and social events took place. It served as a marketplace, a site for public speeches, and the stage for elaborate ceremonies and celebrations.

Every step I took within the Roman Forum was a discovery of another historical wonder. From the iconic Arch of Titus, commemorating the Roman conquest of Jerusalem, to the majestic Temple of Saturn, dedicated to the god of agriculture, each structure spoke volumes about the lives and aspirations of the ancient Romans.

The archaeological remnants that remain within the Roman Forum are a testament to the incredible engineering prowess and artistic excellence of the Roman civilization. The grand columns, intricate marble carvings, and the remnants of ancient temples and basilicas stand as a testament to the empire's architectural marvels.

As I wandered through the ancient streets and squares, I could almost feel the echoes of the past reverberating around me. Imagining the vibrant marketplace, the heated political debates, and the awe-inspiring religious ceremonies that unfolded here added a depth of understanding to my visit. I couldn't help but marvel at the undeniable influence and power that the Roman Empire once held.

To enhance your experience at the Roman Forum, I highly recommend hiring a knowledgeable guide or availing yourself of audio guides on offer. Their insights and detailed explanations will bring the ancient ruins to life, allowing you to truly appreciate the historical context and significance of each structure and artifact.

It is worth noting that the Roman Forum can be quite expansive, so wearing comfortable walking shoes and allowing ample time for exploration is essential. Additionally, I suggest visiting early in the morning or during the shoulder seasons to avoid large crowds and fully immerse yourself in the awe-inspiring atmosphere.

The Roman Forum is a must-visit for history enthusiasts, architecture admirers, and anyone seeking a deeper understanding of the foundations of Western civilization. Its rich history and stunning remains offer a unique opportunity to step into the world of ancient Romans and gain a profound appreciation for their achievements.

My visit to the Roman Forum was an unforgettable journey into the heart of Ancient Rome, and I wholeheartedly encourage every traveler to include this historical gem in their Rome itinerary. Prepare to be transported through time, unravel the stories of the past, and witness the enduring legacy of the Roman Empire within the ancient walls of the remarkable Roman forum.

title: Active history in the centre of the city
text:
Most people won't even realise that their Colosseum ticket includes entry to the Forum and Palatine Hills, and they'll be missing out! We explored the site ourselves as we were already familiar with the history, but there are also multiple information boards to provide further information, so don't feel pressured into joining an expensive tour if you're worried about it simply being an information-free space. Make sure you have your walking shoes on as the site stretches far and wide!

There are multiple potable water taps around, often near toilets, so you can top up water bottles and cool down, especially if you visit during the middle of the day.

Be aware of scammers and pickpockets outside of all entrances - there is no such thing as a free lunch after all, and anyone offering you a free piece of jewellery will surely ask for money as soon as you take it. The same goes for fellow 'tourists' stopping you and asking for help, or thrusting a map in your face to hide your view from your handbag or pockets - walk away, or at most direct them to the clearly uniformed staff, and keep a hold of your belongings at all times when moving between the Colosseum and Forum/Palatine Hills.

Not too much of an ancient site "in terms of size" due to its location at like right in the middle of the city, but this is still a fairly sizeable rectangular-shaped area (especially its "sprawling length" for a nice walk from the end near the site entrance to the far end of the site) and where among the ruins was kind of quite a bit fascinating sight (to me that is) of these "whole structures" still standing which can hardly be called ruins (from their outward appearances although no entry inside those buildings) and one of those intact structures called the Temple of Romulus was actually built only about a thousand years after its namesake ruler (so to reflect on the fact that these ruins are very likely not all from the same time but from "various times" in the long history of the Ancient Rome).  And yes, it was also a "nice idea" I would say (likely by the site management) to create a little garden-like area in one part of the site with some flowers beside a nice lawn & some mini-pools on the lawn (with also a row of "ruined statues" on one side of the lawn).  And also great to see for like a "nice photo-op" was a number of pillars some in like small groups & some just by themselves (all of which likely once had been parts of structures no longer in existence).

And apart from the ruins but very close to them (just off one side of the site's length after going up like a ramp way) is also the site's "rest area" with plenty of outdoor seating (tables & chairs), a good-sized shop (for refreshments & miscellaneous) and nice bathrooms.

Just after arriving here with my tour group (which I joined "just upon arrival" outside the Colosseum) and after first visiting the Colosseum as part of the same group ticket (with really quite a breathtaking "big open area" inside to view all the way down to its underground area since there's no amphitheater floor "as of yet"), I split up from the group to do this site before going up the Palatine Hill (with a nice "viewing deck", which is actually right above this site, and some ruins of its own on the hilltop) although yes doing it that way requires a "walk back" from the far end of this site since the only way up the hill is near the entrance to this site.

title: Visite fantastique du Forum Romain

There is also no talking inside the chapel as it is considered one of the most holy places of the Catholic church (where they elect the popes) but that too has to be managed by officials as most people cannot be trusted to follow the rules for this as well. title: The Vatican have perfectly encapsulated being in hell
text:
Possibly the most stressful experience of my life.  I can imagine hell being in a museum with thousands of other people who didn’t want to go to a museum, being ushered through, following signs to a destination (the chapel) which seemingly never comes, and paying for the ‘pleasure’, and the Vatican have encapsulated that with staggering precision.

 When, after looking at more roman clay work than an ancient IKEA, the moment to enter the ‘holy place’ does finally come, it is impossible to enjoy it for even a second as you are quickly ushered through and out the other side.  You are then into the second wave of hell, following the exit signs which seemingly lead to nowhere.  Holy prayers were finally answered when we saw the light of the exit door and made our escape.

The building and artwork are spectacular, of course, but completely ruined by the amount of people let in and the narrow route you’re forced to be funnelled through.  Save your time, money and sanity, go round the corner to St Peter’s, it’s free, and a billion times better

title: The largest church and the largest dome in the world
text: No, we didn't see Chicago's Pope. Robert Prevost, aka Pope X1V, the kid from south suburban Dolton. He was at his summer retreat. So we had to visit St. Peter's Basilica in Rome's Vatican City without him. It is the largest church in the world and features the largest dome in the world. The original basilica lasted from the mid-14th century to 1506, when Pope Julius 11 laid the first stone of the current basilica, which is famous as a place of pilgrimage and for its liturgical functions, often drawing audiences numbering from 15,000 to over 80,000 people. The numbers are staggering. As you walk in, the gold-coffered ceiling is 150 feet high. The height of the dome is 136.5 meters, so tall that you could fit the Statue of Liberty inside it. Built in the shape of a Latin cross, the Basilica is 720 feet long, the length of two football fields, 490 feet wide and 448 feet high. The upper level covers 76,391 square feet while the lower level and crypt covers 129,910 square feet. Ninety-one popes are buried here, including John Paul 11, who died in 2005, and Francis XV1, who died on April 21, 2025. Of all the masterpieces of architecture that can be observed by visitors, none is more awesome than the dome, which was conceived and built up to the drum by Michelangelo and brought to completion, after his death, by architect Giacomo della Porta, who worked with Domenico Fontana from 1588 to 1590, raising the dome in just 22 months with the aid of 800 laborers. Michelangelo, the iconic Renaissance artist who sculpted the David statue and painted the ceiling of the Sistine chapel, sculpted La Pieta in 1497. It depicts Jesus after his crucifixion laying in Mary's lap. The Altar of the Confession is a sacred place that opens up in front of the main altar of the Basilica, enabling the tomb of Saint Peter to be seen from above. The tomb of Saint Peter, who was killed by the Emperor Nero in 64 AD, is located beneath the main altar. The Cathedra of Saint Peter, his episcopal throne, an ancient wooden chair. And the Necropolis, under the central nave, features ancient Roman and early Christian tombs and reveals an ancient path leading to Saint Peter's tomb. The original church over Saint Peter's tomb was built by Emperor Constantine and stood for over 1,000 years before being replaced by the awe-inspiring structure we see today, which took 120 years to build and finally was completed in 1675.

title: St. Peter's Basilica
text: St. Peter's is epic! It's massive! Whether you are Catholic or not, St. Peter's is worth a visit. I recommend getting a ticket to tour the tombs or dome climb because that will be a shorter security line during major tourist time.  The structure itself is nearly unbelievable and will leave you in awe of how in the world did they ever build this place and also so long ago! If visiting the tombs under St. Peter's you enter those through a stairwell in the basement by the lockers and bathrooms. Otherwise you enter St. Peter's through the main entrance or if you're lucky this year, one of the holy doors of Rome. title: The grandest cathedral in Christendom
text:
This basilica, which has the largest interior space of a Christian church in the world, according to Catholic tradition, is located over the burial place of Saint Peter, the first of the pontiffs.  Churches have stood on the site of the basilica since the 4th century, with the current building being constructed between 1506 and 1626, with some of history's most renowned architects working on it, including Bramante, Michelangelo, and Bernini. 
The truth is that you currently have to be patient to enter this temple, as they now check backpacks, so it's advisable not to carry them with you, especially on busy days.
Personally, the most striking thing inside is Bernini's baldachin on the main altar, as well as the wonderful sculpture called The Pietà, made by Michelangelo. Although in previous years its vision was clearer, when it did not have protective glass (in itself very useful today, to avoid possible damage).

title: Watch Your Pockets, Put Your City Face On, Ignore the Crooks
text:
I first visited Rome in 1998 and it was an enjoyable experience.  Not very crowded and only a few hustlers trying to sell you something.  Tell them no once and it was a done deal.  Not today.

I was in Rome about 4 years ago and had the same crappy experience as I did just now in the Roman Forum and Colosseum areas.  Both areas are full (and I mean they are everywhere) of young black men trying to swindle you out of your money, phone, passport, anything they can get their hands on.  They address you and try to get your attention, welcoming you to Rome or commenting on your shoes.  If you fall for this they will engage you in conversation while their partner is picking your backpack or pockets.  If you are fooling enough to get your wallet out to buy a fake charger, cheap bracelet or something like that..be prepared for a hard sell or more harassment.

I did not fall for any of this then and I did not now...but it totally destroys the experience when you have to have your guard up all the time.

Here are some of things said to me.

(First two guys, working together, started towards me.  Looked just like a couple that I kept running into a few years ago.  When I steered hard away he jinked back toward me.  I turned hard away again, he intercepted my path again.  "Hey Man, I like your shoes!" and got in my face.  I told him to get the f away from me and I moved on.  He said, "Why don't you like me?" Last time I told him he was a thief and I don't like thieves.  There were so many around I ignored him and his partner.

5 minutes later, near the entrance to the lower area by the Colloseum, several other men, one called out, "Hey, nice shoes." (Ignored him.). "Where you from?" (No response.) "You don't like black people?" I let that one go too.

2 minutes later, "Hey, where you from?" No answer.  "You from Africa?" (I'm of Italian-Norwegian descent.)

And it goes on and on.  

Trust me, these people have NO desire to improve your experience in Rome.  They are a bunch of thieves and swindlers and should be banished.  They know where the Carabinieri are stationed and (imagine this!) they avoid those areas.  But they have nothing in mind but relieving you of your cash, cards and whatnot.  (A friend of mine was pickpocketed in Rome last week...that issue is a whole other story.) 

If you want to get a sense of the "real" Italy, and not this haven of non-locals who are ruining the experience of "the eternal city" then visit elsewhere...Orvieto, Moltepulciano, Lecce, Bari...the list goes on.  Oh, there's a few malcreants there too, but nothing like you're going to find here.   If it weren't for the fact I have a class in Italy next week and I wanted some Italian practice beforehand I would not have come here.  This is my last time in Rome.  Back to the small cities and towns for sure.

title: Tour Group Visit
text:
I visited the Sistine Chapel twice in the month of March with two separate group tours.  Our tour groups visited when it opened in the morning and we didn’t have to wait long in lines.

There are benches lining the walls.  If you are lucky to see an open spot on the benches, sit in it.  It is much more comfortable staring up at the ceiling while sitting.  It wasn’t too crowded during my two visits.  Photography is not permitted and silence is encouraged.  Our tour groups were given about 20 minutes in the Sistine Chapel.

There is a partition dividing the Chapel in two.  When tour groups are ready to leave, members of tour groups meet together in the back section prior to leaving the Chapel.

There are 3 panels in the Pinecone Courtyard prior to entering the Vatican Museum featuring the frescoes in the Sistine Chapel that provide a good summary of what each images represent.

title: The chapel is amazing, but the experience itself was less so
text: The Sistine Chapel itself is stunning. I was so happy to get to see it myself. However, the Sistine Chapel experience is not very pleasant.  You are herded in the door to an area in the middle of the room designated for people to stand and view the masterpiece. There is no stopping along the perimeter as it needs to remain clear for people to enter and leave the area. The security were constantly moving people from there which caused a little bit of pushing within the crowd. There really just wasn’t enough room in the viewing area for the vast number of people, but luckily we quickly found a place at the back of the standing area. Although we were squeezed in shoulder to shoulder with what seemed like 100s of people, I tried to ignore that and take my time to see everything. It was very warm in there and there was constant reminders not to take photos (probably because so many people felt the rule did not apply to them), but you can still appreciate the beauty of it all. I still recommend visiting just be prepared for the crowds.

title: La chapelle Sixtine
text:
La chapelle Sixtine fait partie des incontournables de la visite du Vatican et un lieu de passage obligé pour les visiteurs.
Elle fait partie des Musées du Vatican, vous y accèderez lors de la visite des Musées : Musées du Vatican.
Elle abrite les célèbres fresques de Michel-Ange, réalisées au début du XVIe siècle.
En soi, l’architecture de la chapelle Sixtine est assez simple. C’est en effet une salle rectangulaire de 40 mètres de long, 13 mètres de large, et environ 21 mètres de hauteur. Au plafond, une voûte, et 12 fenêtres sur les murs. Ensuite, le sol est recouvert de marbres polychromes. Ce qui fait la renommée de la chapelle, ce sont en fait les nombreuses œuvres d’art et fresques qu’elle abrite. Les plus connues d’entre elles sont sans doute celles de Michel-Ange, mais des artistes tels que Luca Signorelli et Sandro Botticelli ont également contribué à sa décoration.

There are also quite a few toilets before you enter the chapel which would be the end of the Vatican Museums tour. At the end of your visit you can choose to go back through the museums by going through the left door or out to the gift shops and St. Peter's Basilica through the right door. title: Grandest of all Catholic churches in the world
text: I consider this as the grandest of all Catholic churches worldwide not so much in terms of physical dimension (though the church is huge!), but more in terms of historical, artistic and religious significance. Visiting this church is like stepping into the very heart of Christianity where the Apostle St. Peter, upon whom Christ founded his church, is buried and venerated. The place is also like a museum, full of Renaissance masterpieces -- the works of the likes of Michaelangelo, Bernini, Bramante, and many others. Not to miss are Michaelangelo's "Pietà" and Bernini's canopy over the main altar. But do find some time to pause in silence and pray. Remember that you are in a church. Finally, if you have time, climb up the dome ("cupola") and admire the city of Rome from above and the Papal tombs on the lower level of the basilica.

title: Climb the 300+ steps up to the Dome! TOTALLY WORTH THE EFFORT!!! Come Early to Avoid the Crazy Crowds!
text:
We visited Rome and Vatican City for the first time in May 2025. We signed up for a guided tour with The Tour Guy, which included a Dome Climb, visiting the Crypt and the main hall of St. Peter's Basilica, visiting the Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel. This tour started at 7.15am and ended at around 3.45pm. With a guided tour, we skipped the line and went straight through security without any hassle. After clearing security, the first activity on the itinerary was the Dome climb. We took the elevator up to the roof terrace of the basilica and entered the lower section of the dome to admire the beautiful mosaics. Then we walked up 300+ steps through very narrow passageways and 2 spiral staircases to reach the 360-degree circular outdoor viewing platform of the dome. The views from this platform are ABSOLUTELY SPECTACULAR! IMPORTANT NOTE: For those who are claustrophobic, obese and out of shape, you might want to think twice before doing this climb. If you are not on a guided tour, you should purchase your tickets for the dome climb online a week before you visit Vatican City. Otherwise, you will have to stand in line for a very long time to purchase the tickets at the venue!

Next up was going down into the crypt of the basilica. Our guide brought us through the crypt while pointing out the sarcophagi of several former Popes and spiritual leaders including the sarcophagus of Saint Peter himself and we eventually ended up inside the main hall of St. Peter's Basilica right under the main dome which we had climbed up earlier! This basilica is the largest basilica in the world today and it is just a marvelous example of Christian architecture and ornamentation! Visiting St. Peter's Basilica should be on the travel bucket list of everyone on this planet, Catholic or not! Our guide also brought us to walk through the Holy Door of St. Peter's Basilica, after all, 2025 is a Jubilee Year and one only gets this opportunity once every 25 years! Make sure you see the Pieta sculpture by Michelangelo and capture a few photographs as your keepsake or souvenir of your visit to this magnificent basilica and Vatican City!

This is definitely a MUST-VISIT tourist attraction and place of worship for everyone who comes to Rome. Put this on your bucket list!!!

title: Well worth the effort
text:
My wife and I visited the Dome as part of a pre-booked online Bassilica with Dome and Lift ticket. Although entrance to the Bassilica is free, pre-booking (for an extra 7 euros) allows you to choose a time slot for the Dome visit, plus the added advantage of being in the shorter line for entrance to the Bassilica itself.

The lift cuts out the need to take the first 200+ steps and takes you to the terrace of the Basilica, where you can enjoy a unique view over the Eternal City. 

It also allows an opportunity to admire up close the mosaics of Saint Peter's Dome, from the same vantage point as the artist who designed it.

The next stage is not for the fainthearted or those with health and mobility issues. To reach the top of the Dome, you must continue up 320 steps, which can be quite steep and narrow in places.

However, if you make it to the top, the 360° views over Rome are truly spectacular, especially out over St. Peter's Square and beyond.

placeInfo.address: Piazza San Pietro, 00120 Vatican City Italy

title: Book a time slot via official St. Peter's Bassilica website
text:
We purchased a Dome with Lift ticket online, which allowed us to choose a specific time for accessing the dome. I opted for 3.30pm as this ensured that the sun was behind the dome, giving better light for photos of the square and beyond. 

The Dome with Lift tickets were 22 euros each, which included an audio guide that you could download 90 minutes before your dome time slot. In the end, we didn't use the audio guide, so the extra 7 euros were effectively a booking fee. Well worthwhile to be able to take the pre-booked queue, which was almost non-existent, as opposed to the always very lengthy 'normal' line.

Once inside, the first thing that strikes  you is that the biggest church in the world appears quite small. However, as you move around, exploring all the side chapels and areas within the Bassilica, and then as you look up and gaze at the ceilings and dome(s), its vastness becomes all too clear. 

The architecture and art combine to make a truly breathtaking spectacle. Yet it is still possible to find a quiet space to stand or sit and reflect on the spiritual dimensions and purpose of this building, a place to worship God. 

As with many sites in Rome, there were a couple of frustrating and annoying matters. Firstly, the number of people who need to be the centre of attraction in their online world and therefore choose to take wholly inappropriate selfies. Secondly, there are those who deliberately flout the dress code for a place of worship, pushing the definition of respectful beyond belief!

When our time slot for the lift arrived, there was no queue at all, so my wife and I travelled up, accompanied only by the Bassilica member of staff on lift duty.

I have a separate review of the Dome, but let's just say that it was equally breathtaking.

title: Die Morgentour buchen - dann ist es wirklich einmalig
text:
885152588

Wir haben die erste Tour am Morgen mit Frühstück online zwei Monate im Voraus für knapp 200 Euro für 2 Erw. und 1 Teenager gebucht. Wir mussten dafür um 5 Uhr aufstehen; die Tour ging um 7:30 Uhr los. Bitte bedenken, dass der Startpunkt draußen (ohne Überdachung) ist und man dort ggf. bei Kälte/Regen/Sonne ungeschützt steht. Gegenüber ist ein Cafe, dort kann man ggf. einen Espresso trinken und noch einmal die Toilette nutzen. Wir hatten das Glück und waren tatsächlich die erste Tour am Morgen, die in den Vatikan kam und konnten somit alles ganz toll fotografieren und hatten niemanden vor uns. In der Sixtinischen Kapelle ist das Fotografieren verboten, sonst ist es überall erlaubt. Unsere Führerin war sehr gut und sprach ein gutes Englisch. Das Frühstück nach der Tour war eher eine Katastrophe. Man musste lange warten, der Sitzplatz wurde zugewiesen. Pancakes und Marmelade/Honig musste man sich holen (Warteschlange) und die Pancakes waren schon kalt. Alles andere (Croissants/Brötchen, Kaffee, Wurst, Rührei (ebenfalls kalt), Kartoffelspalten (ebenfalls kalt) wurde nach und nach an die Tische gebracht. Bis wir alles hatten, waren die ersten schon fertig. O-Saft mussten wir 2 x bestellen und ewig darauf warten. Das Frühstück können auch wir nicht empfehlen und wer die Möglichkeit hat, sollte die Frühführung ohne FR buchen. Wir hatten gelesen, dass es von der Sixtinischen Kapelle einen Zugang für Gruppenführungen zum Petersdom gibt und sind nach dem FR mit den ganzen anderen MASSEN von Leuten wieder zur Sixtinischen Kapelle, um diesen Zugang zu nehmen. Zwei Wärter haben uns aber unmissverständlich klar gemacht, dass es dort nur Zugang mit einer Gruppenführung gibt. Also, der (Insider-) Tipp funktioniert leider nicht mehr .

title: Jaw Dropping!
text: Around 4 Million visitors see the Sistine Chapel each year and this of course means that it is very packed and in the height of summer not very quiet or serene. Setting this aside, it is still the place to see. You are lead through the Vatican museums in what will seems like endless rooms and ceilings and sign posts toward the Sistine, until you finally reach the stair case that takes you inside.  It is heavily marshalled and you are literally herded along with the flow; it it is marvellous to behold. What you cannot do is to take video or photo's - The prohibition against photography has been in place for several decades, and while many assume that the no-photography rule is in place to prevent the flashing of cameras from affecting the art, the real reason dates back to the restoration of the chapel's art that began in 1980 and took nearly 20 years to complete.  In return for funding the renovation, Nippon TV received the exclusive rights to photography and video of the restored art. You will almost constantly hear the security shouting "no photography" but you still have your eyes (and memories) to enjoy eye-popping art that adorns nearly every inch of the walls and ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

title: Ruins?  Many.  Stories?  More.  Imagination?  Needed.
text:
Visiting the Roman Forum is akin to touring an open-air museum of the Kingdom, Republic, and Empire all at once and having to peel back the multiple layers of history contained in almost three millennia.  It takes some effort!  Many temples, shrines, and residences from the Monarchy were located here including the Regia (royal residence, from the 8th century BCE) and Temple of Vesta (likely from the 7th century BCE).  In the early days of the Republic the area was a vibrant social center containing businesses and food stalls; this economic and communal nexus then morphed into more of a ceremonial nucleus during the Empire.  Like many Ancient Roman sites, it fell into disrepair after dissolution of the Empire and modern excavation was started in the early 1800’s.  If there is one unifying characteristic of the area it is certainly change, and in its current reincarnation Roman citizens have given way to innumerable tourists and modern archeologists.  

I visited Foro Romano on no less than three occasions.  The first was on a solo visit after wandering around Palatine Hill, and the second was as part of a small group tour that included a visit to the Colosseum’s underground chambers.  Both of these visits left me almost more confused about the area than before my trip.  The third and most comprehensive outing was through a private tour organized by the Hotel Eden (see separate review), and it was on this occasion that I truly began to appreciate what was before me.  Starting at the entrance by the Arch of Septimius Severus, we methodically walked through Via Sacra, branching off to visit the Basilica Julia, House of the Vestal Virgins, Temple of Castor and Pollux, and Julius Cesar’s funeral pyre (among others!).  We ended with a stop at the Basilica of Constantine and Maxentius before ascending to Palatine Hill and stopping for a sweeping overview from above of the area we had just seen on foot below.

In summary, this was not an “easy” place to visit largely because it suffers from the same deficit that many ancient ruins do, mainly that one needs quite a bit of personal augmented reality to picture the area anywhere close to what it was in its (multiple) heyday(s).  While it is easy for me to picture gladiators fighting in the backdrop of the ruins of the Colosseum, it is much more difficult to picture law courts functioning from rows of columnar stumps.  Not having an audio guide readily available makes a human guide a necessity, and I would highly recommend a private or small group tour for those coming here, along with a bit of reading about the area before your outing.  Add the number of people jockeying for photos and, well, my return on the time invested was average at best.

Everyone’s going to visit anyways, right?  Just be prepared to put some mental muscle into the experience.

title: I really think that almost everyone can find something here to like
text:
I guess that there isn't much that I can add about St. Peter's Basilica.  It is mind-blowingly awesome.  It is so big, has so many little details, so many little nooks and crannies and little surprises.  It is an absolute feast for the eyes on multiple scales, and I don't think that there is anything else like it on Earth.  So if you're asking if it is really that big of a deal, then my answer is 'yes'.  It really is that big of a deal.  

I have been to St. Peter's a few times, most recently January 2025 for a jubilee papal Mass.  The liturgy was amazing.  We also attended a smaller Mass in the chapel behind the main altar the next day-- again, truly wonderful.  Our children (15, 11, 8yo) were also wowed by the liturgies and the church, so I would say that St. Peter's has a wide appeal age-wise, even if it is sometimes difficult to keep track of all of the symbols, iconography, and, yes, Latin.  On that note, if one is not familiar or has limited familiarity with Catholic symbology or iconography, having some kind of book or guide would make your visit more edifying (honestly, even if you know something, there is an awful lot there).  

I once paid for the tour up to the top of the dome, and I enjoyed this very much.  One gets to see the church from some of the upper galleries, which provides a nice change of perspective.  Going up progressively smaller halls and stairs, one finally emerges in the cupola atop the dome, and the views of Rome and the Vatican were a really nice treat, but this was 25 years ago, and I haven't done it since.  

If you really, really hate Catholics or churches, then I suppose that perhaps St. Peter's is not for you; it's not subtle.  (I would also question your decision to visit Rome, though perhaps you could stick to the Classical parts.) However, I think that there is plenty to appreciate even if your real interests lie more in art, architecture, decoration, anthropology, the Renaissance, or something near related rather than Christianity or religion.  It really is a special place.

title: Incredible building
text:
We purchased a skip the line ticket with a self-guided map and audio guide on our phones, which
worked fine, and gave us all of the information we needed.
There is a lift you can take to get part the way up, which we took but to get to the dome you have to
take the steps. The staircase to the dome required a level of fitness, and turning back is not an
option as there is a queue of people following you. Part of the staircase does get increasingly narrow
as you get closer to the top, probably not ideal if you are claustrophobic.
At the top there is stunning panoramic view of the city, great for taking pictures. Whilst it was quite
busy most people were accommodating and moved round the dome top to allow people to take in
views from all areas. It was truly breathtaking and worth going.
You descend the same was, so lots of steps, but you can stop before the lift and take in the city
views half way down.
Our tickets gave us skipped the line to get into the main Basilica, which was breathtaking It was very
busy but nobody was in a rush so you were able to take in the amazing architecture and sculptures
An absolute must visit.

title: No Photography Inside and gotta be quiet!
text:

But I understand the rationale though. Being there in person is exponentially better than seeing it through pictures. The Creation of Adam itself is relatively small with a lot of paintings within the chapel and it took me a few rounds to find it.

Photography is allowed within the rest of the Vatican museums though, just no flash. And again, no photography of any form is allowed within the Sistine Chapel and don't make any noise within the chapel as well! The staff will make a scene if you're caught violating their rules!

title: Too much people. Don't go on a busy day, you will regret.
text:
We had an awful experience. Only because there are too many people inside. 

It starts by standing in line for over two hours, while loads of groups go inside. While waiting there is a man (slightly bold, nervously smoking cigarettes) who wants you to buy priority skip the line tickets. You will be paying over 100 euro. He does get rude if you reject him.

When you enter the museum, it is packed with people. There's no way to enjoy all the art and employees are rushing you through the museum. There should be a maximum of entrants and this museum should be available for all people. You will have loads of advantages if you pay more. That's not ok.

I wouldn't recommend on a busy day. If you are visiting on a quiet day, this museum is probably the best in the world.

title: A must-see
text:
Truly something that stays with you! When we visited, a priest led the entire room in prayer for peace. I'm not a religious person (nor was I raised Catholic) but it was an incredibly moving experience. It is, of course, very busy and the chapel was very crowded, but most of the other visitors were respectful of the request for silence.

There's a great story behind the reason why you can't take photographs - I won't spoil it for you, but I looked it up out of curiosity after our visit as we didn't have a tour guide.

My only criticism is that the maps that the Musei Vaticani hand out aren't the best design. I was confused trying to follow it, so gave up and went via signpost instead (we didn't get a chance to take in the entire museum as we didn't have long to spend in Rome, so if you do visit the Musei Vaticani, allow an entire day). Of course, I'd have liked to have stayed longer to just admire and absorb this beautiful artwork too, but wouldn't we all!

title: Crowds ruin the experience
text:
Don’t get me wrong- St. Peter’s Basilica is magnificent in size and beauty. The basilica is absolutely beautiful! And being able to pass through the Holy Doors was beyond special. We also got to see the Pieta, which was spectacular. However, the crowds are IMMENSE.  Luckily we bought the skip the line tickets from the Vatican website, which helped a little. Once inside though, it is a sea of visitors being ushered through a set flow. You can’t really see things at your own pace and if you try to break away from the flow of visitors, staff promptly push you back into the flow. 
We were lucky to find a side chapel where we could participate in Adoration for a while, but otherwise the massive crowds and crowd management strip a lot of spirituality out of the visit.  They had most if the seating inside roped off, so we couldn’t even sit and enjoy the church. They just hustle visitors through because they have to. 
There are plenty of gift shops, mostly overpriced and nowhere to get things blessed.
My advice is see St. Peter’s for its physical beauty but go to Basilica of Mary Major and Basilica of St John of Lateran for the religious experience. Both of those were profoundly more  religious experiences.

title: There are hits and misses.
text:
Finally, I got to visit St. Peter’s Basilica! I purchased a ticket that included access to both the basilica and the dome. However, since I didn’t opt for a skip-the-line entry, I had to endure a nearly 1.5-hour wait in the cold—a torturous experience.

When it was my turn, I had a choice: climb all the way up via the stairs or take the elevator partway and tackle the remaining 331 steps on foot. I chose the latter. As I ascended, the staircase grew increasingly narrow, with no railings for support. The walls seemed to close in on me, and as someone who is claustrophobic, I ended up having a panic attack.

Reaching the top, I was greeted by a stunning panoramic view of the city. However, my excitement was dampened by the metal safety grilles, which partially obstructed the view. In the end, while the experience was unique, I personally didn’t find it worth the anxiety.

Descending the same way, I finally stepped into the basilica itself—and it was absolutely breathtaking. The intricate artwork, the grand architecture, and the sheer historical significance of the place made it a truly awe-inspiring visit.

title: Definitely visit the Basilica when in Rome
text:
St. Peter's Basilica was the highlight of our trip to Rome. We were so confused about how to purchase the best ticket option as my husband wanted to climb the stairs to the Dome & I did not (for health reasons). We eventually settled on buying from the official site which included the lift to the terrace and a self audio guide.
We arrived around 10am and pretty much got straight through the security scanners. The outside view to the Basilica is a splendid sight but once inside the Basilica it is breath taking. We used the Audio guide which was very informative, you need your own ear pods for this as it is a download available after booking the tickets. 
The Dome for me personally was a disappointment, I took the lift up to the terrace level which did not have the views over the city that I was expecting...this could be me misunderstanding what was included. On reaching the terrace level we had to climb a small staircase and then we were able to walk around less than half of the Dome [ perspex screens also obscure taking photos down into the Basilica and there is no view to the outside which is what I was expecting. There are some wonderful mosaics to enjoy.
My husband continued up the staircase to the top level and he did say that the views were amazing although it was congested so he couldn't really enjoy it.
Overall we would 100% recommend going to the Basilica

text: Ottimo sito archeologico e sicuramente da visitare se di passaggio per Roma. La mia esperienza la voglio però condividere per evitare ad altri la mia disavventura. Dopo un centinaio di metri dall'ingresso (lato piazza Venezia), mi accorgo che non ho più il portafogli che avevo attentamente riposto nella tasca anteriore dei pantaloni. Premetto che, data l'ora mattutina, vi erano pochissimi visitatori all'interno del sito. title: No visit to Rome would be complete without a trip to the Forum
text:
The Roman Forum comprises much of the Ancient Rome's most important structures, from shrines to government houses to monuments. Although much of the complex is in ruins, you can see the remains and imagine the former glory of the Arch of Septimius Severus, the Temple of Saturn, the Arch of Titus and the House of the Vestal Virgins, among other structures.  Ancient Rome's most important center of commerce, government, and religion; and probably the entire Empire. 
Entrance fees for the Roman Forum depend on what tour you take and what kind of ticket you book. It's possible to book a ticket to explore on your own (which usually includes entrance to the Colosseum and Palatine Hill). I would advise that you do this but through an agency/tour as you will get the fast track entry and this will save you a lot of time. You can also decide on either a tour guide, headset, or phone app or just do your own thing.  The Forum is open daily at 9 a.m. and closes at 3:30, 4:30 or 6:15 p.m., depending on the season. The closest metro station is Colosseo.
