title: A Profound Journey Through Faith and Art—St. Peter’s Basilica
text:
Visiting St. Peter’s Basilica as part of a pilgrimage retracing the steps of St. Francis of Assisi was nothing short of transformative. As an artist, filmmaker, photographer, and devout Catholic, I found myself overwhelmed at every turn by the sheer beauty, history, and spiritual significance of this sacred place.

The moment I stepped inside, I was struck by the grandeur of it all—the soaring ceilings, the intricate mosaics, and the way light filters through the windows as if divinely orchestrated. It’s not just a building; it’s a living testament to faith, crafted by hands that were undoubtedly blessed. Every detail feels purposeful, like a physical manifestation of devotion.

Walking through the basilica, I was particularly drawn to the chapels—each a masterpiece in its own right. Michelangelo’s Pietà took my breath away. Standing before it, I felt an indescribable connection to both the artist and the divine, as if the sculpture itself was alive with emotion and grace.

Beneath the grandeur of the basilica lies a quieter, more solemn experience: the catacombs and tombs of popes past. Walking through these sacred spaces was humbling. The tomb of St. Peter himself, the rock upon which the Church was built, filled me with a deep sense of reverence and awe. It’s hard to describe the feeling of being so close to the foundation of our faith.

Our tour group lingered in these spaces, absorbing the history and the palpable sense of sanctity that seemed to emanate from every stone. The guide’s recounting of the basilica’s creation only deepened my appreciation. To think of the artists and architects who dedicated their lives to this work—it’s clear they were inspired by something far greater than themselves.

From a creative perspective, St. Peter’s Basilica is a marvel. The way every line, curve, and detail leads your eye upward—toward the heavens—is nothing short of genius. It’s the kind of place that makes you feel small, yet profoundly connected to something infinite. As a photographer, I was in paradise; every angle seemed to tell a story, and every shadow and beam of light was a reminder of the divine interplay between creation and Creator.

Spiritually, this experience was moving beyond words. Standing in the heart of the Catholic Church, surrounded by centuries of faith and devotion, I felt a renewed sense of purpose and connection to my own journey. St. Peter’s Basilica is not just a place you visit—it’s a place that stays with you, a reminder of the power of faith, art, and the human spirit united in worship.

If you have the chance to visit, don’t rush through it. Take your time to absorb the atmosphere, reflect, and let it move you. This isn’t just a bucket-list destination—it’s a pilgrimage, an encounter with history, and a glimpse of heaven itself.

title: Some tips for your visit
text:
Not going to write about the history and the breathtaking beauty of the cathedral, that goes without saying, obviously. But just a few tips: 
We got there early, around 9:30am on a Friday in November. You don’t have to pay to enter the cathedral, but you do have to go through security check, like at an airport. That can take some time. We waited around 15 minutes. As you face  the security booths, don’t line up for the one in the very right. This is the one that moves the slowest as the security guards add people to this line who skip the wait (attending the mass, pregnant or with little children. More about that later). 
We used Rick Steve’s’ Pocket guide to Rome to guide us through the cathedral and it was more than enough to learn about the major highlights. 
The gift shop is located to the left all the way in the back. There are also shops as you exit the cathedral on your right. Items are different. The Holy Water bottles are only sold inside the cathedral. You can also get them blessed. There are quite a few chapels inside that you can attend for a prayer or a mass. No photos or touristy stuff when you do that and the guards are very strict  and vigilant about that.
We came back at 4:30ish pm to attend a mass. The line to get through security was much longer than in the morning. However, you can tell the  guards you are here for the mass and they’ll let you cut the line (you’ll still have to pass the security, they’ll just let you go ahead   of everyone else). You can also cut the line if you are pregnant, I’ve seen people do that. We attended the mass in Italian an also did the confession (they offer that in English as well): 
The restrooms are to the right when you exit the cathedral. They are free.

Once you enter, you lose yourself among the vastness of the Basilica, you almost do not feel the number of those present. Don't miss the tombs of the Popes (that of John Paul II is in the Basilica), the basements and even the visit to the dome. What else to say? Michelangelo's Pietà, alone worth the trip!

title: Beautiful, but the crowds are almost surreal.
text: A visit to the Vatican is a must, despite the crowds. We were a bit early and feared a long line, even with a skip-the-line ticket from get your guide. And in some rooms there are famous paintings by Van Gogh, Rubens, Picasso and many others, and 90% just walk on with an eye only for the "Sistine Chapel" signs. You can also take pictures all the time during the two-hour walk through all sorts of rooms, both up and down, and then you finally arrive at the famous chapel, where guards shout that you can't take pictures in this one room only... a bit surreal. But the organization was fine. And the artwork is beautiful.

title: A museum that honors cultures, but must go further in recognizing injustices
text:
I visited the Anima Mundi Museum at the Vatican and was touched by the wealth of exhibits, especially those from Amerindian cultures. It is valuable to see these traditions promoted and respected.

However, it is important to recall that the Vatican has recently acknowledged the wrongs caused by colonization and the “Doctrine of Discovery”, which have profoundly affected indigenous peoples. I would have liked to see a more explicit mention in the museum of these historical injustices and of the ongoing efforts at redress.

A place like Anima Mundi has a key role to play: to celebrate cultures, but also to educate on the mistakes of the past to build a fairer future.

title: Crowded, hot, and not worth it
text:
We were supposed to have our tour at 8am, but the Vatican cancelled all tours until the afternoon (presumably because the Pope was going to be on the move), so our tour was changed to 1pm. A nightmare. The amount of people at that time, especially because anyone who was booked in the morning, was also now there at 1pm, made it impossible to enjoy. 

The tour guide wasn't bad, but she didn't focus much on the history of the Vatican itself. But honestly, even if she was the best tour guide in the world, it wouldn't have mattered much, because there were so many groups smashed together, it was almost impossible to walk or focus.

Even the tour operators from all the different companies were snapping at each other, due to the crowding and trying to get around each other.

By the time we got to the Sistine Chapel, I was hot, tired and unimpressed. We were told at the beginning of the tour that there is no talking while inside the chapel, but good luck with that when you have thousands of people in a small area. It was loud and packed in, and security was snapping at everyone who didn't listen about not taking photos in there. Also, you can't even exit until you find your tour guide. They literally won't let you exit without your guide. Talk about feeling a little claustrophobic and trapped.

The grounds outside at the end were the best part. It's a beautiful area and they were setting up for an event. Once we got outside of the Vatican, we noticed many law enforcement around and were told the Pope was either leaving or coming back from somewhere. 

If I were to come back to Rome, I'd pass on the Vatican City tour. They allow way too many people in. Not to mention, there's no exits anywhere if you get to the point where you want/need to leave. You're stuck until your tour is over. And although it was a beautiful day outside, it was hot as you-know-what in the Vatican.

title: Take time to enjoy the Vatican Museums

It was quiet and peaceful with extraordinary views of St. Peter's Basilica.  Our Vatican Museum guide took us through the gardens, past a few museum highlights and then straight to the Sistine Chapel.  We were allowed to go back and visit all the areas of the museum that were skipped by our tour guide.  Prior to buying our ticket, I could not figure out if we were forced to directly exit the museum complex after visiting the Sistine Chapel.  The answer is NO!  You can start over and visit the whole complex at your own pace. There is also a cafeteria where lunch can be purchased and eaten either inside or outside on a patio.  Just be warned!  There are aggressive seagulls that will try to steal your food if you take it outside.

There were minimal opportunities to take much time to admire the art and once we entered the chapel, we were in and out within a few minutes. The time spent in the museum and chapel was about 3 hours, but honestly, you could easily spend a day admiring everything so whilst what we saw was amazing, it seemed just a method of maximum revenue over allowing visitors an opportunity to really appreciate the museum and Sistine chapel. 

We had booked the Basilica afterwards, but that was cancelled so we felt a bit deflated.

title: Extraordinary Experience and a Highlight of Rome. Arrive Early in the Morning
text: Visiting St Peter's Basilica is an extraordinary experience and is a highlight of a visit to Rome. Not only is the interior of the Basilica beautiful but the sheer size of the cathedral leaves you awestruck. The highlights include viewing Bernini's stunning altar with its bronze baroque canopy and dove window in the apse and viewing Michelangelo's Pieta. It is also well worth making the climb to the top of the dome. This is a strenuous endeavor but is so worth the time and effort as the views from the top are spectacular especially if it is a sunny day. It is free to enter the Basilica but there is a 10 Euro charge to make the climb. An elevator takes you to the roof avoiding the first 231 steps. However, you must then climb 323 steps to get to the top of the dome. St Peter's can get overwhelmed with tourists. It is essential to arrive early in the morning. You first need to go through a security check and a huge line starts forming on St Peter's Square after 9am. Once through security, I would recommend doing the dome climb first as a separate slow moving line forms for it. The dome was open as early as 730am when we visited in November. Plan for 1 hour to complete the dome climb including waiting in lines and another 1 hour to tour the interior of St Peter's. Remember that appropriate dress is required. No shorts or bare shoulders. If visiting on a Sunday, time your visit so that you are still around at noon as the Pope will usually appear at his residence window overlooking St Peter's Square and give a blessing to the crowd below. This was pretty special.

title: Spectacular Views and Well Worth the Effort
text: Climbing to the top of the dome of St Peter's Basilica was an amazing experience and well worth the effort and time involved. The views from here are spectacular. It costs 10 Euro and only cash was accepted. The line forms just outside of the entrance to St Peter's Basilica and was very slow moving so I would recommend going early in the day before crowds build. It was open as early as 730am when we visited. Try to pick a day when the sun is out, and the sky is blue for the best experience and photography. There is an elevator to the roof that allows you to avoid the 231 steps. If someone in your group doesn't want to climb any further, this vantage point still offers really great views of St Peter's Square and is worth experiencing. However, the truly spectacular experience involves another 323 steps to the top of the dome. Certainly, a strenuous workout but so worth it. Plan for an hour for the whole experience including waiting in line, making the climb and enjoying the views.

title: Unmissable Masterpiece of Art and History ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
text: The Vatican Museums are simply unmissable—an extraordinary journey through centuries of art, history, and culture. From ancient sculptures to Renaissance masterpieces, every room holds treasures that leave you in awe. The highlight, of course, is the Sistine Chapel, where Michelangelo’s ceiling is breathtaking beyond words. Despite the crowds, the scale and richness of the collection make the experience unforgettable. Plan at least half a day to explore properly and book tickets in advance to skip long lines. A must for anyone visiting Rome—this is where history, spirituality, and art converge in the most spectacular way.

The Raphael Rooms were particularly striking, and, of course, the Sistine Chapel — seeing these masterpieces in person is something words can’t fully capture.
I recommend going early in the morning to avoid the crowds and definitely taking an audio guide — otherwise, you might miss some fascinating details. The museums are huge, so plan your route in advance and don’t try to see everything in one day.

title: Overcrowded and money spinner
text:
Whist the museum is fabulous to see this is clearly a money making scheme for the Catholic Church. The architecture and artefacts are amazing to see however, you’ll be hard pressed to see it all without someone in front of you or next to you. Time slots are every 30 minutes and it is massively overcrowded in every room. 
Having been to the Louvre and the British  museum the Vatican is disappointing. Not for the art but the way they pack everyone in. 
Do not try to enter prior to your time slot. Book tickets in advance. 
Expect it to be extremely crowded and difficult to see everything with no air conditioner and very limited fans. 
The Sistine chapel is so packed you can get a glimpse and on your way. No photography allowed in the chapel. 
My advice, spend your money elsewhere and google the images.

title: 551 steps - be there early, the upper steps are steep and narrow
text: We were at St. Peter’s Basilica shortly after 8 am and then had to queue for about 15 minutes at security, another 20 minutes to buy our tickets for the Dom Dom Dome, so it went quite quickly. There are 2 options: 1. Save the first 204 steps with elevator - for 10,-€ or 2. to run the whole 551 steps for 8,-€ (as of June 2024). I decided to run up the whole 551 steps, with the first 204 steps really easy to run. Approximately halfway along the way, you then stand on a balcony just below the dome, similar to Florence Cathedral, and can admire the frescoes up close, which is super impressive. The upper part of the steps then becomes quite steep and narrow, not for people with heart problems and claustrophobia. The view from the top is just spectacular and worth the effort. Absolute highlight. Highly recommended.

title: Too many people and misadventure at the entrance
text:
Too many people. Entries should be subject to even more quotas. I understand that the demand is so great and you want to please everyone, but so you do not fully appreciate the beautiful place.

All the staff met both outside and inside were kind and professional. All but one...
At the metal detector check, between 10.30 and 10.45, in the middle row, I was treated badly and rudely by the security officer.
I state that I am a frequent flyer and through the security checks of every airport in the world without problems and with awareness of the procedure.
Not seeing trays where to place all the objects together I placed only backpack, keys and cell phone.
The metal detector then played as I passed by and I then stepped back to place the wallet on the tape in question.
The metal detector rang again as I passed, but before backing down to place my belt and glasses I headed to the tape to retrieve the wallet that was sliding individually on the same as there were no trays in which to place all the objects. I obviously informed the employee in advance of what I was doing and that I would recover the wallet to pass everything together. The attendant in question, a man in his forties suffering from eye misalignment (mentioned only to identify a specific characteristic and not to harm those who do their job politely and professionally), pushed me back not allowing me to recover the wallet and I managed at least to communicate to my partner already beyond the controls to take her wallet because in the confusion anyone could have taken it and taken it away. What is unacceptable, however, is that from that moment, unjustifiably, the security officer began to take an aggressive attitude and repeat to me in a rude tone out loud three or four times “you don’t tell me, I’m not your brother, you have to take your wallet”.

I am always very respectful of the authorities and sympathetic to the stressful situations to which they are subjected and realizing the altered state of the subject I preferred not to say a word, but having traveled far and wide believe me that I have never experienced such a paradoxical situation. I believe that that person is not fit to do that job if he must treat in a rude and unprofessional manner those who come to visit the Vatican Museums with respect and eager to live a pleasant day. The impact it risks leaving on many tourists is bad. My Asian Companion, who is accustomed to many other types of Processing in every situation, was dazed all morning.

title: Vatican Museums. The best of art and history in one place. / Lo mejor del arte y la historia en un sólo lugar.
text:
We've had the good fortune to visit several museums in different countries, from the Metropolitan Museum in New York to the Prado in Madrid, but the Vatican Museum exceeded our expectations. The wealth of art and historical works it houses makes this a must-see for those traveling to Rome. Some advice: get your tickets online on the museum's official website. Be careful, as some websites mimic the official website and tend to be confusing. In the case of the Vatican Museum, the words are in Latin, so it's MVSEI VATICANI. A second piece of advice is not to arrive too early, thinking you might get in early. Tickets are timed, and the line for your turn only forms 15 minutes beforehand. My wife and I arrived at 2:30 and ended up having to wait an hour for our turn. It was worth the wait. Highly recommended. The Sistine Chapel is unforgettable; I just arrived with such a sore neck from looking at the murals on the ceilings that I could barely enjoy it.
————

Hemos tenido la dicha de visitar varios museos en diferentes paises, desde el Metropolitano de NY, o el Prado en Madrid, pero los Museo Vaticano superó nuestras espectativas. La riqueza de obras de arte e históricas que acoge hace que este sea un lugar de obligada visita para los que viajen a Roma. Algunos consejos: saque los tickets online en la pagina oficial del museo, cuidado que hay algunos websites que imitan a la pagina oficial y tienden a confundir. En el caso del museo vaticano las palabras las encuentran en latín por lo tanto es MVSEI VATICANI. Un segu do consejo es que no vayan demasiado temprano pe sando que pueden entrar antes de tiempo. Los tickets tienen hora y solo uno 15 minutos antes se hace la fila para el turno. Mi esposa y yo llegamos 2:30 y resultó que tuvimos que esperar una hora para nuestro turno. Valió la pena la espera. Recomendado altamente. La capilla Sixtina es inolvidable, solo que llegé con tanto dolor en el cuello de mirar murales en los techos que casi no pude disfrutarla.

title: This visit makes me grateful I don’t live in Italy
text:
If there was any doubt the Vatican’s first and foremost priority isn’t money, this visit put that to bed. We bought a “skip the line” ticket which was technically true as the security checks only took a few minutes however Vatican museums would’ve sold 5-10 thousand of them for the same time…..now given some of the very carefully designed walkways to ensure it’s an eternity before the Sistine chapel were extremely narrow, my wife who’s a diabetic felt dizzy in one of those walkways, so we stopped and I give her some sugar, only for her to be pushed along by what I can only describe as an Italian “Karen” of a tour guide saying no stopping, at which point to told her she’s a diabetic and to walk way. But it gets better, we were travelling with a toddler in a stroller and there were lifts, however to get one you needed to summon the one operator they have there which can take 5-10 mins depending on how busy they were, otherwise it was carrying the stroller up and down stairs.

Then once we reached the Sistine chapel (which was amazing but ridiculously crowded as per vaticans $$ driven business model) that same Karen tried to grab my wife’s phone off her claiming she was trying to take photos of the ceiling (which is apparently forbidden) but she was simply sending a text. I confronted her a second time, after showing me some ID she told he she works for the pope and was going to call security. Later I learned she’s a tour guide employed directly by the museum, it’s like saying the mailman works for the President 😂. She did try to get security involved who clearly get paid too little to care and just shrugged it off. But given we were in a sacred place I bit my tongue (was ready by then to completely let loose on her) and we left. 

So the combination of the Vatican allowing such overcrowding and this SOB it made what was meant to be a great holiday experience a rather dreadful one. 

Buyers beware

title: Organisation = scam
text:
The museum is more than complete and beautiful.  It is the organization that is a catastrophe. Contrary to what I read on the reviews, the official Vatican booking site can only be accessed one month before the date of the day of the visit.  By going there several times that day, in the morning , we only managed to validate the 5:30 p.m. slot knowing that on the site it is specified that the museum closes at 8 p.m. with a start of evacuation at 7:30 p.m.
We wanted to go into the queue which was huge at around 5.15pm as the ticket controller had told me earlier. And finally all the people who had a ticket at 5:30 were turned away because they still accepted people who had a ticket at 5:00 p.m. and who arrived late (whereas on the site, it is specified that delays are not allowed), results at 5:30 p.m. we only begin to accept people who have a ticket at 5:30 p.m. which corresponds to about 300 people, so if you wisely queue you can very well enter the Vatican after 6:00 p.m. Contrary to what is said on the Vatican website it is not possible to avoid some rooms (or very little then ) to save time on the tour and there is no point in inquiring about the plans or buying a plan because you are obliged to follow a circuit ,which would have been interesting to know in advance. the beginning of the tour is very very badly indicated .once you have started the tour you follow it with the a flock . As you now know that you only have 2 hours left to visit , you hurry into the first rooms and then you realize that they were perhaps the most interesting , but you say to yourself "it doesn't matter I'll go back to them at the end" (for example the room on Egypt ) left at 7:10 p.m. of the circuit , we head for the stairs to return only to the room Egypt and there we realize that the guards have already closed the barriers of all the rooms , even the ones below , so from 7:10 p.m. , and not half an hour before the end , you can no longer access any room . they close 45 minutes before the end. with guards in each room, I think that in half an hour, they would have plenty of time to get everyone out before 8:00 p.m. so tickets sold by 5:30 p.m., contrary to what they say on the sites, it's a big scam you enter at 6:00 p.m. well passed and you leave at 7:15 p.m. And there are no fewer people because time is not limited so those who have been there since the morning can stay all day.  Combined with those who enter at the same time as you, you can not breathe.

title: Must-see but too many groups
text:
2nd visit to this place, still beautiful. I came home around 12:15 and left at more than 6:00.
However, the management of schedules and entrance queues needs to be improved (too many groups and the visitor does not know which queue to take, depending on when to enter; so many people have to wait in full sun).
Once you get home, don’t hesitate to drop off your things at the cloakroom and just keep a bottle of water and your hat with you (you’ll have to get out of the building). 
Not all rooms are air-conditioned or ventilated, which can make the visit painful depending on the heat. I am not sure that opening the windows of some rooms in the middle of the afternoon by more than 35° improves this situation
You should make a separate entrance for groups or improve it because it frankly disturbs the visit of individual people or families (you just can not pass or see anything). In a medium-sized room I counted up to 7 groups (or rather 7 Flags), it is clearly far too much and it also leads to a permanent hubbub and in several languages at the same time. Some groups or visitors are also embarrassed by pushing others or touching objects/sculptures.
I was looking forward to depositing my postcards at the post office after my visit. Curiously the post office was already closed when I went out. Couldn’t we align the post office’s schedule with the museum’s closure so that visitors can send their shipments after the visit?
Try to get an entrance ticket before 1pm. Without this you will not have time to go around. Once you’re launched to the Sistine Chapel, even if you want to shorten your visit, you won’t necessarily be able to do so given the world (and groups).

title: No good if you have mobility issues
text:
Pros:
Went with my mum with mobility issues. We managed to get lifts which was helpful 
Some great prices of art here we especially liked all the Egyptian artefacts 
The bistrot is lovely, not overpriced and not long to wait for a seat 

Cons:
Signage is not great, if you are looking for toilets lift etc it can be a trek to find .

Lifts often took you against the one way system which made it hard to navigate with the crowds. You could only use a lift if operated, no self service.

Lifts somewhere nowhere near attraction. My mum wanted to visit the Sistine chapel but it was a good 10 mins walk from where the lift dropped you off. No good 

The Sistine chapel, kept being badgered to move by rude staff when I was trying to look at the ceiling ( not near a doorway). It was far too busy . Maybe they need to lower the number of tickets allowed in a day and not be so greedy for money.

Overall, there is some artifacts were amazing and some staff were lovely but some staff were rude and maybe they should explain no access to areas like Sistine chapel if have mobility issues.

title: St. Peter's Basilica /Vatican City, Italy
text:
The Papal Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican (Italian: Basilica Papale di San Pietro in Vaticano), or simply Saint Peter's Basilica (Latin: Basilica Sancti Petri; Italian: Basilica di San Pietro, is a church of the Italian High Renaissance located in Vatican City, an independent microstate enclaved within the city of Rome, Italy. It was initially planned in the 15th century by Pope Nicholas V and then Pope Julius II to replace the ageing Old St. Peter's Basilica, which was built in the fourth century by Roman emperor Constantine the Great. Construction of the present basilica began on 18 April 1506 and was completed on 18 November 1626.

Designed principally by architects Donato Bramante, Carlo Maderno and all round genius Michelangelo, with piazza and fittings by sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini, St. Peter's is one of the most renowned works of Italian Renaissance architecture and is the largest church in the world by interior measure.

While it is neither the mother church of the Catholic Church nor the cathedral of the Diocese of Rome (these equivalent titles being held by the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran in Rome), St. Peter's is regarded as one of the holiest Catholic shrines. It has been described as "holding a unique position in the Christian world",and as "the greatest of all churches of Christendom.

Catholic tradition holds that the basilica is the burial site of Saint Peter, chief among Jesus's apostles and also the first Bishop of Rome (Pope). Saint Peter's tomb is directly below the high altar of the basilica, also known as the Altar of the Confession.
For this reason, many popes, cardinals and bishops have been interred at St. Peter's since the Early Christian period.

St. Peter's is famous as a place of pilgrimage and for its liturgical functions. The pope presides at a number of liturgies throughout the year both within the basilica or the adjoining St. Peter's Square; these liturgies draw audiences numbering from 15,000 to over 80,000 people.

St. Peter's has many historical associations, with the early Christian Church, the Papacy, the Protestant Reformation and Catholic Counter-Reformation and numerous artists, especially Michelangelo. As a work of architecture, it is regarded as the greatest building of its age.

St. Peter's is one of the four churches in the world that hold the rank of Major papal basilica, all four of which are in Rome, and is also one of the Seven Pilgrim Churches of Rome. Contrary to popular misconception, it is not a cathedral because it is not the seat of a bishop; the cathedral of the pope as bishop of Rome is at the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran.

Entrance is absolutely free and my humble advise would be to not join a tour but go very early (service hours starting from 7:00am until 6:30pm) in the morning to avoid crowds ( lines during peak season can easily take 2 hrs and more to get in) and just get inspired but this extraordinary, magnificent building.

title: The grandest collection of art that you've ever seen
text: The Vatican Museums not only house the extensive collections of art, archaeology and ethno-anthropology amassed by Popes from the 17th century onwards, they also contain some of the Apostolic Palace's most extraordinary and artistically significant rooms. It is awe-inspiring to view artwork by such masters as Michelangelo, Da Vinci, Raphael, Caravaggio, van Gogh, Chagall, Bacon, Carra, Matisse and Reni. Today, the collection of Modern and Contemporary and Renaissance art consists of 8,000 works. The most famous artwork is the Sistine Chapel ceiling, The Last Judgement, St. Matthew, Liberation of Saint Peter, The Annunciation, Transfiguration, St. Jerome, The Victory of Christianity Over Paganism, The Colossal Statue of Augustus, The Statue of Hercules in Bronze, The Crowning of the Virgin, Artemis of Ephesus, Augustus of Prima Porta. But, as our knowledgeable guide is eager to point out, any history of the museums' collections should begin with the history of the rooms that the Popes over the centuries chose as places of residence or private prayer and reflection. Most important are the Niccoline Chapel and the Borgia Apartment. The Noccoline Chapel, which was built between 1447 and 1449, is one of the great works of 15th century Italy and is probably the peak of what may be defined as Florentine painter Fra Angelico's "Christian humanism." The Borgia Apartment, built between 1277 and 1280, with six monumental spaces, was transformed into artistic greatness in 1494 by Pinturicchio's stunning cycle of frescoes decorating the various interconnecting rooms. The Vatican Museums are open to the public from 8 to 8 Monday through Saturday. Allow at least three or four hours to see as much as you can.

title: Caveat emptor!
text: Where do I start? We had "skip the line" tickets with a guided tour for 7:45 a.m. This does not mean that there is no line - you will be in a horde of people at the entrance who also have "skipped the line." They give tour guides priority to enter, but there are countless guides with groups of people following them. The mob does not ease once you have passed through two ticket checks and picked up your audio headset. With thousands of people you are herded through miles of long, hot corridors, everyone inching along towards the prize of the Sistine Chapel. Our guide, to her credit, tried to point out and describe certain artworks, but the art you are passing is almost impossible to see due to the incredible press of people. There are signs for the Sistine Chapel along the route, but it takes two hours to get there. Despair begins to set in! Everyone's faces were bathed in sweat and showing signs of misery. There is no air conditioning. There is scarcely any air moving in from the occasional open window. I think it is quite a dangerous situation, to have so many people packed into this space with little egress - a disaster waiting to happen, God forbid. It is not an educational or uplifting experience - it is an endurance contest. I wound up getting separated from my group once we (finally!) made it to the Sistine Chapel. The route back was much less crowded, as most people seem to go on to St. Peter's Basilica right from the Chapel. I recommend skipping the Sistine Chapel if you really want to look at the amazing art collections in the museum, and find galleries away from the corridor that leads to the chapel. Once I found my way out of the museum (and past the requisite gift shops), I enjoyed sitting in the beautiful gardens, which were pretty much deserted.

title: What a marvel!
text:
Photos don't do this justice - you really need to see this site in person to appreciate its majesty! Even though, of course, it's been thousands of years since its heyday, you can really imagine this being a hub for ancient Rome. In particular, the temple in dedication to Faustina is stunning. We only did a tour for the Colosseum but one wouldn't have gone amiss here either - we like our own pace but there's so much here that you won't want to miss. 

Tip: We did the Forum alongside the Colosseum and the Palatine Hill, recommended as not only is it in the same area but it's likely if you pre-book you'll get all three at once. However you'll need a pretty good level of fitness to do this big trip and some decent ankle-supporting boots with a good grip (not fashionable perhaps, but let the history be your Instagram post). There's a lot of stairs, and if you're lucky enough to get some rain during your visit, it can get slippery.

title: Amazing place to visit.
text:
A visit to the Vatican Museums and the awe-inspiring Sistine Chapel is an absolute highlight of any trip to Rome, though it requires some strategic planning to make the most of it.
First and foremost, heed this advice: avoid peak times of day at all costs! The Vatican Museums are among the most visited in the world, and they can get incredibly crowded. We saw queues stretching for what looked like two hours for those without pre-booked tickets, so trust me when I say, book your tickets in advance!
For the best experience, I highly recommend booking a guided tour directly on the official Vatican Museums website (museivaticani.va). This provides fantastic value and ensures you're with a knowledgeable, well-organized group. Our guide brought the immense history to life, navigating us through the vast collections and offering insights we would have undoubtedly missed on our own. It made the experience far more enriching.
The sheer amount of history and art contained within these walls is mind-boggling. From ancient Roman and Egyptian artifacts to Renaissance masterpieces, every corner holds a treasure. We spent nearly three hours exploring, and honestly, it still wasn't enough to fully absorb everything. Be prepared for a lot of walking, and note that there are lots of stairs, so be mindful if you have mobility issues.
The crescendo of the visit is, of course, the Sistine Chapel. The artistry of Michelangelo's frescoes is truly breathtaking, a masterpiece that demands quiet contemplation. However, it was disheartening to see that despite the signs and repeated announcements, the rule of silence was largely ignored by many visitors. It's also important to remember that no pictures are allowed in the Sistine Chapel, a rule strictly enforced to preserve the artworks and the reverent atmosphere.
On a practical note, the facilities within the museums are good, with a couple of cafes serving food. These are a welcome respite, offering a chance to refuel and rest your feet amidst the extensive walking.

title: Overcrowded but Totally Worth it! Take an Exclusive Guided Tour!
text:
My uncle & I visited Rome for the first time in May 2025 and we took a guided tour of St. Peter's Basilica, the Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel.

The Vatican Museums started in 1506 and today, they consist of 54 museums that display the immense collection of art and artifacts amassed by the Catholic Church and the Papacy throughout the centuries. You have to walk through 17km of corridors, hallways, passageways and staircases to see all the exhibits in the 54 museums! In 2024, the Vatican Museums received over 6.8 million visitors. In 2025, an average of 35,000 people visit this place each day, making the Vatican Museums the 2nd most popular museum complex in the world, after the Louvre in Paris. First-time visitors usually get lost in this enormous place if they do not take a guided tour, and they will miss seeing the top attractions here!

The 10 must-see attractions in the Vatican Museums are:
1) The Sistine Chapel
2) Raphael Rooms
3) The Gallery of Maps
4) The Pinacoteca
5) The Pio Clementino Museum
6) The Gregorian Egyptian Museum
7) The Carriage Pavilion
8) The Ethnological Museum
9) The Pieta Sculpture by Michelangelo
10) The Bramante Staircase

My uncle and I saw all these attractions thanks to our awesome guide, without wasting any time wandering around. The corridors and passageways of the Vatican Museums are always very crowded. The Sistine Chapel is the last hall in the Vatican Museums and in the daytime, it is constantly SERIOUSLY OVERCROWDED! There are usually around 10,000 visitors inside the Sistine Chapel at any time during normal operating hours. We had great difficulty getting to the exit on the other side of the hall, we had to literally push our way through the crowd! Prepare to be squashed like sardines in a can inside the Sistine Chapel! Photography & Videography ARE STRICTLY PROHIBITED inside the Sistine Chapel. Visitors and tour guides are NOT ALLOWED TO TALK inside the Sistine Chapel!

Since we couldn't enjoy the Sistine Chapel on the first visit with that enormous crowd, we returned to the Vatican Museums on the 2nd day and took an exclusive after-hours guided tour of the Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel. This 2nd tour was very expensive BUT TOTALLY WORTH EVERY PENNY!!! There were 20 guests with 1 tour guide for this night time guided tour and we were accompanied throughout the tour by a museum security guard. We had the entire museum complex to ourselves! When we arrived in the Sistine Chapel, we were the only ones there! WE HAD THE ENTIRE SISTINE CHAPEL TO OURSELVES!!!!!! We spent around 45 minutes inside the Chapel while our guide explained the meaning of each and every detail of Michelangelo's paintings on the ceiling and the walls of the Sistine Chapel, especially the Last Judgement. This exclusive tour was the highlight of our vacation in Rome!!!

title: Sistine Chapel is worth what you have to go through to get there
text: There is one reason to go to the Vatican Museums and it is called the Sistine Chapel. If you are looking for a comprehensive collection of world art and culture, you are better off going to the Met, the Louvre or the British Museum. This collection skews conservative, and as you might expect ecclesiastical, which is the Vatican's brand. Nonetheless, there is there is an overwhelming sense of materiality in this space built on ideas of immortality and spirituality. The ancient sculpture, which popes seemed to have loved to collect, includes 'Laocoon and His Sons.' In person it is clear why this sculpture was so influential for Renaissance sculptors. But the reason you and everyone else is here is to see the Sistine Chapel. For that reason it feels a bit like a cross between a museum and an IKEA, in that regardless of the direction you first take,  you are put on a fairly controlled path that ends with this masterpiece. There are many interesting diversions along the way and like everyone says, go early, buy a timed ticket online in advance and the crowds will be much less severe than later in the day. The path towards  the chapel is interesting as it gets narrower and the ceilings get lower, going through a contemporary collection (that seems to lack any major works) until you are in what appears to be a back hallway (with marble stair treads of course.) Since we were there early this was a reasonably easy walk, but I can imagine that it is designed to control and hold a long line. At the end of the stairway there is a reasonably plain doorway that you walk through and suddenly you are in one of the most incredible spaces in the world. It is transformative and the sense of space cannot be described or photographed adequately. It has to be experienced. The Vatican admin wisely does not allow talking above a whisper or photographs, so the tour groups with flags on sticks and the selfie posing that clogs the rest of Rome completely drops away. It is just you and this immersive experience of color, dimension and movement from the early 1500's.

title: What's the point?
text:
I would love to say I enjoyed my time sat the Vatican museums, but the truth is it was really just one big hassle. The museum is basically a very long, narrow hallway, lined with exhibits on both sides with an ornate ceiling above. Problem is, it’s a solid mass of people and, unless you happen to be walking on one of the sides, all you can see is the ceiling. They tell you to keep moving, so even if you happen to be on one side to where you can see something, you’re being bum rushed through so fast that you don’t have time to take it all in, so it becomes meaningless. And don’t even think about moving to the other side to see what’s over there….it’s impossible to get through the solid mass of humanity. Yes, the ceiling is beautiful, but you really have no time to stop and look at the detail. 

The Sistine Chapel? Another exercise in futility. It’s super crowded and poorly lit with limited seating. All that certainly takes away from the awesomeness of the place. Yes, the ceiling is pretty incredible; however, because the place is so dark it’s hard to really see it. I ended up having to buy a guide book afterwards just to see and learn about the place.

On top of the chaos most of the staff were downright rude. They were pushy, condescending, and obviously on a power trip. I get it…dealing with the public day in and day out can be exhausting, but it was their idea to apply for the job, not mine. 

In the end, my visit was more annoying than anything else.

title: Stunning! Time your visit and watch out for street hawkers.
text:
St Peter’s Basilica is stunning. It is definitely worth a visit, whether you have Christian faith or not, and anything else I say would spoil the visit!
I will say two practical things, though.
Firstly, timing your visit is important, unless you don’t mind queuing for 2 hours or more. The day we went, there was a Papal audience in the morning, and so the public weren’t allowed into the square until shortly after 12 noon. This meant that we waited for about 30 minutes in a non-moving queue before anyone was allowed in.
Once we were allowed in, prepare for a mad scramble! Everyone headed straight for the entrance to the queue for the Basilica, and it was a slightly scary crush of people trying to get through a pretty narrow entrance. Be brave and make sure your group sticks together! (Relatively easy for us, being only 3 of us). Helps to enter the square at the Via di Porta Angelica entrance - the closest entrance to where the queue begins. Once you join the queue, you’re waiting to go through security scanners, and then you can explore the Basilica at leisure. We realised how well we’d timed it when we came out about 45 minutes later to see the entrance queue literally stretching around the whole square.
The second thing to be aware of (and this is true at any major tourist areas) is the aggressive nature of the street hawkers. They are very persistent, and use the tactics of literally putting something into your hand or on your wrist, saying it’s “free” but then demanding money from you. Be very firm in refusing - we’ve learnt to note where they are and steer clear of them, and if that’s impossible, avoid eye contact and keep hands in pockets. You find them everywhere, but they are especially prevalent in St Peter’s Square. Keep alert!

title: The Papal Basilica in Vatican City
text:
This is one of the four Papal Basilica's around Rome. St. Peter's forms part of the Vatican complex and residence for the Pope and as such is probably the most important church in the Catholic World today. It is also an immensely popular place to visit, meaning queues to enter can be quite long. Thus planning your day of sightseeing around St. Peter's can be wise. Opening hours are 7am to 7pm daily. 

St. Peter's Basilica was built between 1506 and 1626 and was graced by the hands and minds of Italy's finest architects during those times including Bramante, Michelangelo, Carlo Maderno and Bernini amongst others. It is both a Renaissance and Baroque masterpiece of enormous scale including the massive dome which can be seen from various vantage points throughout Rome. 

There are many highlights, far too many to mention all. The exterior facade is worth spending time to enjoy. The interior includes masterpiece mosaic artworks and sculptures including Michelangelo's Pietra, Bernini's tombs of Pope Urban VIII and Pope Alexander  VII, Baldacchino, the ancient  St. Peter Enthroned monument. You can learn about the various monuments within St. Peter's on the church website. 

The St. Peter's website is also the place to pick up information about various mass services, Papal audience attendance as well as information related to the upcoming 2025 Jubilee year which will see the Holy Door opened for the first time in 25 years a part of the Jubilee celebrations.

title: Two motives: to look from above inside the cathedral and to look around the cathedral.
text: Dome of the Cathedral of St. Petra is a hotel attraction. Its height is 119 meters with a diameter of 42 meters. Almost perfect proportions 1:3. The construction of the dome is associated with the name of Michelangelo, whose construction leadership of the cathedral is associated with its construction. However, despite a long creative life, only a drum was erected under the genius of the Renaissance. The dome was completed by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana. The dome itself was erected in 22 months by 800 workers, commissioning it in 1590. But covering 3,000 square meters of the dome area with mosaics took 15 years. There is a fee to climb the dome. As often happens when climbing different towers, there are 2 ways: on your own for 8 euros and by elevator for 10. However, lovers of comfort should not delude themselves: the budget method is 550 steps, and the elevator does not eliminate the need to climb 320. However, you must stand in line. Little difference. The ascent is in some places along very narrow stairs, so the recommendation to refrain from climbing for those suffering from claustrophobia is not abstract. There are 2 reasons for going up to the dome: to look inside the cathedral at the main altar from above and to look around the cathedral. title: A great cathedral created by great artists...
text: It is paradoxical, but it is a fact that for all its greatness, the Cathedral of St. Peter's is neither the cathedral church of the Diocese of Rome nor the main basilica of the Catholic world. This status is reserved for San Giovanni in Laterano. However, so many celebrities worked on the construction of St. Peter's Cathedral that in the eyes of the rest of the world, nothing was and is not more important than San Pietro. In addition, in terms of area (total 21 thousand square meters, useful 15 thousand) the Cathedral of St. Petra is in first place in the world. The significance of the cathedral was also in the fact that it was built on the site of a basilica, built on the site of the supposed burial of the remains of St. Peter, the founder of the Catholic Church, who suffered martyrdom in the circus of Nero in 66. And the church was built in 326 under Emperor Constantine. Distance - 260 years! Mozart died in 1791, from which we are separated by 233 years, and we have no chance now, with all our methods, of finding in which mass grave in Vienna the great composer was buried. But in Christianity there is such a concept as a “miracle”, which can explain everything that is inaccessible to logic... In general, by the era of the early Renaissance, the Basilica of St. Petra became very dilapidated, and Pope Nicholas V raised the question of its replacement, or reconstruction. This dilemma became the main one for subsequent architects. Although attempts to fit the old church into the new cathedral, as a rule, always ended badly (see the story about St. Isaac's Cathedral in St. Petersburg). The decision to build a new cathedral was made by Pope Julius II. In 1506, he appointed Bramante as chief architect with the idea of giving San Pietro the shape of a Greek cross. Subsequently, Raphael, Sangallo, Peruzzi, Michelangelo, Bernini and Maderna were architects. Each of them contributed something to the cathedral, but the contribution of Michelangelo and Bernini was especially great. Michelangelo proposed a dome, solving the problem of how many there should be (Fra Giovanni Giocondo proposed five, like the Venetian San Marco). At the age of 25, he created a magnificent Pieta, which was later placed in the cathedral. This is the only sculpture in the cathedral behind armored glass, after in 1972 a madman, shouting “I am Jesus Christ,” cut off the Virgin Mary’s nose and fingers with a hammer. Bernini's contribution is no less extensive. Firstly, it was he who came up with the famous semicircular colonnade, without which the world cannot imagine either the cathedral or Piazza San Pietro. The best way to appreciate it is from above, going up to the dome. Bernini created the altar of the cathedral, inventing the pulpit of St. Petra with his supposedly chair. The huge canopy above the altar is also his work. Not everyone likes him for his pomp. Well, and finally, the tomb of Pope Alexander VII is also the work of the great Bernini. The Pope turned out so-so, but the statues of Truth, Mercy, Prudence and Justice are magnificent and erotic. Bernini is also the author of the tomb of Urban VIII. However, just tourists like me and believers have different preferences. Catholics especially prize a bronze statue of a seated Apostle Peter, probably from the 13th century, by Arnolfo di Cambio. His right foot has been licked for centuries to a shine. However, the first thing a tourist sees is the façade of the cathedral, which was completed in 1614 by Carlo Maderna. He placed an attic on massive columns, which is decorated with 13 sculptures. There are five gates in the columns of the portico: the Gate of Death, Good and Evil, Philaret and the Gate of the Sacraments and the Holy Gate. The latest ones, Porta Santa, open once every 25 years. Those who pass through them are freed from all sins. They last opened in 2016. So next time in 2041... Through the Gates of Death, the Vatican sends the deceased pontiffs on their last journey. True, Benedict XVI broke the centuries-old tradition of dying in office and resigned “before”... In addition to examining the interior, it is necessary to climb to the dome of the cathedral. From there you can see not only the splendor of Piazza San Pietro with Via Concellazione, built under Mussolini, but also Bernini's altar. You can take the elevator or the stairs for a couple of euros cheaper. But it’s not about the money, it’s about maintaining tone, isn’t it? For those who don’t have enough of this, you can also visit the necropolis of the cathedral, but I’m not a fan of such things, and even there you need a reservation.

title: A walk through history.
text:
Entering the Forum is like stepping through a time portal. The history is extraordinary, and the ruins hint at how impressive this area was 2,000 years ago. We spent about an hour wandering the site on our own, which was enough time (especially for our teenagers), although it would be easy to spend more time. 

TIP - Watch out for private “tour guides” offering you tickets outside the Forum, especially near the Colosseum. Some will even approach you as you wait in line at the ticket office (which sits between the Forum and the Colosseum). If you can plan ahead, it’s best to buy your tickets online from the official website (for the Parco Archeologico del Colosseo). If you are looking for tickets on the spot, start with the official ticket office, where tickets are least expensive. If they are sold out, a private tour guide may be able to get you in on a tour, but it will be much more expensive.

title: Il cuore della città romana
text: E' la vasta area archeologica che si estende sotto al Palatino, dal Campidoglio al Colosseo, alla dx di via dei Fori Imperiali (andando da piazza Venezia verso il Colosseo), tranne la prima parte a ridosso della citata via che è il foro di Cesare, il primo dei fori imperiali. D'altra parte è difficile separare il foro romano (repubblicano) dai fori imperiali, che vennero creati dai diversi imperatori per allargare il perimetro originario del foro repubblicano, non più sufficiente all'aumentata crescita dell'Urbe. In età imperiale, pertanto, il foro occupava tutta l'area della depressione posta tra il Campidoglio, il Palatino e l'Esquilino. Con la costruzione della via dei Fori Imperiali, che passa sopra parte delle rovine antiche, si è creata una divisione artificiale tra i fori imperiali (sulla sx venendo da p.za Venezia) e il foro romano (sulla dx), con l'eccezione del citato foro di Cesare. Girando per Roma in tutti i quartieri centrali sopravvivono rovine e resti, talvolta maestosi (cito per tutti il Pantheon), dell'antica Roma, ma in questa area, alle pendici dei menzionati tre colli, vi è la maggiore concentrazione delle antiche vestigia (minimamente interessata da sovrapposizioni successive, per lo più solo alcune chiese): dal fori al Colosseo, all'arco di Costantino e alle ville imperiali del Palatino, che dal versante opposto al foro, scende verso la grande arena del Circo Massimo. A parte gli archi di trionfo (di Settimio Severo e di Tito), quasi nessun altro edificio/tempio del foro è giunto a noi in modo integro, ma la distesa delle rovine, con alle spalle il Tabularium sul Capidoglio, la collina del Palatino che si erge dritta sulla dx, sopra i resti del palazzo di Tiberio e di fronte la grande mole del Colosseo, è uno spettacolo meraviglioso; ci sono vari punti per osservare questa distesa, anche da alcune parti sopraelevate all'interno del foro stesso, ma i posti migliori sono le terrazze panoramiche nei pressi del Campidoglio e quelle del Palatino negli Orti Farnesiani. Passeggiando per le vie del foro, per lo più sui basolati originari, passando tra le antiche e imponenti rovine, non si può non essere suggestionati sapendo che qui una volta era il cuore della città "caput mundi", il centro della vita politica, giudiziaria, commerciale e religiosa di una metropoli di un milione di abitanti. Qui vi erano gli incontri pubblici e le parate, vi si riuniva il Senato, si dibattevano le questioni giudiziarie, si riscuotevano le tasse e si svolgevano gli incontri d'affari, vi erano alcuni dei principali templi e la casa delle vestali, e poi botteghe/bancarelle tutte intorno. Bisogna fare uno sforzo di fantasia per trasformare le rovine in edifici e templi scintillanti di preziosi marmi policromi, decorati con fregi e statue, e le strade/piazze affollate da una variegata e multiforme umanità: avvocati e magistrati, politici, tribuni, sacerdoti, funzionari, filosofi e uomini di lettere, ma anche commercianti, gente comune, vagabondi e questuanti. Per visitare il foro romano esiste un unico biglietto cumulativo con i fori imperiali e il Palatino, acquistabile solo on line, che al momento costa 16 euro, con l'aggiunta di 2 euro per i diritti di prenotazione (il prezzo aumenta se nella visita, mantenendo la possibilità di vedere anche i siti super del foro e del Palatino, si vuole aggiungere anche l'entrata al Colosseo). Certo il prezzo non è modico, ma è sicuramente più che adeguato a quello che si va a visitare. Si può inoltre approfittare delle domeniche ad ingresso gratuito (le prime domeniche del mese), ma in tal caso sappiate che restano chiusi i siti super come, ad esempio, per il foro romano, la Curia Julia, la Rampa di Domiziano e la chiesa di Santa Maria Antiqua (il tempio di Romolo è invece chiuso tutti i giorni per manutenzione: si può vederne l'interno dalla basilica dei SS.Cosma e Damiano, con entrata da via dei Fori Imperiali, ma in ogni caso non si riescono a vedere le decorazioni parietali, che però non sono del periodo romano, bensì pitture medievali). Sempre con riferimento alle domeniche gratuite, se non siete interessati a vedere anche il Colosseo, consiglio di accedere dalla Colonna Traiana, con visita dei fori imperiali, del foro romano e del Palatino, tutti tra loro collegati, in quanto qui non c'è fila; per vedere invece anche il Colosseo, il biglietto gratuito va ritirato per forza ai box in piazza del Colosseo, dove si forma una bella fila fin dalle prime ore della mattina, fila che diventa quasi chilometrica già a metà mattina.

Don't be discouraged by the endless queue, the cost (10 euros for the lift) or the hundreds of steps that, despite the lift, you still have to climb. The climb is not suitable for everyone, some passages are narrow and the spiral staircase with the only handhold, a bell rope, was a cult moment! However, it is priceless to see the interior of St. Peter's from the top of the dome, close to the mosaics, but above all, once you reach the outside... words are not needed. The images are enough!
However, better organization would be a must: online tickets are currently not available and, if you too happen to have a single ticket operator,... equip yourself with lots and lots of patience!

title: A must-see in Rome

Saint Peter's Basilica is one of the jewels of Rome, it is a must! Everything about the basilica is stunning and leaves you speechless. You feel small inside and out because the architecture is breathtaking.
All in the basilica is full of history, in every part of it a story is told. Between the architecture, the gilding, the moldings, the mosaics and the paintings you won't know where to turn, the place is so majestic.
Also remember before leaving the basilica to climb into the dome.
A good 551 steps, but don't panic for the lazy, there is an elevator.
The exterior view offered by the dome is exceptional. You have a 360° view of Rome and these main monuments.

We recommend visiting the Vatican (with the Sistine Chapel of course) before visiting the Basilica because and taking "skip the line" tickets because this allows you to enter without waiting and under the sun we know that that can be quickly exhausting.

title: Visiting The Roman Forum?  Don't Overlook This.
text:
What can I say that countless others have not already said. One thing springs to mind. If you visit the Roman Forum be sure to take time to visit the new museum that has opened not far from the Arch of Titus and is housed in Santa Francesca Romana--Museo del Foro.

The museum's holdings go hand in hand with the wonderfully uplifting account and archival records of the archaeologist Giacomo Boni to whom all of us, who visit the Forum and marvel at its structures and are humbled by the intelligence and tenacity of humanity evidenced by the ancient Romans, owe a huge debt of gratitude and a place in our hearts and minds. There is a short film about his excavations, using still photos from the end of the 19th century and early years of the 20th century and quotes from the man himself.

title: Beware of long queues and scammers outside!
text:
Possibly one of the best museums in the world, however! This is also a detriment as it is absolutely packed at most times of the day. Definitely visit off season! You will be moving in a continuous queue all the way through the museum towards the Sistine chapel, and once you get to the Sistine chapel you will be herded out before you get to take in the art. Not a good experience. Most tourists also do not treat the place with the proper respect it is owed. Loud talking etc.

The line is very long to get into the museum if you don’t buy a ticket beforehand. And there are scammers who pretend to be museum staff who will try to lure you away from the queue. title: Beautiful artwork overshadowed by criminally negligent overcrowding
text:
I had originally purchased tickets for a 7:30 am entrance but was unwell on the morning of my ticket, which promised entry and breakfast before the crowds arrived, so I had to cancel. I rebooked for the next day for Happy Hour which included drinks and snacks and please believe me when I say that was the highlight of the evening. 

We dutifully followed the signs to the chapel and it felt like we were walking forever to get there. When we finally arrived in the room there were hundreds, and I mean hundreds of other people in the room, and over their hushed exclamations of wonder there were Vatican employees  bellowing “No Photos” “No talking”   The chapel was very warm and stuffy due to the number of people in the room - I felt faint. 

It took well over five minutes of shuffling - not possible to take normal steps due to the crowding -  to funnel out of the room through a REGULAR-SIZED doorway, (a doorway which was nowhere near as wide as necessary for such a crowd) into a regular-sized hallway, which was not even as wide as a school hallway which might have hundreds of students moving freely while going from classroom to classroom.. Had there been a fire, the crushing deaths would have been catastrophic.  People using wheelchairs were completely surrounded by other people trying to leave. Getting out was like going through a labyrinth. 

The Catholic Church is wealthy, almost indecently so, and Vatican City itself is wealthy - they have sources of income other than tourists.  There was no need to cram as many people as possible into that space. I understand crowd theory and I know that even peaceful crowds like this can become volatile if a panic starts for any reason.  Moreover, the moisture from that many peoples’ breath in the room surely can’t be good for the artwork.  Other famous art galleries in Italy limit the number of people who can enter at any one time.

I believe that this overcrowding seriously exceeded the number of people who should legally  have been allowed to be in the space. It’s a catastrophe waiting to happen.  

My recommendation, if you aren’t satisfied with photos, is to book the 7:30 am breakfast and chapel ticket.  If you aren’t an early riser I seriously suggest that you don’t go - it isn’t worth the risk.

title: Amazing Art but poor experience
text: Call me naive - I normally research vacations well but this was below expectations. Firstly the Sistine Chapel is not part of the Basilica which is a seperate tour. The museum prior to the Sistine Chapel is enormous . It  holds many pieces of roman remains and a massive collection of religious art. I am sure that the artists are all reknowned but quite frankly after the first half hour of ressurection pictures I had had enough. As you move towards the Sistine Chapel the ceilings are amazing but this is spoilt by the increasing crowds. The tour guides block your way and make navigating the crowds impossible. They should have a seperate lane. Given that we are just coming out of Covid there was no thought for crowd control or mask wearing and given that I am not a regular mask wearer even I felt let down. Photographs are permitted throughout the museum but the minute you enter the chapel they are not. There must have been 500-600 people crammed in - the tours take over the central section and everyone else is herded around the edge. The chapel does not have a chapel/sacred feel about it and the staff are constantly shouting "silencio" . Not very silent. There are plenty of churches in Rome with equally stunning murals , apologies to Michaelangelo, but it would have been more pleasant to roam Rome ( excuse the pun) and explore than be crammed into a Vatican Disney. No doubt others will disagree.

title: An awfully long (and needless?!) walk
text:
The Vatican has now totally rearranged everything since we came many years ago. At this point, the only way to see the Sistine Chapel is to walk about 100 miles, the entire length of the Vatican Museums, and back again. The physical location of the chapel is literally through the wall from St Peter's Basilica, but no, you can't do anything as obvious as have a door - that would be too easy. Also, there is nowhere to sit down until you get very near the Sistine (Sala Matisse), and nowhere on the slog back. A drink of water? Nah...

To start with, Apple phone maps didn't give us good directions, which led us up the Viale Vaticano, instead of down, which was a bad start in very hot weather. Inside, the layout must be easy, once you already know it, but the map they hand out is not particularly clear as to where you are at the beginning, or what's the "sense of the visit" as it is usually described. It seems as though there are elevators, but they are only for the handicapped. 

Once you do get to the Sistine Chapel, it is bereft of any pews, or other appurtenances of an actual chapel. For some reason it is announced by loudspeaker every two minutes or less that no photos or videos are allowed. In general, although there is a brief blessing offered every twenty minutes or so, it feels more like a tourist attraction than one of the Holy of Holies. 

This is not to say that you should deprive yourself of the opportunity to see the Chapel, and the Raphael rooms (which would equally be very accessible from the basilica, instead of only at the end of a long hike through way less interesting exhibits). I suppose an imposed Calvary is the price of seeing the chapel; only rarely do I wish I were 21 again, but this was one time.

title: Majesty Lost in the Madness!
text:
When in Rome... you have to see the Vatican. The art is breathtaking, the history overwhelming—it’s truly one of the world’s great treasures. But sadly, our experience was not a pleasant one.

The entry queues were chaotic and exhausting. Once inside, we were funneled through a one-way system, crammed shoulder-to-shoulder with hundreds of others. Over four miles of passageways, jostled and bumped along, with little chance to pause and take in what we were seeing.

By the time we reached the Sistine Chapel, it was packed beyond belief. There was no room to stop, no quiet moment to absorb the beauty. We were inside for less than a minute before being shuffled through a small exit—herded like cattle.

It left me feeling disappointed and sad. Such profound art deserves reverence, not rush.

title: My Top Ten Tips
text:
What can I add to an incredible place that has over 24,693 reviews?  Here’s my starter for 10….

1.  Book a Tour.  Trying to gain entry on the day lead to disappointment.  Or be very expensive.

2.  Book your tour early to get what you want.  There is a mind-blowing choice of options, so take the time to research what’s on offer.

3.  If you can afford it, book onto a tour with small numbers.  We booked a guaranteed ‘Six Places’ through Livtours (highly recommended, and reviewed separately), combined into a Colosseum tour.  Less time in queues and a much more personal than following the herd of a larger tour group.

4.  Don’t forget your photo ID.  That can lead to serious disappointment.

5.  And try to pack light, lots of airport style security on entry, plus it’s no fun resembling a Himalayan Sherpa

6.  In summer, it can get really hot.  It even hit 34 degrees Celsius on the day of our visit, early September.  Sun cream and a hat.

7.  And a water bottle.  You can refill at several recharging points inside.

8.  Try to do a bit of reading on the Forum before visiting, I think that by doing this you will appreciate so much more from your visit.

9.  And outside, be mindful of pickpockets.  They don’t always look like the stereotypical street urchins either.  Be wary of the beautiful people, working in pairs, designer clothes and immaculate make-up.  With labelled shopping bags, empty until they become useful cover for newly acquired wallets, phones and sun glasses!

10.  It can all be a little overwhelming, so take your time.  After our tour had finished, we took a snack-break in the (surprisingly good-value) café before reappearing to revisit some of the sites and walk around Palatine Hills area.

Had a dreadful visit to the Vatican yesterday.  Had bought tickets and guided tour pre booked .  Took 45 mins to get in so we missed our slot.  Had to protest to get next available tour.  So after 2 hrs of queuing and waiting time we finally started our tour.  We then were corralled into over crowded corridors managed by surly guards.  Several times we were blocked from going down normal tour routes due to over crowding, and then had to climb and descend several flights of stairs on detour .
No time to stop or really look at anything and the whole time was being pushed and shoved by others .  Found the whole experience deeply unpleasant and ultimately felt unsafe as many of the doors were single file only and crowds of people pushing to get through them.  Definite fire hazard. Was told by guide that there were probably 25 thousand people  there that day.
Scitine chapel also packed with one tiny door to exit and guides are not allowed in there to discuss images so had to remember what she had said 2 hrs before.
Couldn’t wait to get out of there and exit also took unnecessary long route as we had to move through 5 gift shops along the way.  Experience has done nothing to restore any faith in Catholic Church.  Just felt the whole this is a money making exercise and I felt that ultimately exhibits could get damaged  with so little space to move around.

title: Marvel at everything… but get a tour guide!
text:
Art. Art. Art. And more art. Literally, everywhere you look, there is art all over the Vatican. Incredible place to visit, though I cannot urge you enough to book/reserve your ticket in ADVANCE. A lot of advice I’d read about visiting the Vatican said to book an early time slot and had referenced that it would always likely be crowded. This year, 2025, is a jubilee year and at present, the Pope is ill, so I thought we would run into huge crowds. In actuality, Rome did not seem any more crowded than any other major capital city I’ve been in, though we have come during the ‘shoulder season’ rather than high season.

Still, it was worth it to book tickets to the Vatican in advance. We booked an 8am tour through the Vatican museum website directly (which I highly recommend doing), and were advised to arrive 30 minutes in advance of entry. So, at 7:30am, we got there, and there was already a line forming for those who had not booked a ticket in advance. They were only just setting up 3 separate lines for those who had booked in advance (which was indicated on our entry ticket which one to stand in), and we wound up first in our designated line. I’m unsure what the first line was for (maybe just those who booked entry tickets?), but ours seemed to be for those of us who’d booked tours with the Vatican staff directly, and the third was for third-party tours. As such, both of the other lines still had to line up further after they initially passed the staff, and our line was released to walk directly into the Vatican Museums. 

Our tour guide was Santi, an extremely knowledgeable guide who was also extremely funny. He expertly navigated us through crowds, explained the Sistine Chapel and what to look for in advance of entering the Chapel since it was at the end of the tour. Then, he took us through the museum on a whistle stop tour of the major works of art and statues held inside of the museum. It is a truly breathtaking amount of art and it can become easily overwhelming to try to view and understand the significance of the works held there, but with Santi directing our path, we were able to efficiently view the most important and compelling portions without getting too overwhelmed. We especially enjoyed seeing the Basilica from the terrace, the outdoor courtyard with varying statues of antiquity (the snakes winding around a Trojan man whose face was twisted in agony was memorable, as was the one with Perseus with the severed head of Medusa), and Nero’s wife’s enormous marble bath! We were also taken through the Raphael rooms and marveled at the stunning color of his paintings, and ultimately finished in the Sistine Chapel where we were in awe of Michaelangelo’s most famous work.

It’s well worth the visit, but heed the advice of the many travelers who’ve gone before — book for an early morning tour (it was getting crowded by the time we finished) and absolutely	100% book a tour guide to help you navigate through. Without one, you may be meandering aimlessly with no concept of what you’re viewing (unless you studied a lot in advance) and you can appreciate it more when you know more.

title: A splendid museum, but saturated with visitors...
text:
Before our stay in Rome, my girlfriend surprised me and offered me tickets to visit the Vatican Museum. It's not that I love this kind of thing, but it's always interesting to discover and learn.

We arrived 10-15 minutes early and came back in the process. But I'm full of people who didn't have reservations. The lines were quite long and chaotic...

We stayed approximately 3 hours to visit everything taking our time. It's a really nice museum. Rooms, paintings, sculptures... A lot of things are really beautiful and definitely worth a visit! 

If I had to make a point, it's because there are too many people for the visits. It's black people! It's impossible to visit without a minimum of stress. Not really time to savor the visit or take beautiful photos...

Sixteen Chapel? We were all packed in the center of the room, I didn't even know how to turn around without touching someone... The guards shouted every 2 seconds: "MOVE PLEASE" or "DON'T TAKE PHOTOS".

I also find the ticket price quite expensive (more than 30€) without the audio guide we also took to understand everything (the sound was clear and good quality). The different outlets to buy souvenirs and things like that were also overpriced.

In short, I still recommend doing it once. You just have to keep in mind it's probably gonna be black people!

title: Vatican Museums and st Peter's basilica - impressive
text:
It is definitely remarkable place and must visit site. We had to wait in a line before entering, but it totally worth it. 
The beginning of the exposition of the Museums was a little complicated for us - we did not understand at once where to start. But then followed the crow ;) and enjoyed the collection very much. 
The exposition is rich and impressive. I strongly advice not to "run through the rooms" just to "check" visit to Vatican. Take your time. There is a lot to see :) 
As about Sistine chapel - after all gold and bliss of Rome churches and tressures of the museum - at first sight it was not the most impressive part. But then you stand and look at the painting and the magic happens. You see the masterpiece. It is something unreal.
And st Peter's basilica - I have no words. It is so impressive, it is difficult to believe that people build it. 
We had been there in the beginning of February. There were quite a lot of people, but not overwhelming. We expected a lot of people, so the crowds did not spoil our visit.

title: Underwhelming?
text:
Years and years of art school, art history, pop culture, images, et cetera, have coddled me into thinking that this would be like some sort of life goal, to finally see the Sistine Chapel.

First of all, you're forced through an entire place and museum before you actually get to the chapel. And once you get to the chapel, it's kind of just there. And it feels smaller than I expected. 

The artistry is beautiful and is all over the walls (we have all seen pictures) but as for the experience of being there and seeing it in person... it left more to be desired. For me personally. 

Factors could have included the hot day, the overabundance of tourists, my weakened physical state from walking the past two weeks. I even had a seat along the side of the chapel but still felt like it was underwhelming.

Maybe a place with a reputation like this simply cannot live up to its own expectations. 

I will say definitely worth a visit if you're in Rome, but I think for me it was more of a checklist sort of thing. Images you'll find online far exceed the viewing experience once there.

title: Unique experience but organize your route well!
text:
Visiting the Vatican Museums is an unmissable experience for anyone passing through Rome. The amount of artwork is impressive: from Raphael’s frescoes to classical sculptures, to the magnificent Sistine Chapel, which alone is worth a visit.

However, you have to be prepared for two things: a lot of people and a very long journey. If you go at peak times, the tourist flow can make it difficult to fully enjoy the most famous rooms. I highly recommend booking tickets online: you pay an extra pre-sale fee (5€ per person) but it allows you to avoid the long queues at the entrance. We chose to make the visit in the late afternoon, and it was a good choice.

To appreciate them at best it takes at least 3-4 hours, but you could stay all day without seeing everything! Comfortable shoes and a little patience in the most crowded rooms are indispensable.

Overall, an amazing experience that I recommend to everyone, but with good planning!
