title: Highlights - Curia, Arch of Septimius Severus & Temple of Saturn
text:
The Roman Forum is a large, sprawling and often confusing archaeological site. I don’t think I’m alone in finding it confusing. For starters, there are several forums in the same general area. It can be hard to tell where one ends and one starts and what’s left is mainly in ruins. To get the most out of it, you need a guide or really good guidebook and map of the layout.
For the most part, what you see are isolated groups of columns, missing statues, patches of flagstones and discarded blocks of marble and stone.
However the Roman Forum was once the beating heart of ancient Rome and despite the passing centuries, there are still some fairly substantial structures here. 
The most impressive are the Curia (Senate House), the triumphal Arches of Septimius Severus and Titus, and the Temple of Saturn (see separate reviews). These are the better preserved buildings and structures and can clearly identify them. You can actually go inside the Curia, where you find remnants of the original marble flooring, some frescos, mosaics and relief fragments.
ENTRY: 
* It is worth noting that you cannot buy a separate entry to the forum. It is included in the combo Colosseum/Roman Forum ticket. You have two days to use the pass but it's essential to book ahead. 
* It is also possible to see quite a lot from the roadside, without buying a ticket, if you are walking up the to the Capitoline Museums

title: Some tips for your visit
text:
We bought tickets on the official site, we got a package that included audio guides and tickets to the Vatican museum and the Sistine Chapel. We visited St Peter’s Basilica on own own at around 9:30am with barely any crowds (last week of November) and then simply walked to the Vatican Museum. Had lunch at a cafe inside Vatican. Our tickets were for 1pm. Lines get a bit confusing at the entrance. There are lines for people with tickets and no tickets. Then those who have tickets, they split into lines of people who have guided tours with tickets and another line with just entrance tickets. These two lines form right at the main entrance, not along the long Vatican wall.
We were told to check in our backpack (standard size, not hiking, but eventually a guard let us take the backpack in 🤷🏼‍♀️)
We opted out of any guided tours and just followed Rick Steve’s Pocket Guide to Rome. To be honest, it was quite sufficient to us. We even barely listened to the audio guide as the museum has good signage with information. The only place where we did listen to the audio guide was the Sistine Chapel. 
There are a few gift shops inside, they all seem to carry different merchandise.

title: Art heaven. Tourist hell.
text:
This being the Vatican, perhaps it's appropriate that you'll be thinking a lot about God during your visit to the Vatican Museums. You'll be thinking "God, I can't believe how many people they've crammed in here," or maybe "God, that woman just elbowed me in the ribs/stepped on my foot/farted," or perhaps "God, why is this river of humanity not stopping?" Perhaps it's appropriate that you be thinking of Dante and his Inferno, because this is surely its sixth circle, and like Tantalus, you'll have exquisite artistic and architectural treasures dangled briefly in front of you as you're rushed past in the inexorable cattle chute designed to stuff you and thousands of others in the Sistine Chapel.

We booked "skip the line" tour with an official Vatican guide, first thing in the morning, as we'd been assured that this would also help us "skip the crowds." It didn't. We were met on the narrow piazza outside the entrance by a swirling mass of humanity, some being disgorged by a long queue of tour buses, others trying to buy tickets, and others, like us, just trying to find a way to skip the line as we'd been promised. We didn't get to skip the line altogether, but the one they told us to join moved quickly--we were inside in 15 minutes. Finding our guide was easy. She was the older woman who looked like she hated tourists and hated having to be awake at the crack of dawn to guide them through a giant, Renaissance-era petri dish. 
Her vivacity continued throughout the tour. She muttered something about Lacoon as we spent 30 seconds in front of one of the Classical world's most astonishing statues, mumbled about St. Helena's sarcophagus, wearily said something cursory and about the Hall of Maps (it was too crowded to see them anyway), and finally deposited us in the Sistine Chapel, with the usual warning not to take photos or talk. Truth is, once crammed into the chapel, you'd have to shout over the constant bellows of the guards reminding you not to disturb the sanctity of the place. 
So we left the Sistine Chapel after a few minutes. It's beautiful, but impossible to appreciate. I feel no need to go back unless I'm seeing it by candlelight while listening to a live, invitation-only performance of Allegri's "Miserere." Since no papal invitation is likely to arrive, that means I feel no need to go back.

However, I WOULD go back to the Vatican Museums, because after leaving the Sistine Chapel, we decided to double back and retrace our steps. We discovered that getting off the literally beaten path took us to empty galleries like the spectacular (and empty!) 16th century Borgia apartments. Similarly (and inexplicably) empty were the galleries housing the museums' extensive Etruscan collection. We even got a chance to see Lacoon in relative peace, as well as a number of sculptures in side galleries that we missed with our guide. The crowds also seemed to thin some as the morning progressed, so I'm not sure how effective showing up as the museum opens is. I agree with previous comments here that most exhibits are poorly labeled--I'm guessing that an audioguide would have helped. While I would buy my ticket online again, Next time, though, I'll skip the tour.

title: An invitation to reflect on art, history and our shared humanity
text:
The Vatican Museums are one of the most valuable cultural treasures in the world. With more than 70,000 works of art and a history dating back to the 16th century, they offer a unique journey through centuries of beauty and spirituality. Visiting the Vatican Museums means immersing yourself in a constant dialogue between art and faith, on a journey that touches Egyptian civilization, ancient Greece, the Renaissance and beyond. In our visit we selected only some of their most emblematic wonders, to better appreciate them. After the entrance and the beautiful ribbon ramp, among the ancient treasures, we find the Egyptian statue of Tuia, symbol of the meeting between the East and Rome. This sculpture, with its enigmatic charm, testifies to the refinement of Egyptian art. Continuing, we find ourselves in the Octagon Courtyard, the heart of the classic collection. Here stand iconic sculptures such as the Belvedere Apollo and the Laocoon group. This open space invites you to contemplate the harmony and perfection of Greco-Roman sculpture. In the foreground, the group of the Laocoon narrates the drama and suffering of the Trojan priest and his sons. It is a masterpiece that captures the human pathos, symbol of Hellenistic art at its peak. Then we entered the Round Room, inspired by the Pantheon, which enchants with its floor mosaic and monumental statues. In the center, the colossal porphyry crater, emblem of grandeur and majesty. Moving forward, we immersed ourselves in the Tapestry Room, where intricate fabrics recount biblical and historical episodes. The delicacy of the details makes these tapestries works of art alive. Following, the Hall of Geographical Maps offers a fresco of the world as it was conceived in the sixteenth century. Its painted walls tell a journey through Italy, combining art and science in a unique visual harmony. And here are the most anticipated works. The Signature Room: We dwell on the Sacrament Dispute. This fresco by Raphael Sanzio celebrates the Eucharist, with a play of lights that unites the earth to the sky. Next door, The School of Athens represents the triumph of philosophy. Plato and Aristotle dominate the scene, surrounded by the great thinkers of antiquity. A tribute to the human intellect. turning our heads, we admire The Parnassus, where Apollo, surrounded by Muses, celebrates poetry. The composition conveys a sense of balance and grace typical of the Renaissance. And finally we came to what represents one of the greatest masterpieces of world art: the Sistine Chapel. In this Michelangelo Buonarroti, with his extraordinary mastery, transformed the ceiling and wall of the altar into works of unique visual and narrative power. On the vault Genesis (1508-1512), a journey into the origins of humanity, with scenes depicting biblical episodes such as the Creation of Adam and the Separation of Light from Darkness. Michelangelo uses vivid colors and monumental figures to enhance divine dynamics and energy, emphasizing the direct relationship between God and man. On the altar wall, The Last Judgment (1536-1541) shows a dramatic and terrible vision of Judgment Day. At the center, Christ appears as a judge, surrounded by a whirlwind of resurrected or damned figures. The composition impresses with its emotional intensity and strong sense of movement, offering a raw and realistic reflection on the human condition. The tour ends with the helical staircase by Giuseppe Momo, a contemporary work that, inspired by the famous Bramante staircase, combines functionality and beauty.
The Vatican Museums are not only a place of memory, but a timeless source of inspiration, an invitation to reflect on art, history and our shared humanity.

title: Dall'alto e dall'esterno
text:
Area paludosa nell'antichità.Diventato in seguito centro della vita pubblica per oltre un millennio.
Nel corso delle varie epoche sono stati costruiti i vari monumenti e costruzioni per le funzioni politiche, commerciali, religiose.
Diventato in seguito incapace a svolgere la funzione di centro amministrativo e di rappresentanza della città perchè troppo piccolo gli imperartori che si sono susseguiti decido no di vi aggiungere  solo monumenti di prestigio tipo il Tempio di Vespasiano e Tito, quello di Antonino Pio e Faustina  e il monumentale Arco di Settimio Severo, per celebrare le vittorie dell’imperatore sui Parti.
L'ultima realizzazione è stata nei primi anni del IV secolo d.C.  realizzata
dall’imperatore Massenzio-
Diventata in seguito un pascolo perchè l’area subì un forte interramento.
 Bisogna aspettare sino a dopo  1860 per vedere i primi lavori di scavo nell’area.

title: One of the places that, in life, you must absolutely visit
text:
Forgive my ignorance, but often, the Museums, after a while bore me (after an initial enthusiasm). Quite the opposite of my wife adoring them.
Strangely, for the Vatican Museums, this has not happened.
In fact I was enthusiastic and admired.
Last January 7, also thanks to a mild and pleasant sunny winter day, I could admire them in all their beauty (gardens included).
It would be impossible to describe them: the Pinacoteca, the Egyptian Museum, the Galleria dei candelabra, that of tapestries, the part reserved for animals. But, for me, the top is reached with the Gallery of Maps before reaching the Sistine Chapel.
Overcrowded and overvisited, the Sistine Chapel is the masterpiece of masterpieces.
The Last Judgment stands there, but everything "smells" of art: Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Perugino.
Photos (only in the Sistine Chapel) are not allowed, but you cannot, in life, not visit it at least once.

title: Vatican Museum Tour
text:
We added a guided tour of the Vatican and Sistine Chapel for our family of 5 (two adults, 21, 20, 17 kids) through the museum directly. We initially just bought tickets but added the guide later. Our tour time was 4:30pm so we queued at 4:00pm. It was a little confusing in the waiting area outside but there were attendants helping move things along. Our guide was Patrizia. She had about 20 of us to keep track of and we did notice the headsets had a short range so you really had to keep up to hear the information. Patrizia was very thorough in her tour and we learned a lot about the history of the popes and the works of the masters. Our favorite rooms were the hall of cartography and the Rafael rooms, which had just recently been unveiled after a restoration!
The tour lasted about 3 hours including the Sistine Chapel, which is where we exited the tour, Patrizia did not join there as guides stay behind for that. Be aware it is a holy place so no talking or pictures. I did see people chastised for snapping pictures on their phones. All in all it was a great tour with a lot of interesting information to absorb. We did get tired but I think it was overstimulation from the sheer volume of art and crowds. Despite that, if you are interested in Catholicism, history and/or art I recommend going!

title: Great museum but be prepared to be herded in the crowds
text:
To get there, the signage wasn’t great and we landed up on the wrong side of Vatican City which resulted in lots of walking and tired feet. 

You can book tickets on the day, however, the queue is exceptionally long so rather book tickets online. If you do so, queue in the line on the right hand side. We also booked the audio guides online.

The Vatican museum is one of the most beautiful museums that I’ve seen. However, it was exceptionally crowded and hot inside with no option to exit  without completing the entire route. We felt herded by crowds and it became a bit claustrophobic.

Be sure to wear very comfortable shoes.

All in all, great museum but be prepared to wait in queues and be herded by crowds in the same direction until you exit.

title: Great works, absolute zero for the organization
text:
Our rating is an average between the maximum score for the works present and the absolute zero of the organization.
Here there is a magnificence of endless art, culminating in Raphael's Rooms and the Sistine Chapel. So much art all at once that makes you drunk and breathless! There are no words to describe what it feels like to be faced with all this.
About the organization much is already written in multiple reviews... with skip-the-line tickets (among other things at a high price) you bypass only the queue at the entrance, and then stay in the queue throughout the visit to museums, where you are forced to follow a path that crosses all the rooms without being able to choose what to see or not to see, or be able to linger calmly in the rooms of your interest, pushed by hordes of people crowded and guides who invite you to continue fast.
At the end after at least two hours of crowding you arrive at the Sistine Chapel exhausted... 
Given the online booking they should quota and limit the entrances in order to allow people to visit these masterpieces in peace and above all in safety, but unfortunately it is just an endless business, really sad...

title: A work like no other
text:
Highly highly suggest going with a tour group. We had a lecture in the Pinecone Courtyard as guides aren’t allowed to speak inside the Chapel. The ceiling was Michelangelo’s first painting assignment and he didn’t want to do it. He told the Pope he was a sculptor, not a painter. Rafael was alive at the time but the Pope wanted Michelangelo and made him an offer he couldn’t refuse. What came out of it was pure genius. Only Michelangelo could paint God. Part of the ceiling near the Pope’s door was damaged over 400 years ago. It will never be repaired. The painting above the Pope’s door were damaged at the same time. The originals were by Rafael. The repainting is awful. That’s why Michelangelo’s work will never be repaired.

Photography and videography are strictly forbidden.

title: Breathtaking! (Literally and Figuratively!)
text:
Bucket list checked!

It was in my bucket list and it did not disappoint!

It’s hard to put into words the beauty of this place—-a lifetime indeed is not enough to marvel the astonishing works of the masters here. You have to spend more time just to take everything in—- plus the scale and the thousands of steps are enough to let you know how difficult and challenging to finish all the masterpieces inside must be! And yes, it’s a very (really!) long walk to get to Michelangelo’s famous work! 

I just hope the security would find a way to allow a safe spot to take a picture inside(after all we did travel a long way to get there!) just like the way they do it in France with Mona Lisa. The people who took the time, effort and money to get there deserves at least some memorable photos to take home to share with family and friends.

Will I recommend it? I will tell you this, if you have not even included this in your bucket list, then do so now as it would totally change your perspective in life in general once you see what a real product of sweat and blood really looks like!

I will definitely come back! (Once is just NOT enough)

text:
Firstly - we booked a ticket for Vatican Museum and managed to queue up in St Peter’s Square for 30 mins going through all the checkpoints only to find out we were in the wrong place and the actual museum is a 15 minute walk away. We ended up missing our museum time slot quite significantly but they still let us in. The Vatican museum is huge, you will walk and walk. It is also hot and yes it’s crowded but it is nowhere near as bad as the Tower of London in the summer!!!

It is a must see, just incredible art, history and the Sistine Chapel breathtaking.

title: Amazing Collection of Art Highlighted by Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel
text: An amazing collection of art highlighted by experiencing the Raphael Rooms and the Sistine Chapel which is breathtaking. You can easily spend several hours in the museum, and I would budget at least 2 1/2-3 hours. Purchase tickets well in advance online allowing you to select a specific entry time. Otherwise, you could stand in line for hours to purchase a ticket. When you arrive at the museum, make sure you don't stand in this line if you already have a voucher. There is a separate line for those with a reserved time. You will still need to go through a security check and then will need to exchange your voucher for an entrance ticket at a designated ticket window. All of this takes time so plan accordingly. It is very worthwhile to rent an audioguide for an extra charge. This can be purchased in advance as well and picked up at the top of the spiral ramp after showing your entrance ticket. The tour ends in the Sistine Chapel. Ideally you should try to exit through the short cut into St Peter's Basilica. This is usually only for tour groups so assume the guards will stop you but give it a try. Otherwise, you will need to make the long walk taking 15 minutes back to where you entered the museum.

title: An assault on your eyes
text:
Be realistic this is an extremely popular location. We went early in December and whilst it was busy it was ok and we definitely did not get herded around as described in other reviews. 
Buy your tickets online prior to coming! The website has different options. Bring ID, you will be required to produce it. I would not recommend a guided tour, it takes forever, instead pay 7euro for an audible tour. You get a handset in the language of your choice and a map of the route. You can choose what to listen too. Many exhibits have a red label and a number. Enter the number and you get the explanation, it’s that simple.
The museum is vast, there is a huge amount to see so do expect to be there for at least two or more hours. Cafes and toilets are onsite so you can rest. The history is staggering and some of the statues and other exhibits are awesome. Whilst there can be crowds it is worth it. 
The culmination of the route is the Sistine Chapel, wow! Security is tight but comforting. After the Sistine Chapel the exit is another 10 minute walk away passing gift shops and cafes. The exit is next to the entry point.

title: Pre-book a time slot. Take the Audio Tour and go at your own pace.
text: Go in the morning if you can as there is so much to see. Pre book rather than hope for a ticket on the day. The no ticket line didn't look too long on the day I went, but I don't know how long people had to wait. I also recommend the audio tour. You can go through at your own pace. I can't speak for every guided tour I saw, but they looked as if they were rushing in places and giving edited highlights. I guess if you are short of time it could be good, but I prefer doing my own thing. Some rooms were lovely and peaceful as few to no tours passed me. I was glad I could slow down and take it all in - after all, the tickets are not that cheap and I wanted to make the most of my day.  There are rooms filled with fantastic sculptures, works of art and religious stuff (not religious myself!) A lot seemed to have been "acquired" by the Vatican. Room after room filled with all sorts of things . On paper, the map given looks easy to follow, however, I am sure I managed to miss some bits. It looks as if there is a short cut to the Sistine chapel - I think it could be the wheelchair access as with the crowds it is almost impossible to backtrack if you bypass the rooms the route shows. I stopped for a snack and the toilet before entering the chapel. I am glad I did as, like everywhere in Rome, preparations are happening for the jubilee next year and some areas are closed. I just had a coffee and a small pizza. Not over priced, but nothing fancy.  I think they were the first open toilets since near the entrance. Then, to be honest, the Sistine chapel was a bit of an anticlimax. I could see why people are hearded into the room by staff, but despite the signs telling people it was a sacred space, it felt more like a noisy cattle market. I was expecting quiet as people wandered around respecting the space. However, the tour guides were talking to their groups and every few minutes there was a recording in at least three languages telling people to be quiet. It rather spoilt the atmosphere. I was glad to get out. Don't miss the Papal transport in the garden. There is an entrance down some steps where sedan chairs, carriages, miscellaneous cars and the more modern Pope mobiles are on display. I went in at 9.30 and emerged at around 2.15. You exit close to the museum entrance. If you then want to visit St Peters Basilica, it is a 5-10 minute walk around the block to get to the main square. I am glad I have been, but it is a one time thing. Plenty to look at even if you aren't religious.

title: Unimaginable
text:
What you can see, admire and contemplate in this place is difficult to do elsewhere.
How much it is possible to reflect on Michelangelo's greatness thanks to his Last Judgment of the Sistine Chapel is possible only here.
After the visit to the Vatican Museums I came out intoxicated, almost dazed and drunk by so much beauty expressed in the most varied forms: from paintings to statues, from archaeological finds of the most disparate cultures to the richness and beauty of the Vatican Gardens, up to the wonderful creation of Michelangelo. Almost as if to say that after the abundance combined with the splendor of what is possible to find in the Museums, the only worthy conclusion is to lose yourself in the enchantment and poetry of a wonderful and unique work in the world.
I think everyone should be lucky enough to visit the Vatican Museums.

title: Vatican City Review
text:
Vatican City is an awe-inspiring destination and the spiritual heart of the Roman Catholic Church. It’s filled with some of the world’s most remarkable art, architecture, and history, making it a must-visit for anyone traveling to Rome. The highlights include St. Peter’s Basilica, the Sistine Chapel, and the Vatican Museums.

The experience of standing beneath Michelangelo’s painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel is surreal. Every corner of the chapel is filled with intricate details, and the vibrant colors make it hard to believe it’s centuries old. St. Peter’s Basilica is equally breathtaking, with its soaring dome and countless sculptures. Climbing to the top offers a panoramic view of Rome that’s worth every step.

Tips 
1. Book tickets ahead of time to avoid long lines, especially for the Vatican Museums.
2. Consider a guided tour to get the most out of the visit and learn about the art and history.
3. Dress appropriately, as strict dress codes apply within religious spaces.

Whether you’re interested in art, history, or spirituality, Vatican City offers an extraordinary experience and a unique look into a world apart from everyday Rome.

title: Capitalism at its worst!
text:
I have visited a lot of museums in my time but this has to be the worst. You have to follow a one way system, there's no freedom of movement so your essentially moving at a snails pace with either staff shouting at you to move along or people jostling you if you stop to admire something.
It took an hour to finally get to the Sistine Chapel. Before going in there are signs reminding you that it is a holy place, to be respectful etc. Again, we were herded like cattle into the overcrowded chapel. It completely ruined the experience. Unlike other churches in Rome there are no mirrors so you can see a magnified image of the ceiling. Don't get me wrong the ceiling is stunning but it would have been so much nicer if there had been fewer people and no staff shouting at everyone! It feels like the Vatican has fallen victim to capitalism and are just trying to pack as many people in as possible. We visited other churches that had equally beautiful ceilings where it felt like the art was actually being respected not commodified.

title: Museums among the richest in the world
text:
Like other museums of this level, it would take weeks to visit it in depth. For a day tour we relied on an official Guide with a 150-minute tour, at the end of which you are free to continue the visit independently. The highlight of the museums is obviously the Sistine Chapel, always crowded (you can hardly see the mosaic floor). Equally crowded is the Gallery of Geographical Maps, which is the main access road to the Sistine.
Incredibly almost empty instead the three rooms, such as the picture gallery (with works by Van Gogh, Caravaggio, Titian, Giotto, Fra Angelico, Perugino, Pinturicchio, Raphael, Leonardo, ...). Also interesting is the Carriage Museum, where in addition to the carriages are collected the Papamobiles since 1930, and also the Missionary Ethnological Museum, with artifacts and indigenous art from Oceania, Africa and America. 
Inside the museums there is also a showcase with football memorabilia given to the popes (shirts of Maradona, Messi, Pelè, Italy, ...).

title: Absolutely incredible walk through some of the most significant ruins in history
text:
The Roman Forum and Palatine Hill was by far the highlight of our visit to Rome. This incredible archeological park has you walking the 2000 year old roads of ancient Rome, getting up close with the remains of temples and other major structures of this important area. You really feel the energy of history flowing.

The view from Palatine Hill (the platform through the garden) is fabulous, with the dome of St Peter’s Basilica at one end, sweeping around to the Colosseum at the other.

 The park opens at 9.00 and highly recommend getting there early as you can enjoy much of it, including the Hill view without the crowds and the heat which build by mid morning. We spent around 3 hours.

Online booking is required unless you have a free slot on the Roma card or are visiting as part of the Colosseum ticket.

title: Roman forum
text:
With the colosseum, the Roman forum was easily one of my favourite places in Rome.
It is very big and disperse, we only explored for 2hours, but would definitely spend more 1 or 2 hours just walking in the forum.
There is a drinking water fountain inside the forum, which was nice in a hot day.
The magnitude of the buildings was unexpected, and the fact we were walking and seeing buildings (even if in ruins) of a Roman "downtown" of more than 1800 years ago, was mind-blowing.
From the palatine hill, to the temple of saturn, to the supposed site of Julius Caesar's assassination, to the tomb of Romulus, the Roman forum defined itself as one of my favourite sites for sure.

title: Amazing place, with poor interpretation and bad customer service.
text:
An excellent site, however it is unfortunately marred by the visitor experience being unworthy of such a gem.

There's a lot to see, but be aware that visitor interpretation on site is poor. 

They may publish a closing time of 16.30 and you might budget your time to get round the site based on that information but be warned... the staff would seem to wish to go home at exactly that time, so will start closing off sections of the site and sweeping visitors toward the exit 45 minutes before, telling you that the site is closing by 16.15, but because there are a lot of people in the archaeological park (hardly any one visitor's fault - and let's face it, when is it not busy) they have to start pushing people out well before the published time, being prepared to lie about the true closing time to get you out.

Apparently in March they move the closing time later due to longer daylight, but this doesn't happen till then. So if you go in February especially to avoid summer crowds, be aware of the closing time being an hour before sunset- and be warned that what time they publish they close is not what time you have.

title: Crowded, but must-see
text:
Vatican City has two entrances, one for the museum and one for St. Peter's Basilica. To avoid the outdoor line to the Vatican Museum ticket booth, we booked tickets online in advance. Since the general admission tickets online were already sold out,  we opted for the Guided Tours for Individuals through the official Vatican website. This ticket allowed us to get in the security line and enter. 
This tour was with a Vatican tour guide, about 2 hours, and was not expensive compared to what some other "skip the line" tours websites were charging. 
The tour starts with  general historical and artist information at a kiosk style area, proceeding through the hallways needed to get to the Sistine Chapel, and ending prior to entering the Sistine Chapel. The tour did not include going through the Egyptian collection. Once exiting the Sistine Chapel we were able to go back and see the museum areas again. If you exit the museum at the ticket area you cannot re-enter with the same ticket, nor can you go directly and enter St Peter's Basilica. Simply walk around the outside city wall and wait in this line to go through different security to get in St. Peter's Basilica and Dome areas. The Museum has a cafeteria and toilet area.

title: Everywhere is full of rude staff.
text:
At the beginning of the tour, while trying to validate our guided tour tickets, almost all the employees in the entire place, except for the polite lady who chatted with me in line, were rude and uncaring. They constantly treat people like sheep to be herded. We understand that the place is already making money, but at least treat people like people. The only thing missing from the museum staff is the sheep herding sticks.

Apart from that, the cafe inside is a disgrace. We decided to rest for a while, take a breath, and get our bearings, but we were disgraced. I have never seen a cafe with such uncaring employees in my life. The place is empty, you have to enter from a closed area! You sit and wait, and the employees throw the menu in front of you. We ordered coffee and croissants. The coffee was the most mediocre and cold coffee in the world (we ordered hot coffee). The croissant was supposed to be plain, but it was orange and chocolate (I think they mixed up the orders), in short, it is ridiculous.

The number of toilets is clearly insufficient. There is an incredible queue. It is unacceptable that there are only two or three toilets in a place visited by thousands of people every day and that they are tiny and poorly maintained.

In the Sistine Chapel, they are constantly trying to get rid of people. Our guide explained it in detail but we could barely stay inside. All the officers are constantly trying to herd people like sheep, telling them to move forward, move forward, and almost trying to get rid of them.

In short: If you want to be treated like a human being, don't waste your time and energy here. If you want to be herded like sheep, this is the place for you!

title: Vatican Museums: Where You’re Herded Like Sheep… But Without the Holy Blessing
text:
My visit to the Vatican Museums left me with mixed feelings. Before coming here, I had high expectations, but the actual experience didn’t live up to them. It felt less like a museum and more like a huge “government office,” where I felt restricted and controlled.

Firstly, the whole process made me feel like we were “paying to be allowed to see treasures” rather than being welcomed as guests. The strict rules and crowd control made the visit feel rushed, as if we were being herded through. My friend needed to use the restroom, so we had to skip several exhibits and rooms, and when we tried to go back, a staff member coldly told us no. There were many “Exit” signs everywhere, and if you accidentally took one, you could miss entire sections of the museum. Thankfully, we had a simple map and asked both staff and other visitors for directions to see everything.

The crowds were overwhelming, packed with tour groups. However, surprisingly, some of the less talked-about halls were quiet and beautiful, which was a pleasant surprise. It’s worth noting that the routes are adjusted based on how busy it is. At one point, we arrived at an empty Roman exhibit, only to find out later that the entrance had been closed after we entered. This made us feel like the museum wasn’t treating visitors as guests but rather as paying tourists just there to check things off a list.

In the end, this visit left me somewhat disappointed. I don’t think I will return to this museum. Goodbye, Sistine Chapel.

title: Consider your clientele
text:
1:) the “bouncers” outside organising the lines/groups of people are rude. Remember who and what you’re serving. The short, skinny, dark haired man with glasses was a jerk. 
2.) entry and direction are confusing and chaotic.  I understand this is an old facility, but signage… proper signage makes all the difference. I still do not know where I walked.
3.) the museum is incredible. One could spend an entire day roaming its halls and seeing history. We are limited physically, so our goal was the Sistine Chapel. But what absolutely incredible art: paintings, sculptures, tapestries throughout. 
4.) the Sistine Chapel is beyond words. A long, long, confusing walk to get there, thru mysterious hallways, up and down eerie stairs, crowded and hot…but then, there it is. Wait for a rare seat on the perimeter benches, and ponder history. I’ve studied it and read of it for over 50 years, and to finally be there….. wow.
5.) the walk to the exit is lined with money changers selling religious garbage in the name of faith. Store after store of the same crap. The same tables Jesus would be overturning in the temple. Embarrassing, offensive, vulgar…
In conclusion, one has to do it, along with everyone else in the world. Be prepared for a long day full of tested patience, incredible art, and religious contradiction… along with people, thousands of people. Is it worth it? I still don’t know the answer to that question.

title: Reservations are a must!
text:
I was told that waiting two or three hours was commonplace without Reservations, so I made a Reservation as soon as it became possible to make a Reservation two months before the visit date on the official website.
Some of the time slots are already closed, perhaps due to Reservation with the tour company. It fills up quickly during the tourist season, so it's a good idea to make Reservations first and then schedule the rest of your trip.

It was a 9am Reservation, but the line without a Reservation on the day stretched hundreds of meters, and I still felt a Reservation was a must.

The exterior and interior of the building are wonderful, and the mosaics of floors here and there are beautiful. If you are not particularly interested in art and just want to know the famous places, 90 minutes is enough.

I went there a few years ago during the evening hours, and the exhibits and luxurious interiors with natural light are great, preferably during the day, and if you'd like more, by Reservation until 9am, when there are fewer people.

title: Amazing place,  be prepared for a long walk and lots of people
text:
Visiting the Vatican was a highlight of my trip.  The sheer scale, quantity and quality of breathtaking art in the Vatican museums and the Sistine Chapel is amazing. 

But... and it is a significant but... you don't get much chance to really appreciate where you are and what you are seeing.  Surrounded by hundreds of people and dozens of tour groups, the best you can hope for is to glimpse art that anywhere else would be the centre of attention. 

Here,  understandably given its reputation, everyone wants to get to the Sistine Chapel.  The only way there is through a couple of miles of corridors with world class artwork at every turn.  But everyone just seems to charge forward as fast as humanly possible. 

Once in the Chapel itself no photos are allowed and you are moved through quickly.  We managed to take about 4 minutes in awe of the surroundings before we were herded onwards.

title: A waste of money
text:
A crushing disappointment

We purchased a ‘Skip the Line’ small group tour starting at 7.30 am. booked through Tiquets. If it wasn’t sad it would be funny! The small group tour consisted of 22 visitors!

The first half hour of the tour was simply padding - standing in St Peter’s Square being given an explanation of the structure. Then another 1/2 hour was wasted in the line with the thousands of other tourists who had paid for a skip the line tour to the Vatican. We wasted a whole hour before we even entered the Vatican Museum! Once inside we were taken to the outside courtyard for another 20 minutes to have the Sistine Chapel explained by looking at several large posters! Now nearly 1.5 hours wasted and as yet no significant art had been viewed live. 

Our guide, touted as an art historian, then lead us into the museum, quickly ushering us past some of the most famous art pieces with not a mentioned of them made. Ours was an English-speaking group and our Italian guides’ accent was so thick that most in the group gave up trying to understand her constant talk as we were swiftly corralled  through the museum corridors amongst throngs of other crushed patrons. Her objective - to get us through the museum as swiftly as possible to reach the famed Sistine Chapel. As we passed through the Stanza de Raphael not a mention was made by our guide of the highly significant works such as the Academie! 

We were herded like sheep to the only art that seemed to matter - the Sistine Chapel. We arrived to a room suffocating with people and Vatican staff herding everyone to the centre of the room in tighter and tighter clusters of humanity. Then our guide stated after 15 minutes as we tried to listen to her inaudible commentary that it was time to exit the Museum. In fact our experience was designed as a singular tour of the Sistine Chapel - not of the Vatican Museum!

This was our third time that my wife and I had visited the Museum, and was by far our worst museum visit of all time. Crowds now destroy the experience and tours like this are a complete joke - except my wife, my daughter and I paid an extortionate AU$600 for the privilege! It borders on false advertising! 

Advice - watch a video on the Vatican Museum or gain the services of a true art historian as a guide on a private tour outside offical Museum opening hours. Our experience - a complete waste of money though we did support the Vatican finances!

title: PLEASE DO NOT IGNORE MY REVIEW
text:
I first visited the museum 7 years ago late september. It was an unforgettable experience.   Museum has a huge collection of statues, paintings, ethnological items from all around the world, also many things about Christianty history of course. I remember that time I looked at every piece one by one, in a relaxed environment, with a lot of free time. The whole visit took maybe 4-5 hours.

And wait…

Yesterday I visited it second time after seven years and IT WAS WORST MUSEUM EXPERIENCE OF MY LIFE. WORST OF THE WORSTS.

Huge queue outside Vatican was not a problem. You may expect it. But inside the museum… Oh my God. It was like doomsday. All corridors were too crowded. Believe me or not It was nearly impossible to take step forward. Do not think about looking the collection items. Just look straight and try to walk if you can. I'm not exaggerating. You will miss %80 of the items between huge human flood. Sensitive people can experience anxiety attack also. So strange. Security employees were also helpless, they were also seemed like lost in the crowd. They only gestured with their hands like “move on” so they were like shepherds and we were like sheep flock :))

Vatican Museums is a complex structure already in normal time. It’s hard to follow the right path if you don’t know area well, or you are visiting it without a guide. Hard but not impossible. And normally very joyful. It must be one of the best experiences of someone’s life despite it’s hardness. But yesterday… The only goal of our visit was reaching the Sistine Chapel and leave the museum after first few minutes. So meaningless. The whole visit took 1 hour this time and we hated every second of it. It was the last museum on our programme and previous days I always told my wife “just wait for Vatican, your mind will blow away”. And then pfffffff. I was ashamed.

I don’t know what changed in 7 years but I think this situation is harmful for visitors, for employees, even for collections, items and buildings themself and finally Italy’s image.

I can not say “do not visit Vatican Museums” because it is a must. But if it goes like our experience, you’ll hate it. I can not lie.

Authorities, do something about it!!!

title: Horribly disorganized, and dangerously overcrowded.
text:
Don't bother going to the Vatican if you're not super religious. I feel like that is the only way you could enjoy it. Otherwise it's just 2.5 hours of shuffling through endless tiny hallways in a herd of thousands of people to see the chapel for a few minutes, because by the end you'll just want to get out of there as soon as possible. It was horribly disorganized, and dangerously overcrowded. You couldn't even stop to look at any of the exhibits because there was a throng of bodies behind you pressing ever forward.

Be aware there are no "fast track" or "skip the line" tickets. There are reserved time tickets (2:00 PM time slot, 2:30, etc.), but you still have to wait in a line with everyone else from that time slot. There were easily hundreds of people for each time and they have time slots every half hour. The line did move quicker than expected, took about 15 minutes past our time slot to get in and we were like the middle of the line.

There was a separate even longer line for people that were trying to buy tickets that day and I would definitely not recommend that.

I totally understand they are dealing with thousands upon thousands of visitors every day, but just a few well-placed benches were needed earlier in the tour.

Also DO NOT choose the ‘Lunch included’ option… it’s an absolute RIP OFF (22 Euros). Instructions for how to access the lunch were non-existent (no information at all was provided on the ticket or at time of booking) & even the staff didn’t know where we were supposed to go to redeem the voucher. I was not the only person encountering that problem - many I saw were asking & being turned away from the Bistrot.

The menu was extremely limited & it was in the food court - where I could have gotten (more or less) the same thing for cheaper. Basically - bowl of very ordinary pasta & a bit of chicken with some baked eggplant - mostly tasteless. Plus a bottle of water & a kiwi fruit! Worst meal I’ve eaten in Italy - by far.

Just book your entry ticket & audio guide (a must & totally worth it) & once you’ve seen the museums (takes about 4 hours)… sit in the garden with a beer & then head out to lunch somewhere in Rome nearby. You’ll enjoy the food so much more.

title: It would be useful for the "Vatican Museum" to learn from the Louvre or Versailles about its organization.
text:
Confounded by the curious Vatican Museum.
The entrance is not professionally managed, with no ropes or signs indicating where to place or where to pass. It is necessary to refer to employees who are the numbers of 1 to understand something. 
Once placed in an approximate queue, we wait for our passage time, but visitors who arrived on the wire grill us the place without going through the queue box. Ticket controllers with no qualms for visitors waiting their turns. 

Once inside a forest of signs indicate the exit without ever indicating WHERE the tour begins.       
Nothing is intuitive. 
No map of the museum is available.
The signposts are of no help. 
A “toilet” sign is located next to a door plastered in a prohibited sense.     
A sign near an elevator lists things to see without specifying which floors these things are on. 
Several others indicate "MUSEO" followed by different surnames. To be mistaken, it seems that several museums are to be visited when they are simply the different wings of the Vatican Museum. A real headache. 
Far from discovering the history of the Vatican and its popes, we end up with Egyptian mummies and Chagall paintings, which is not quite what we came here to find.      
It is also not possible to organize your time or choose what interests you, because the museum is thought like an Indian queue that forces us to see everything and trample for several hours without taking the time. The Sistine Chapel which is the most interesting thing to see is only accessible if the entire museum has been passed through before. 
I dare not imagine the state of the elderly and children in there. 
Once inside the chapel a vigil is charged with saying “chuuuut chuuuut” constantly and continuously, difficult when 300 people cram into the same room.        
Ah and the audio guides are 8€ extra outside of the Admission Award. 
In short, an experience far from living up to an institution as old and important as the Vatican.

title: Incredible Experience, Definitely advise the official Tour
text:
I'll review this in a few parts.

Firstly the Vatican Museums are HUGE. So much art and culture from ancient history to modern contemporary art. Could probably do with a few more signs as to what things are and, at some point after the Sistine Chapel, signs seemed to stop having English translations although you're basically done by then anyway. Definitely set aside a full day at least if not a couple to see everything.

We had an official Tour which I would recommend to anyone and everyone. By official tours I mean one only booked through the Vatican Museum website. They start with a walkthrough of the art on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel because there is, and I quote, "Absolutely no talking in the sistine chapel" (I'll come back to that) but there was plenty of time to hear about the art and about how Michaelangelo did it with plenty of room for questions. I believe our guide said his name was Jad, he was incredible. Very knowledgeable and engaging. He also gave us plenty of time to take the tour at our own leisure despite our tour being 20 people from 4 or 5 different groups on the day provided we weren't in a bottleneck area. He definitely gave more insight to the works than we'd have been able to get by general admission.

The Sistine chapel was incredibly well preserved. Not sure what other reviews referred to about being "herded" as there were literally chairs around the edge that you can sit on and enjoy the art for as long as you like, or not being able to take pics to make you "but something from the shop"... There are so many pics of the chapel on the internet, just enjoy being where you are. Our tour ended just before the chapel specifically so that we can take as long as we want in the chapel.

My biggest issue however was other people's conduct within the Sistine Chapel. It is such an important place to Catholicism which is why I imagine there is not talking or taking pictures. There are signs, guards and a tannoy all attempting to enforce these rules however the disrespect shown by the general public was outrageous. There were guided tours going through where the tour guide would be talking throughout. Other reviews have said about how their "official Tour guide" was told to be quiet by the guards to which I would reply with "this was not an official Tour". If it was up to me, there would be no tour guide technology at all in the Sistine Chapel and anyone found talking or taking pictures should be escorted out by the scruff of their necks. The Vatican are well within their rights to charge extra for entry to the chapel or even stop access altogether so I felt very privileged to have had access via general admission. I'm not a Christian by any means, respect is universal. They asked for quiet, we should give quiet. They ask for no pictures, so we shouldn't take pictures. 

Before the rant about humanity takes over the whole review, I will summarise by saying I really enjoyed my day out. The museum was incredible, the tour was amazing and well worth the money. title: High spirituality
text:
A wonderful experience, despite endless entrance queue. Rich museum of Egyptian, Roman, Greek art, ancient tapestries, pinocytheque and modern art. Magnificent sculptures, paintings, floors, ceilings, courtyards. The Sistine Chapel can be reached after an hour of walking. "The Last Judgment" is a wall. Benches are arranged in the room to sit and observe the ceiling. As always, to access the Vatican Museums you will have to pass under the metal detector and use the wardrobe for backpacks, bags and bulky items.
Important: in addition to health precautions, to access the Vatican Museums it is necessary to wear decent and respectful of the place, so do not show up in shorts (yes shorts at the knee), miniskirts, armored T-shirts and tank tops. Imagine having to enter a Catholic holy place and make no mistake. On the last Sunday of each month, the Vatican opens its museums for free. The exhibitions start at 9.00, but the queue for those who want to enter forms much earlier. The museum is normally closed on Sundays, but on these special days it is open until 2pm, with the last admission at 12.30pm. To reach the famous Sistine Chapel, you have to walk for an hour through the inner rooms. The ordinary ticket costs €17 and a reduced ticket €8 which is exclusively reserved for children aged 6 to 18 and university students, while children under 6 years do not pay. If you buy your ticket online on the official site, you can add €4 per “skip the line” and €2 per transaction.

Durante il Rinascimento papa Giulio II utilizzò l’area come cava: i materiali furono presi e portati via o distrutti per  essere poi utilizzati per rinnovare la città come lui stesso aveva stabilito.  Il valore e l’importanza del foro furono valorizzati nel Cinquecento anche grazie ai pittori di vedute romane che dipingevano  le rovine affioranti nell'area del pascolo. Ci furono una serie di scavi nel corso dei secoli che portarono alla luce ciò che oggi si visita.

text:
I recommend anyone coming to Rome to visit the Vatican museum. 

You will see lots of beautiful exhibitions and art. The Sistine Chapel probably one of the most beautiful things I have seen. If you are a Catholic you should visit the Vatican once in your life. However, the big downside is the amount of visitors, it is very difficult to really give yourself to the tour because there is always someone pushing you, blocking you from seeing the paintings and exhibitions.

However, remember a few things :
1) First of all, always book your tickets in advance, the queues to buy tickets at the stations are very long.
2. it is better to visit the museum in the morning because the queues are smaller and it is easier to see the art
3) You have to be dressed so that you have to cover your knees and shoulders because if you don't, you won't be allowed in.

title: Vatican Museums/ Vatican City, Italy
text:
Book tickets directly via Vatican museum (Musei Vaticani.va) webpage ca. 60 days ahead (they go very quickly), saves money and stress about fake ticketing, semi honest tour operators etc...

If you have limited time, skip a guided tour all together. 

There's so much to see you will not be able to see most in one visit anyway, plan ahead to determine what you really want to see/don't want to miss. 

Go super early (arrive at least 45 mins prior opening, opening hrs are 8am to 7pm) and avoid the later morning crowd or go in the later afternoon/evening before closing. 
During summer peak times (early June-August) it is usually a terrible idea to visit. 
Dangerously overcrowded, hot and miserably herded through endless small rooms and dark corridors like tourist cattle. No room to stop, breathe or to enjoy museum, just being moved forward during that season. By the time you finally get to the Sistine chapel you’re so desperate to escape the masses, noise and claustrophobia… except the exit’s another 45 minute trudge. Nevertheless it is a must to see when in Rome....

The Vatican Museums (Italian: Musei Vaticani; Latin: Musea Vaticana) are the public museums of Vatican City, enclave of Rome. They display works from the immense collection amassed by the Catholic Church and the papacy throughout the centuries, including several of the most well-known Roman sculptures and most important masterpieces of Renaissance art in the world. The museums contain roughly 70,000 works, of which 20,000 are on display, and currently employs approx. 640 people who work in 40 different administrative, scholarly, and restoration departments.

There are 24 galleries, or rooms, in total, with the Sistine Chapel, notably, being the last room visited within the Museum.

Pope Julius II founded the museums in the early 16th century.

The Sistine Chapel, with its ceiling and altar wall decorated by Michelangelo, and the Stanze di Raffaello (decorated by Raphael) are on the visitor route through the Vatican Museums.

In 2023, the Vatican Museums were visited by 6.8 million people.
They ranked second in the list of most-visited art museums in the world after the Louvre, and third on the list of most-visited museums.

title: Carla Zaia -- excellent Roma private tour guide
text:
We learned about Carla from Rick Steve's Rome book, and we were very fortunate being able to tour with her on those days we wanted. We did a tour at the Colosseum, San Clemente Basilica and the Roman Forum. We then did another at the Vantican Museum / St. Peter's Basilica. 

The 4 of us, including two school aged kids were thoroughly impressed by the depth of knowledge and the amount of energy Carla has! Yes, that's a lot a lot of positive energy that reflected her passion for what she does. It was certainly like touring with a Roma local who can't wait to share all the good things about the city she loves. She also helped us out in detail for recommendations on where/when to go to for good food and stuff, even after all the tours were over.

She is also very good at controlling the tempo and to keep our kids engaged. Our kids are naturally interested in ancient history of Rome but still, we were impressed that at their age (primary and middle school), they kept their attention with Carla through these 3-4 hours long each, non-stop walking tours -- and one of the outdoor tours was done when it was raining!

Last but not least -- remember the good old days doing business when people really honored their words more so than a contract etc.? That's how it felt like working with Carla when we booked her time, and all the way throughout. No middle man or cranky billing company / web portals / mysterious, thousand-miles-away customer service involved. You communicate with her via email directly and things got settled nicely, straight and clear. 

We highly recommend having Carla Zaia to tour Rome. Rick Steve's book is superb too for self-touring, which we did ourselves for many other sites there. (By the way, we also used Lonely Planet for more restaurant / Gelato recommendations, but Rick Steve's is better as a "tour guide book" as you stroll through the sites) But, for places with too much to see under limited time, and especially when traveling with kids or in a group -- we felt that the time would be much better spent with a professional guide, like Carla. title: Overcrowded and poor organisation
text:
The queues outside are poorly organised which wasn’t a good start.  They ought to employ someone who is an expert in crowd management.  Miserable security guards shouting at people to get into the right lines.

After showing your ticket and having it scanned, you have to immediately queue again for your ticket to be scanned.  What’s the point of this?

We wanted to reach the Sistine chapel because it was unbearably warm in most of the rooms, but in order to do this, you’re herded like cattle for about an hour, through room after room of art and culture that starts to merge together after a while.  Up and down flights of packed staircases and in and out of rooms with no air con, until we finally reached the chapel which was so busy we decided to leave after just a few minutes. More rude security staff shouting at people to not take photos - why not make this abundantly clear before people reach the room?

Outside, you can see the basilica but there’s no signs telling you how to reach it.  We were so tired by this point we decided to leave.

In summary, given this is one of the most popular tourist locations on the planet, it ought to be ashamed of how poorly it organises and treats paying visitors.

title: Because you know of course the Vatican needs your hard earned money
text:
To begin, let me be upfront, I'm a hard-core atheist, but I love history, and I have visited Vatican City before, way back in 2003.

My experience in 2024 could not have been more different to 2003.

In 2003, we had space, time, and a general sense of wow as we strolled about the place in our own pace. Notwithstanding that the place stinks of unearned wealth. But remember thou shalt not steal.

Now to 2024, and we have a daughter that wants to study art, so we thought let's show her the Sistene Chapel while we're in Rome. Ha, how silly we were.

If you like tonnes of people packed in like sardines around you, bumper car tour guides more impatient and uncaring than a big city commuter that's running late for a 9 am meeting, searing heat and no air con, the usual number of gormless people going in the wrong direction, down trodden beggars being ignored outside whats supposed to be the spiritual centre of a religion that cares, surly staff and guards that want you to stop and cover up (because you know, an exposed shoulder will ruin the Sistine Chapel) but dont stop and hold the line, overpriced tat, endless obstacle courses of gift shops, a nightmarish crystal maze like den of rats tunnels through stolen art, and more greed and vanity than you can shake a stick at, congrats, you'll love the Vatican Museums. 

If on the other hand you're normal, probably better to give it a miss in 2024. The exit came as a massive relief.

title: Organizzazione pessima!!
text:
Venendo dalla giornata precedente dedicata ai Musei vaticani devo manifestare tutta la mia delusione sull'organizzazione di questo sito. 
1) Prenotazione sul sito Internet difficile da trovare per cui si è portati ad acquistare presso agenzie con costi superiori fino al 20%
2) Usciti dal Colosseo, che fa parte dello stesso complesso e che ti obbligano a visitare per primo (perchè??) non vi è alcuna segnalazione su dove sia l'entrata al Foro Romano
3) Infatti le entrate sono 2 (o forse di più, mah?) e non esiste un itinerario prestabilito che ti consenta di vedere tutto secondo una successione comprensibile e razionale
4) sistema audiovisivo pagato caro ma totalmente inadeguato che non consente di comprendere l'evoluzione storica di tutto il complesso
5) la sola possibilità di illustrazione è quella che ti rimanda ogni volta a cliccare sul codice QR del singolo sito o monumento con il tuo cellulare, cosa laboriosa e illogica.
Conclusione: pessima figura nei confronti dei turisti ed il dubbio che il sistema sia mantenuto volutamente inadeguato per obbligare il ricorso alle guide.

title: Un viaggio nel tempo
text:
Il Foro Romano è uno dei simboli della capitale e ci mostra la maestosità delle costruzioni edilizie dell'impero Romano. 
Era la parte della città in cui si svolgeva la vita pubblica e religiosa dei romani.
Con la caduta dell'impero questa area venne abbandonata restando sottoterra per riemergere grazie agli scavi del XX secolo.
Da non perdere la Via Sacra che era la strada principale dell'antica Roma, l'Arco di Tito, il tempio di Antonino e Faustina, la Basilica di Massenzio e Costantino, la Colonna di Foca.
Percorrendo la Via Sacra potrete chiudere gli occhi e immaginarvi di trovarvi li più di 20 secoli fa.
Uno dei posti più belli di Roma dove trascorrere alcune ore passeggiando senza annoiarvi.

title: The trick to visiting the quiet Sistine Chapel
text:
The reputation of this museum is well established, and the only point of this review is to share the excellent Trip Tip I found on romewise.com to visit the Sistine Chapel (almost) alone.  

By booking your ticket in advance (on the museum website), you can choose to enter at opening time (8:00 a.m. at the time of writing), and pass through the museum to go directly to the chapel, which opens 30 minutes later.  You will be there almost alone (there were about 40 people present during my visit. I went back an hour later and there were more than 300 of us). 

I also strongly recommend the audio guide. This will allow you to take the time to contemplate Michelangelo's works quietly and with excellent descriptions.  

You can then return to the museum entrance and resume the circuit to see the other rooms.  Mentions to pinacoteca, Pio Clementino and Raphael halls. Have a nice visit!

title: Do It AND Wait in Line
text:
Don't rush through it! The pathway to the Sistine Chapel is a through walkway, not a loop or an out-and-back. That being said, the museums are a must do. I would recommend standing in the line to buy tickets on site. The line was long, yes, but scammers take advantage of tourists and overcharge. I wouldn't get in line any later than 1330 or 1400. It took my husband and I about 2 hours to get through it during peak tourism season, but it was well worth it. We met interesting people in the line and got a good tan. 

Would recommend bringing a hat and/or fan as there isn't much shade. If you want Vatican museum books, I'd recommend buying them from the bookstore near St. Peter's Basilica. There was a greater quantity of them in English. 

Contrary to what I read from many reviewers, you ARE allowed to take photos inside. There are some exhibits that prohibit it, including the Sistine Chapel, but that is not the case 100% of the time. Additionally, a "General Ticket" purchased at the on-site ticket office includes the Sistine Chapel. One does not need to purchase two separate tickets. 

The amount of tour groups inside the museum was pandemonium. They would all stop walking when the guide would begin talking about something, but they would take up the entire length of the walkway. There was no common courtesy and no consideration for other visitors. 

My last recommendation would be to download the museum map ahead of time. The internet connection on-site isn't great and my husband and I were not able to successfully load the link from the posted QR code.

title: How to visit painlessly
text:
On Friday 7 June 2024, my wife and I visited The Vatican Museum. It was enjoyable and painless. This is how. 
Buying tickets. 2 months before, we bought tickets online from the official ‘Vatican Museums Online Ticket Office’ for 32 Euros each and chose 11a.m. as our entry time. The ticket includes entry to the Sistine Chapel which is part of the museum. On the day it was hot: 30 degrees. As instructed, we printed out the tickets attached to the email. 
Queuing to get in. As we approached the entrance, we walked past a line of people 100m long queuing against the Vatican wall to buy tickets on the day. We arrived 30 minutes early but were not allowed in until our ticket entry time, so we had a coffee in the café on the other side of the road. We did not see any queues to get in unless a tour group turned up. At 11 a.m, the time on our ticket, we were let in on production of our tickets and PASSPORTS. There were only a few people queuing in front of us. We found the guards, outside and inside, friendly and helpful. 
Audio guides. We walked into a very large and modern foyer where we bought audio guides for 8 Euros. They are very easy to use, the information is excellent and, unlike the many guide-led tour groups we saw, you can go at your own pace. You hold them to your ear but they have a headphone socket so you could bring your own headphones. We were given a map showing the route to follow. There are a lot of rooms; If you stop at every object included in the headphones, you would be there for several days, so be selective. Listen to the room overview and then choose the objects that take your interest. We spent 5 hours, but it would take 5 years to view everything; think the biggest and opulent National Trust building you’ve ever visited x 100. Once we had our audio guide, we queued for a few minutes to go through an airport-type scanner. We saw many people allowed entry with rucksacks (so you could bring sandwiches) and wearing shorts.
Food and rest. There are places to sit but not many so keep your eyes peeled. About halfway round, there is a café with airport type food and similarly priced. The Sistine Chapel is about 2/3 of the way round. Anyone wearing shorts or skirts above the knee were given a piece of material to wrap around their legs. Before you leave the Museum, there is a gift shop. Altogether, we were there for 5 hours.
St Peter’s Basilica. We left the museum at the same place we first entered and walked 15 minutes around the Vatican wall to St Peters Basilica. It is free to enter. We queued for 30 minutes to go through an airport-type security scanner. The Basilica is huge and awesome. We spent an hour inside.
Summary: book tickets online from the Museum website; TAKE YOUR PASSPORT; buy an audio guide. Allow at least 5 hours.

title: A few tips for planning visits to the Vatican Museums
text:
Vatican Museums was founded in the early 16th-century by Pope Julius II. It is in the heart of Vatican City adjacent to St. Peter's Basilica and is open daily from 8am to 7pm daily (closed on Sundays). Time slotted entry tickets start around €20 each for general admission although you can purchase various ticket combos as well as a variety of guided tours that come at higher prices. It is highly advisable to reserve tickets well in advance of your travels to Rome. 

Here are a few tips for planning your Vatican Day below. 

Queue management at the Vatican Museums entrance can seem a bit confusing. Ask the friendly staff outside if you have questions about which queue to line up. Probably best to be there at least half an hour prior to your scheduled entry to minimise waiting time outside. Note that the queue outside is just security. You still have to pass through metal detector and valid tickets at the indoor entry to access the actual museums viewing area. 

Entry is free on the last Sunday of every month from 9am to 2pm. I've done this in the past and an experienced extremely long queue well over 90 minutes. Seems it remains impossible to reserve skip the line style tickets on free entry days so best to show up really early and be ready for long queues and entry on the day. 

The Vatican is made up of several different museums, exhibition halls and galleries. It is much more than just the Sistine Chapel and there is a lot to see that can fill an entire day if you have the time and interest. It is very much worth the effort of  researching the various museums and collections before. Know what you want to see and have a plan in mind as you enter, allowing you to maximise your time inside the Vatican. As you are moving through the museums, you will encounter fairly regularly, signage telling which direction to go for different museums as well as important highlights such as the Sistine Chapel, Raphael Rooms and Gallery of Maps. 

There is a cafe  style refreshment area within the Vatican Museum but I've always found it a bit difficult to backtrack and find it during visits. As such, we always eat a hearty breakfast before, allowing us enjoy our time without worrying about food and drinks for at least a few hours once inside. There are toilets and quite a few staff around who will be able to point you to nearest toilet location if needed.

text:

title: So excessive, it's impressive and infuriating all at once
text:
The Vatican Museums are incredible. There is so much to see, you definitely need to set aside a day for it. 
Anything and everything the British Museum or the Louvre didn't get their hands on is in the Vatican. 
There is more marble than I have ever seen in my life combined! And the biggest collection of Greek vases, it's truly incredible.
Definitely opt for taking yourself through, rather than a tour. All the tour groups we saw were flying through, missing some really incredible pieces and all pushing past each other. It's much nicer and you'll see more if you go it alone. 
At first it can be a little mazelike and confusing but once you're in the main part of the museum it funnels you through all the rooms in one direction so it's easy to follow along. 
You finish the visit at the Sistine Chapel which, on the whole, is not as impressive as I thought it would be, but the ceiling is amazing. It is the only room in the whole Vatican that they prohibit you from taking photos, which is disappointing. Everywhere else does no flash photography to not damage the artwork, which is understandable, but to not be able to take any seems a bit rude when that's what most people have come to see.
The irony of them asking for donations when you can see the excessive wealth of the church AND the massive crowds of people who have bought tickets to be there is laughable. Don't fall for that. 
The food inside is very average and overpriced. If you can, wait until you leave to get something to eat. 
I still can't get over the sheer volume of what we saw in the museums but there is definitely something for everyone.

title: How to see the Sistine Chapel uncrowded
text:

	2.	Didn’t book a tour.
	3.	Got in line at 7:30 AM with photo ID.
	4.	Walked directly to the Sistine Chapel, which opens at 8:30 AM. With only about 20 people there, we could truly appreciate Michelangelo’s masterpiece.

Afterward, we returned to the beginning, and it was a nightmare of crowds and tours. Definitely avoid tours, as they take about an hour or more to reach the Sistine Chapel, by which time it becomes unbearably crowded.

title: Vatican City Tour and Museums - Open bus
text:
I arranged for admission tickets on the official website of the Vatican Museums. The "Museum admission ticket only" was sold out a few weeks before the visit. There were seats available for the "Museum admission ticket and Vatican City domestic bus tour EUR40.00", so I reserved this (Vatican City Tour and Museums - Open bus). I saved the email (with the QR code required for admission) in a place on my smartphone where it was easy to show. I also brought a printout just in case.
Students get a EUR12 discount (must make a reservation in advance as a student on the website). The website states that student ID is required. Since I only had a Japanese student ID, I obtained an English student ID card and brought it with me before leaving Japan. This is because the international student ID card was in red. In the end, I only had to present a copy of my passport. By the way, even ordinary adults who are not students need to present identification to enter museums and participate in bus tours. My family did not carry the original passport with us, and visited the Vatican with the intention of getting by with a copy. Please use your own judgment when bringing an English student ID card or a copy of your passport. The decision may vary depending on the receptionist.
It was a rare opportunity to tour the paradise-like city that can only be seen on a bus tour. We plugged the earphones provided into the wall of the bus seat and listened to the audio guide while sightseeing. The languages were easy to understand, such as English, French, Spanish, and German. There was no Japanese. The bus had a roof, but it was an open bus with no glass windows. In case of rain, it might be a good idea to bring a raincoat.
After the bus tour of about 20 minutes, we disbanded and each person went into the museum on their own. I recommend taking a day to leisurely appreciate the museum. There were chairs and tables in the garden that you could sit on for free.

title: Delirium...
text: A delirium! Let me start by saying that I visited the Vatican Museums more or less thirty years ago and I remember the experience as one of the most beautiful of my life... Yes, that's right. Maybe I was young, maybe because I was in a happy phase of my life, maybe... but the truth is that I visited the Vatican Museums calmly and free to linger on the works as long as I wanted, unlike today. I found myself in a crowd of people, a river of people, pushed through corridors unable to admire little or anything, feeling contempt. I realize that times have changed and that greater freedom of movement brings more tourism, but when it comes to a museum where incomparable works are kept, I believe it is right to set limits. I don't know, I think it's all a business now, I don't even want to do the math in the Vatican's pocket of how much it collects per day due to the immense turnout, I would be shocked. Having said this, I invite those who love art and culture to avoid going to museums and look at the works in a good book which is perhaps more explanatory. If you think you can admire, transcend in front of so much divine art, it's better to organize yourself for ad personam visits, perhaps in the afternoon because there are tours in the morning, I don't know, the goal would be to avoid the whole world around you.

title: Wir waren mal dort
text:
Die Karten sollte man im November zwei Tage im Voraus buchen. Leider konnten wir einen Abend vorher nur noch die teuren Tickets mit Führung buchen (42€pP-Ticketservice).
Die Tour durch die Gärten, Museen und Six. Kapelle sollte 3h dauern. Mh - davon waren wir fast 2,5h in den Gärten. Unser Guide war zwar prima und konnte sehr viel erzählen, aber für mich hat die Tour zu lange gedauert. Zwar sind die Gärten hübsch anzusehen, aber viel extrem Beeindruckendes zu sehen gibt es nicht. Ein paar Springbrunnen, die Radiostation, Haus von Ratzinger, ein Stück Berliner Mauer, Mosaikbilder und Skulpturen. Von den Gärten aus hat man aber noch einmal einen sehr guten Blick auf den Petersdom. Meines Erachtens hätte 1,5h gereicht. Bevor es in die Museen geht, werden die Besonderheiten der six. Kapelle erläutert. Anschließend schiebt man sich mit zig anderen Gruppen schnell durch die Museen - vorbei an den geografischen Karten und den Wandteppichen. Wir hätten uns die Museen gerne in Ruhe angeschaut, aber das war nicht möglich. Am Ende kommt man zur Six. Kapelle. Fotografieren ist verboten. Wir hätten sie uns spektakulärer vorgestellt und bei den Massen und Security, die ständig rufen "no foto" konnte man die Kapelle auch nicht auf sich wirken lassen.

title: Choose weekdays to visit!
text:
I visited the Vatican museums for the first time by booking the tour with the guided tour. The drive lasts about two hours and you can visit the Pio Clementino museum, the Belvedere courtyard, Raphael's rooms, the Tapestry Room and finally the Sistine Chapel.
Alas, we chose a public holiday, full of people and tourists. Too much confusion, at least for me, makes the visit a bit stressful and even just two hours seems to weigh a lot. However, there are many things to admire that are unique in the world. It is worth visiting them at least once in your life.
I honestly found the Sistine Chapel smaller and "darker" than I expected and very, very chaotic. There is no possibility to take photos and videos in the Chapel.
I recommend the visit and, if there is a choice, I certainly recommend weekdays and of course the guided tour.

title: Good museum, but blatantly putting making money before showing what it hides.
text:
The museum is amazing, from paintings to statues of incalculable value. It's huge, and you need several hours to see everything. So far so good. The problem is that, despite selling tickets by time slots (which in theory should prevent overcrowding of the museum), we were in the rooms surrounded by excess people, as if it were the subway at rush hour. Even our guide apologized for the situation.
We moved through the museum rooms pushed by the human tide, and it was April. I don't even want to imagine what it will be like in summer...
Even the guards in some rooms did not allow you to stay still, they forced you to keep moving forward.
I understand that there is a lot of interest in seeing the museum, but a limit should be placed on the number of visitors. Right now the only thing they manage to do is earn money without stopping without allowing visitors to see the works on display. Not everything goes.

I repeat, the museum in terms of works on display is magnificent. In organization, a 0.

title: Remarkable!
text:
I opted for a guided group tour. Cost €40. About 10 people.
I recommend booking at least a month in advance. A weekday is better, as on weekends foreign tourists (many) are joined by Italian visitors.
The route I chose lasts about 2 hours and includes: Pio Clementino Museum, Raphael's Rooms, Belvedere Courtyard, Hall of Tapestries, Hall of Geographical Maps and Sistine Chapel.
The Sistine Chapel is sensational! The description of the frescoes takes place outside in front of a totem and I recommend memorizing as much as possible, in order to confirm what you have heard once you enter the Chapel (you cannot take photos or videos, and it is always full of tourists who stay as long as possible). possible). Also noteworthy are the Raphael Rooms!
For the rest, the guide only points out the most important attractions, because a whole day wouldn't be enough to see everything.
At the exit, you can admire the helical staircase.
A visit not to be missed in your lifetime!
