title: Sixtinische Kapelle schön -  aber Abzocke
text: Die Sixtinische Kapelle ist an sich schön zum Anschauen. Man kommt in den Raum und überall hängen Gemälde. Das Personal ermahnt aber immer wieder über das Mikrofon, dass man keine Bilder machen soll, weitergehen soll und leise sein soll. Bei uns war es auch nicht so überfüllt wie hier öfter geschrieben. Um in die Kapelle zu gelangen muss man jedoch ein Ticket für alle vatikanische Museen gekauft haben. Das hat uns für zwei Personen 42€ gekostet. Man kann z.B. nicht nur die Kapelle anschauen. Nein, man wird durch alle Museen geschleust, zwei mal durch das Restaurant und das Café, den Souvenirshop etc. Uns haben die anderen Museen nicht interessiert. Man hat keine interessanten Infos gefunden sondern nur goldene Werke die zur Schau gestellt werden, Briefmarken und für uns lauter unnötige Dinge, die in keinster Weise bereichernd waren. Sondern bloße Abzocke. Wir mussten also erst einmal den Rundweg durch alle Museen gehen, der uns ca. 1,5 std (ohne anhalten und begutachten) gekostet hat um in die Kapelle zu gelangen. Die 42€ hätten wir uns locker sparen können denn nur für die Sixtinische Kapelle zum Anschauen ist es das nicht wert.

title: Many museums in one

It is essential to have a pre-purchased ticket if you don't want to queue for hours at the ticket offices, without even having the certainty of being able to enter. Inside the museums there are two refreshment areas and several bookshops. A visit absolutely worth doing at least once in your life.

title: Happy hour was a bit sad
text:
We prebooked directly with the museum after being told that this was the cheapest way to do it. Booking was easy enough to do.  We got the underground in which was fine and quite cheap - a few euro. However, no signs of how to walk from metro. Once there we managed to get in quite quickly without any issues. We had booked audio tours for €7 each. It was like a phone that you had to keep to your ear. It was very detailed but I found my arm ached from holding it so we stopped using after the first room.  Once in you can not fail to be impressed by the surroundings, it really is beautiful, however it is badly organised. I have mobility issues so followed signs for disabled access, however the only lift I managed to find once in the building was the one on the way out. Mind you it too was beautiful.  Given this I found it very hard going. Due to the numbers of people and the lack of order you couldn’t really spend time looking and appreciating the displays. When we arrived at the Cistine chapel it was carnage. Security shouting at people to get in the middle of the room. It was claustrophobic and I found it to be quite disrespectful. Not the serene atmosphere I was expecting. Everyone was speaking (it tells you not to), I saw several people taking sly photos. If you stood for any length of time you were hurried along.  The cattle market type vibe spoilt it a bit for me. Once through the chapel you walk through several gift shops. 
We had bought tickets for the happy hour as it sounded like it would be a magical experience. Sadly not. One, nobody knew where to go for it or how to get there, 2 people told us it was not on and had closed. Once we got there we were ushered to a table and asked what drink we would like before being given a platter of food. It had a feeling that it was closing and that staff wanted you to hurry up and leave, I was led to believe that they would have music playing and that you would be able to use this time to appreciate the opportunity and reflect on the experience but sadly the happy hour was a bit miserable and expensive for what it was.  
Glad we went but I don’t think I would return if I were to go back to Rome.

title: Beautiful but too crowded.
text:
An unclassifiable place.
The immense collections, the countless corridors and rooms, the unreal atmosphere... Everything combines to offer you an unforgettable visit.
But there are crowds. It's also huge. And the endless queues.
Luckily, I had skip-the-line tickets.
Inside the buildings the crowds are so dense that you can feel in danger, oppressed to say the least. A compact flow that prevents wandering and curiosity.
It's really a shame.
I also did not appreciate the obligatory commercial nature of the journey through restaurants or cafetarias or a bazaar of souvenirs as kitsch as they were futile for the most part. Feeling like a pigeon to be plucked.
My real pleasure was found in the exteriors.
The discovery of the gardens was wonderful, to be done again and again.
St. Peter's Square is magnificent and powerful.
Please note: do not go to the immediate restaurants around the Vatican, they are tourist traps for the vast majority.
A few streets away there are much better options for much less money.

Even more so given that the pre-emption costs €5, I personally consider it an armed robbery!
Furthermore, I would do what other great attractions do, that is, I would put a limited entrance to the Sistine Chapel. It has now become an unlivable situation: you move like a sardine, combined with a lot of noise, you just can't enjoy the wonders that are in this wonderful room. It felt like being at the market come on.
I'm sorry that this review will never be read by those in charge, but it's really a shame to make such impressions and not be up to par with other museums of this level... but alas, money doesn't look in anyone's face...

title: A labyrinth of art
text: Often regarded as one of the world's top 10 museums, the Vatican Museums is undeniably huge. With 70,000 works of art, of which about a third are on display in 54 galleries and across more than 5 miles of corridors, the scale of this museum is indeed mind-blowing! You would easily need no less than half a day to cover this immense collection, from ancient artifacts to Renaissance masterpieces, amassed by the Catholic Church throughout the centuries. As one of the world's most visited museums with annual visitors in excess of 5 million, you would expect the museum to be very crowded, so it's best to purchase your timed tickets online to avoid the long queues. Entry to the museum is via Viale Vaticano on the northern side of Vatican City. Upon entering the museum, you're essentially following the visitors route which will take you from one gallery to another, culminating in the highlight of the visit, ie. the Sistine Chapel with its renowned ceiling frescoes. An optional guided tour may provide a different dimension to your experience as they reveal the fascinating stories and hidden symbolism behind the exhibits. Lovely peaceful courtyard gardens within the vicinity of the museum provide a relaxing respite from the artwork overload. Definitely one of the must-see museum in your lifetime!

You're then shoved into the Sistine chapel with another 1000 people and pushed through like an animal. It's a horrible place. You can't stop and wander around. You can't look at anything. It's just an awful waste of 2 hours. Not worth the money and with the 1000s of people hurrying through to try and get a photo of the chapel at the end (which isn't really that good), it's obviously just a Vatican cash cow. Save your money, visit St Peters, climb to the roof of the dome and see something truly amazing and beautiful. Wander through beautiful architecture and soak in the atmosphere of the basilica for an extra hour and dodge the awful Vatican museum. I wouldn't come back to the Vatican museum or Sistine chapel if they paid me to. It's just not a museum.

title: TOO CROWDED, Vatican allowed sacrilege in Sistine Chapel
text:
We booked directly through the Musei Vaticani website especially for a guide-lead tour for individuals which promised an experience with up to 20 people. We appreciated being able to book ahead of time so that we could report to an entry point at a certain time and be allowed entry bypassing the hundreds of people standing in line. We got ready for our tour and overheard some employees talking about how they would have to add a tour t, our group. It ended up that the tour added to ours was 23 people. This meant we had a tour of 30+ people. Our tour guide was not good at showing or explaining anything to us. However, he must have repeated no less than 10 times "See how lucky you are that you have a tour guide instead of walking around aimlessly without information like all these people?" We were not lucky. He walked too quickly dodging the way-too-full-of people and our group of 30+ could not keep up with him. This also meant that he was out of range for our earpieces. At one point he offered that if anyone wanted to split off that they could. We, along with quite a few others who were visibly irritated with the situation, left. Prior to that he mentioned that if we went to the Sistine Chapel that we would have to be reverent. We slowed our pace and finally had a chance to see some of the museum without trying to keep up with a guide. We made our way to the Sistine Chapel and found ourselves in a room that was loud and full of people standing should to shoulder with Museum employees standing  in various spots yelling to keep moving. I looked up and realized we were in the Sistine Chapel! So much for reverence! We managed to find a bench on the side and marveled the ceiling, trying to ignore the loud commotion that was incessant. We meandered through more of the museum trying to ignore the overcrowded situation.
Shame on the Vatican for selling so many tickets that no one could even enjoy what was in there, especially by allowing sacrilege within the Sistine Chapel.

title: Absolutely amazing and so worth the waiting and the slightly chaotic queue system!
text:
Settle in, this is lengthy!
So we booked skip the line timed ticket entry from the original website about one month before. Our visit was February mind, so you may need to consider this in higher season. Do not be fooled for thinking February is not too busy, quite the opposite. The museum was packed. 

I agree with some of the other views on here, actually trying to find the entrance and your allocated timed ticket queue is a trial. 

We entered Vatican City via the bridge near Castel de Angelo, then turning left to St Peter's Basilica. The view when arriving upon the 'square' is breathtaking. We noticed huge queues for the Basilica but no sign posts anywhere for the Musuem. There is also no one to ask other than 'sellers'. We spotted a chap who looked like a guide so quickly asked. He simply pointed (as you look front on to the Dome) to the right. You then see a super small sign for the Museum which is then a further 1km walk. 

Once you're outside you then need to navigate your queue. Again nothing is sign posted, nothing has any timings signposted. You'll need to ask. We then queued for our alloted time. Essentially depending on where you are staying, allow a good amount of time for all of this. 

Once in there are various security procedures to go through and your tickets will be checked. I never take original ID out, so photocopied our passports. It wasn't needed. 

Right so now your in, you are absolutely in for an amazing visit. Before you start head out on to terrace at the top of the escalators for great views over the gardens. Head back in and follow the paper guide given to you. 

There are some spectacular exhibits and it's hard to grasp the ages of some of the pieces. I won't go into too much detail as you'll need to experience for yourself but there are long corridors upon long corridors of beautifully painted ceilings, huge carved statues, mosaic floors, paintings, tombs and much more. It is said that if you stopped at each piece for one minute, it would take you twelve years to get round! This is true, the place is absolutely overwhelming but in an amazing way. We spent about five hours walking by ourselves using an audio guide. I would not opt for an actual guide, you'll miss things and get hurried along, when actually you might just want to stop longer at something to really appreciate it. Certain exhibits are numbered and you just type this in to your audio guide and listen away. 

Inevitably, you'll end up at the Sistine Chapel. Again I won't give you too much information but it is a spectacular and spine tingling place to be. The artwork is beyond what I thought it would be. You'll need to be quiet and there are no photos! We spent a good amount of time sat in here again to appreciate the art and trying to imagine what happens in this room when a Pope passes. Head out and down the circular steps. These are impressive, take your time getting to the bottom. 

I purchased a Vatican book, it was a heafty weighted book with lots of information for €35. 

This is a truly breathtaking place, just a little struggle to find the entrance but once you're in.....it's absolutely amazing.

title: Busy with lots of walking
text:
Purchased tickets online in advance (because who wants to stand in a queue with a whinging child for an unspecified but long period of time?!) Hubs and I are both ordained Church of England priests so discovered we qualified for reduced entry (after a lot of searching on their website - the conditions weren’t enormously easy to find) so I guess that took some of the sting out of paying an extra €5 EACH for booking online?! The queueing system to get in wasn’t awful but it also wasn’t tremendously well organised. LOTS of touts, and fairly long queues so glad we had booked in advance. 
We hadn’t paid for an audio guide, which meant that there was an awful lot of not-sure-what-we’re-looking-at… and the corridors just go on and on and on and on, with nowhere to sit and absorb (or rest!) 
The main thing we really wanted to see was the Sistine Chapel so headed straight there. It was beautiful and reduced me to tears, even though it was busy. We moved into the centre of the room as we were asked to and spent a good 20 minutes taking it all in. (Which you couldn’t actually take it ALL in, even if you had all day!!) 
Our 9 year old enjoyed the pope-mobile exhibit, which was quite well hidden outside… wouldn’t have found it if we hadn’t gone looking, probably! 
I think we probably could’ve spent a lot longer looking around but having skipped over some of it to get to the Sistine Chapel, we couldn’t find a way back, and were completely shattered by the time we decided to head back to our hotel at lunchtime. 
Overall, it was all quite overwhelming, and very very busy with big tour parties BUT - if it’s a must see then you just have to take it as it comes.

title: Fantastic works but terrible organization
text:
One of the most beautiful museums in the world in the hands of a terrible and amateurish organization!
We started queuing at 3.30pm but after an hour we managed to get in, confident in the fact that, as the last entry was at 5pm and closing at 7pm, we would be able to see at least the most important works. It's a shame that the first hitch has already arisen at the ticket office: the cashier abandoned the cash register, leaving the queue waiting without providing any explanation. Nor did the other cashiers bother to integrate the people abandoned in line. Moral of the story: we wasted the first half hour like this. But let's go by points:
1) it doesn't make sense to have people queue up until 5pm (and then close some rooms at 6.30pm) to visit a museum that takes a minimum of 3 hours.
2) rooms closed before closing time: for example the Raphael room closes shortly after 6pm.
3) none but NO indication on the route to follow or recommended (especially at the entrance it is not clear where you should go to start the visit and many people wander around asking for information).
4) TOTAL ABSENCE of description for many works.
5) chaos (and thank goodness they limit entry without a reservation... it's a shame that then, around 5pm, they let everyone pass through, creating an embarrassing crowd).
In short, in the end, we paid €20 per person for an hour and a half visit instead of the expected two, with many rooms inaccessible after 6pm.
I recommend going in the morning but with a reservation.

title: Vatican has changed many rules for 2024
text:
Starting January 1, 2024, the Vatican Museums have changed their hours.  They are now open at 8 a.m., and NO 3rd party tours are allowed in beforehand.   So, all those 'Pristine Sistine ' advertised tours for $100 are a rip off...you'll just be getting in at the same time as those who bought 8 a.m. €20 tickets off the Vatican website.

Tickets can be purchased 60 days ahead of time directly on the Vatican Museums website. 

And while I'm ranting?  Ignore all that 'skip the line' nonsense.   Everyone who purchases a ticket beforehand 'skips' the ticket purchasing line.  BUT no matter who you are,  you will still have to stand in the security check line.  As of 1-1-24, you will have to show security that your ID matches the name on your ticket.

title: Epic climb to the top of the Vatican City
text: If being spellbound by the splendour of the interior of St Peter's Basilica is not enough to take your breath away, then you should climb to the top of its dome for the breathtaking vista of Rome and the Vatican City that will most certainly leave you jaw-dropped. Designed by the famous Michelangelo in the 16th century, the dome is touted to be the tallest in the world at 136 meters and supposedly can even fit the Statue of Liberty into it. Tickets to the dome can be bought once you clear security after queuing for more than an hour, with the queue for the tickets probably adding another 45 minutes. There are 2 ticket options - €8 to climb all 551 steps by foot, or €10 to take the lift to the basilica's rooftop and then climb the remaining 320 steps by foot. The epic climb to the top of the dome follows a narrow single-file staircase that spirals up as the curve of the dome slants inwards towards you. Claustrophobic beware! Before huffing and puffing through the last 320 steps, you will be treated to another unique vantage - looking down into the interior of the basilica from the internal circumference of the dome. Your stoicism and sweat is finally rewarded as you step out onto the caged exterior of the dome, greeted by the massive circular St Peter's Square down below with multitudes of people swarming in all directions like ants, as well as the panoramic view of the Vatican enclave and beyond that, the Eternal City. The experience of standing at the top of the dome of the world's largest and most famous church - priceless!

title: Centre of Catholic cosmos
text:
From the outside, St Peter's Basilica looks like just another Renaissance building in the massive St Peter's Square, but once you step inside, no amount of superlative words could do justice to the spectacle that greets you. The world's largest and most famous cathedral will leave you spellbound and awestruck with its resplendence, grandeur and splendour. You are literally dwarfed by the scale of everything inside - from the height of the gold coffered ceiling to the size of the statues and even the size of the letters that go around the basilica. As the spiritual center of the Vatican and an important mecca of Catholic pilgrimage, expect the place to be absolutely crowded. Be prepared to queue for more than an hour to clear security, but the wait is definitely worth your time.

Construction of the current cathedral began in 1506 using stones removed from the Colosseum and was only completed in 1626, replacing the old basilica built by Emperor Constantine which has stood for an astounding 1200 years on the same site. The basilica is crowned by an astounding Michelangelo-designed dome, touted to be the tallest in the world. It is so tall that it is clearly visible in Rome's skyline and apparently, you could even fit the Statue of Liberty into it! Best of all, for a worthwhile admission charge, you can actually climb the dome and be rewarded with a panoramic view of the Eternal City as well as the enormous St Peter's Square below.

The basilica sits atop an ancient Roman cemetery and also the tomb of Peter the Apostle (the first pope), which is located under the high altar. Above the high altar, standing imposingly at the centre of the basilica, is the glorious Baldacchino, the Baroque-sculpted canopy by Bernini. Also not to be missed is the underground grottoes beneath the basilica's floor, housing many of the medieval basilica's monuments and a crypt containing the tombs of 91 popes, including that of the popular Pope John Paul II. Another interesting observation is that the "paintings" that you see inside the basilica are not actually paintings, but rather glass or ceramic mosaics. 

In summary, no visit to Rome is complete without a visit to “arguably the finest cathedral in the world” (quoting TripAdvisor) - the centre of the Catholic cosmos.

title: A definite visit if you re in Rome
text:
Excellent place to visit, with so many mind blowing treasures and antiquities. Book ahead to get timed entrance tickets as the queue for walk up tickets is long.   It was busy, more so in some areas than others. The whole place is very ornate and it’s worth taking time to really look at the building interiors themselves as well as the artefacts.  Huge collection of art and some massive tapestries…. Trying to put context into the time it must have taken to produce each of these is difficult.  The Sistine Chapel is the obvious highlight, but do not expect an air of quiet, solemnity, or a strong feeling of being in a holy place.  It is busy and there is a lot of chatter which is punctuated by stewards shouting at people who are taking photos. 

The ticket price may look steep, but you could easily spend an entire day here if you want to really appreciate the place.

Visiting St. Peter's Basilica was a surreal experience that exceeded all expectations. As a traveler, the sheer scale of the basilica is awe-inspiring; the moment I stepped into the vast square, the iconic dome dominating the skyline took my breath away.

text: Since it is free and they don't take reservation for timed entry, you absolutely have to go there early in the morning. If you plan on climbing the dome, I would suggest doing that first, because you have to wait in line as well. title: Book the official Extra Time tour!

For travelers concerned about Vatican Museum crowds I highly recommend the official Vatican “Extra Time” Sistine Chapel/Museum Tour which runs daily after hours starting at 3:45 pm (€75).
No crowds, no lines & our group was alone inside the Sistine Chapel with our knowledgeable guide. It also includes a Happy Hour in the outdoor courtyard after the guided Museum tour. I’m unsure whether it runs all winter. The Happy Hour was chilly for us in December, but well worth it for time alone inside the breathtaking Sistine Chapel. 

The tour took us thru the Pio Clementino Museum, Upper Galleries (Candelabras, Geographical Maps, and Tapestries), the Raphael Rooms and then exclusive entrance to the Sistine Chapel. 

My only criticism is that we should have been permitted to stand and wander inside the Sistine Chapel when we were the only group inside. Instead, our guide kept us seated along one wall for the entire time while she explained every panel on the side that depicts the Life of Christ. title: Welcome to IKEA
text:
There is no doubt about the quality of the works: nothing to say. On the other hand, the route imposed to see the essential parts is a model of the worst of what exists on earth. Even IKEA is less oppressive. We follow a single route more or less signposted, it goes up it goes down it goes up it goes down, we go from the ground floor to the 2nd then to the ground floor then to the 1st, we take narrow passageways, small stairs, nothing to sit on, no toilets but shops everywhere, the elderly are clinging to the railings of the stairs praying not to fall or have a cardiac arrest, the children are screaming and the parents carrying the strollers at arm's length too, hordes of zombies wander limply with their headphones on on the ears and their guide in front with his ponpon at the end of a stick (so cute in the photos): green ponpon, red ponpon, Denver the little dinosaur ponpon, colorful hat ponpon, even the Italians slow down when they see the room of their dreams of a security cordon ready "no ma'am, you have to continue straight and follow the route of 40 rooms and 5km, no shortcuts", we want to go see the Sistine Chapel but we are forced to see Egyptian mummies, works by Chagall or oil lamps lined up for no reason, we understand nothing of the logic of this route and we end up feeling anxious at the idea of a crowd movement because we are against each other with no possible turnaround or exit, carried by the mass …
In short, unless you love Sundays at IKEA during sales, it's really the most rotten organization I've done in my entire life. What would the Italians say if we made them go all around the Louvre for 45 minutes to see the Mona Lisa… it’s grotesque…
Conclusion, beautiful museum but organization to be completely revised.

title: Crowding limits your ability to fully check out the museum
text:
I will preface this review by stating that we had an unfortunate incident en route to our visit to the Vatican. Hence, my mood was not great when we arrived. That may or may not color my judgement of how our overall visit went.  FWIW.

We had purchased tickets in advance for an entry time of 10 a.m. They will let you go in maybe 10 - 15 minutes early but not much before. When we entered, there was a security screening (bag X-ray).  We did not, however, have to check our medium-sized backpack. Next, we had to exchange our vouchers for actual tickets. We tried their automated kiosks for this, but they didn't work. We then got in a short line (maybe 8 - 10 people) and handled it with a staffer in one of 3 - 4 booths. The line moved swiftly. 

We entered and rode the escalator up to the main (first) level.  One of our party had been here before, and suggested that we go and check out the Sistine Chapel first. That was not a bad suggestion, but I'll pause here to discuss how the Vatican handles crowding. The museum has the form of an elongated rectangle (picture it with the long side vertical). You enter at the bottom and the Sistine Chapel is at the top.  The only form of crowd control (in terms of entry) that the Vatican does is via ticket sales.  Once the crowd is inside, there are few means of limiting how many people at once can access a given area.  Their solution to this problem is queuing.  They can only control what route you can follow, so as the day goes on they progressively make the route to the Sistine Chapel longer and longer. One result of this is that if you want to see some things at the far end (away from) the chapel, the queue may start to back up there (thus limiting your access).  I'd humbly suggest that they consider some sort of timed entry to the chapel itself as opposed to the current scheme, but whatever. 

The 'rectangle' is also 2 floors tall. We walked the length of one side to the chapel, looking at various art and decoration along the way.  If I went her again (which I'm not super inclined to do, honestly), I'd book a guided tour. You'd probably get a lot more out of it. There were some interesting segments along the gallery - a 'map room' with part of the Italian peninsula detailed, plus a lot of super-ornate wall and ceiling paintings. We eventually arrived at the far end and happened to skip or take a wrong turn by which we missed a Raphael-themed room (The School of Athens). Given the conga-line method of access control, we were not able later to come back to this area.  

The Sistine Chapel - I found it smaller and more dimly lit than I expected. It was interesting to see, but all professional photos I've seen of it were much clearer and brighter.  You are not allowed to take photos there, also.  The crowding wasn't too bad when we were there, but it seemed to be ramping up.

Supposedly you can access St. Peter's Basilica directly from somewhere near the chapel (which would make sense given its function), but we did not take advantage of this. Honestly, given how long the line to the chapel was later in the day, you might save time by going around the outer wall and getting in via the line outside the church...

There were some interesting bits of art and artifacts spread around.  We were not able to see a few items as the conga-line queue for the chapel got extended all the way back to the other end of the rectangle, such that you'd have to commit to going through it just to see some other rooms...  

We did end up eating lunch in the Vatican cafeteria.  They appeared to have a sort of food court option on one side and (maybe) a table-service place on the other (?). We opted for the cafeteria.  Prices were not terrible, but it wasn't super cheap either. They had multiple stations and options (we mostly got boxed salads).  Other than exiting and finding a restaurant outside, there really isn't another option. 

The exit is via a huge spiral staircase. It affords great photo opportunities near the top looking down, so definitely check that out before you leave.

My summary - if they offered some deal where you could pay extra and tour the place in the evening without the crowds or the huge line for the Sistine Chapel, I might come back. Otherwise, I don't think I need to re-visit this place.

title: Visit out of season if possible, to have best experience, and plan what you want to see in advance.
text: I would strongly recommend planning your visit in advance, reading up and researching what you want to see, as it is very confusing and a tad overwhelming otherwise. You get a map, but the audio guide map was different to the official Vatican route map through the museums, and all signs seem to point to the Sistene Chapel, so easy to lose your way or miss some sections. We did not want to be part of a tour group (these many groups with their flags are very irritating and block the way for people who aren't part of the group) so read up on everything first and knew what we wanted to see.  I recommend just buying a 'skip the line' ticket with an audio guide, so you can listen to whatever section you wish to as it suits you.  We went to Rome the second week of November 2023, and I am not sure if it was just pure luck but we had such a wonderful experience of the city at that time and the only big crowds were around the Trevi Fountain.  We had marvellous weather and were able to stay in the Sistene Chapel for quite a long time, without being squashed or crowded out. The Sistene Chapel was definitely the highlight of the Vatican museums tour, and because it wasn't crowded, we could appreciate the immensity and wonder of the magnificent artwork in the Chapel. We got some great photos of the amazing staircase on the way out - take a photo from the top and the bottom view!  Another highlight not to miss are the Octagonal Gardens at the beginning of the tour - amazingly beautiful sculptures by Bernini.  Lots of step to negotiate, so not good for less mobile people.

title: spectacular
text:
St. Peter's Basilica, located in the heart of the Vatican in Rome, is an architectural masterpiece and an extraordinary testimony to the artistic and religious greatness of humanity. Its majesty and grandeur make it one of the most famous churches in the world, not only for the Catholic faithful, but also for art enthusiasts and history lovers.
The facade of the basilica is a riot of columns, statues and elaborate architectural details. Walking along the vast square before it, one feels small before the grandeur of the structure, while Michelangelo's dome stands out against the sky, highlighting the ingenuity and talent of the Renaissance masters. Inside, the basilica welcomes visitors with surprising magnificence. Works of art by artists of the caliber of Michelangelo, Raphael and Bernini adorn the altars and chapels, creating an atmosphere of sublime beauty and sacredness. The statue of Michelangelo's Pietà, which is located immediately at the entrance, is striking for its grace and the perfection of the sculpture. Entrance to the basilica is free, while you pay to go up to the Sistine Chapel

title: Very much worth a visit - history, architecture, art, etc.
text:
Getting in: We arrived here around 1:15 p.m. on a Tuesday and it took 40 minutes in line to get through the security screening. The line tends to follow the curved porticos that border the oval 'square' in front of the church. I'm not sure when you should arrive for a shorter wait, or if that is an option at any given time...  It is free to enter the church.

Restroom line: The restroom facilities are at the bag check, which is to the right as you face the front steps. There was apparently a 10-minute line for the ladies' room. 

This is very much worth seeing even if you are non-religious just for the art / history / architecture aspects. It is enormous. You definitely feel smaller just by entering, which is part of the point.  It is an awe-inspiring building, definitely. Many people have written extensively, so I won't go on at length. You can just wander at your own pace and try to take it all in. 

One additional attraction is to descend one level to the crypt where many popes are entombed. This is well lit and not at all creepy.  It doesn't take long to wander through. You exit outside to the right of the church (but inside the security perimeter).  You can just wander to the front again and re-enter. 

The other side-attraction we checked out was the dome climb. There is a queue on the left side of the portico at the top of the initial stairs to buy tickets for this. The line took about 10 - 15 minutes.  The cost was, I think, 8 Euros if you walked up the entire way, or 10 Euros if you take the elevator up to the main flat roof and just climb the dome itself. After a lot of walking, I opted for the elevator-assist. The elevator had some odd sound of a chain re-spooling that at first sounded like ping pong balls. Once you get to the roof and walk about 50 meters across an open area, the rest of the climb is inside the dome. It was worth it to me, but beware if you have a fear of heights. The views from the top were nice, though when I was there it was in between rain showers.  If you do it on a sunny day I'm sure it is even better. I skipped the elevator on the way down as there was a short line, and descending was easier. 

If you are looking for the Swiss Guards, there is a small guard post on the left corner of the front façade. They appeared to change guards on the hour also. 

Side note:  you can supposedly access the Basilica from the Vatican Museum (which requires a ticket). However, that has its own set of challenges in that it may be a one-way entry (i.e., you cannot then go back to the museum).  Also, you'll have to pass through the line for the Sistine Chapel instead, which is long. If you are interested, you should research this option in advance.

placeInfo.name: Vatican Museums

title: Hideously busy
text: There are some incredible things in the Vatican but I couldn’t recommend visiting at the moment. We bought tickets in advance and didn’t have to queue to get in but despite arriving at 9am on a November weekday it rapidly became uncomfortably busy. The crowds are made worse by the fact that the majority are in tour groups who trample blindly over small family groups and act as if they have more right to see things than individuals do. We did enjoy the Egyptian museum, many of the Roman statues and the Raphael rooms but it was hard work rather than pleasurable. There is very limited information by exhibits and poor signage throughout. In order to get tickets we had to book ‘lunch at the Vatican’ as normal tickets were sold out. The cafe did have tables but the atmosphere was not relaxing and the food (we’re not fussy) was appalling - incredibly overcooked stodgy pasta, meatballs and tinned veg that were almost cold. I think the place needs a complete rethink - improving the circulation of people would help, adding benches internally (not just in the courtyard) having dedicated days or parts of days that are just for small family groups rather than tour groups. I would love to go back if I knew that the experience would be different.

placeInfo.name: Vatican Museums

title: DISORGANIZATION

The problem is that on the Vatican museums website it is not possible to purchase the service except with lunch or the opening of reserved areas, up to spending up to 500 euros and then another increase to purchase skip-the-line tickets on other sites. In short, the usual stuff for priests to make more and more money..
For the rest, disorganization aside which reminds us that the Vatican State is inside Rome, you can admire Egyptian finds, sculptures, paintings and the Pauline Chapel and the Sistine Chapel which alone are worth the ticket. Moreover, the bloodthirsty and orgiastic Popes had awarded themselves the best artists of the time by seeing long in the investment for the Church...

title: Vatican Museums, extraordinary immersion in the History of Art and our Renaissance in particular
text:
There are very few places in the world where you can find such a concentration of history, art and ultimately beauty.
Over 5 km of rooms, corridors, stairways and courtyards full of architectural, sculptural and pictorial works of inestimable value, a true journey through time and the world, through the millennia of art history and in particular in the incomparable history of our Renaissance.
The Corridors of Tapestries and Geographical Maps, Raphael's Rooms and the famous Sistine Chapel are simply indescribable, they leave you stunned and if you could also access the Vatican Library, Stendhal syndrome would be irreversible.
But for this journey to the Paradise of Art we need a Guide and our Beatrice was Fulvia Valentini, very good at managing the times of the visit without making the hours and kilometers weigh on her, with a profound knowledge of the art she tells you about and with great passion that it transmits to you.
The organization can be improved but it's not bad, you can skip the queues by booking and the crowding almost disappears when you are absorbed in the sensorial bubble of amazement.
Francesco Perissinotto, Treviso

title: Great trip
text:
We visited here as part of a combined ticket. You can see quite a bit of the Forum from the road and there are some information boards around. However I would recommend spending some time here with the downloadable Vox guide/ audio guide to properly understand the context and detail.

There is a lot to see and plenty of walking to be done.  We enjoyed seeing the temple of the Vestal virgins although this was currently under renovation. The arch of Titus and the Temple of Saturn are very spectacular.

The temple of the divine Romulus is amazing for its state of conservation, as is temple of Castor and Pollux.

Well worth a few hours of exploration.

Notice the great views of the Colosseum and the arch of Constantine from here too.

title: Simply stunning
text:
A fantastic trip to the Vatican Museums with a couple of teens. The amount of history held in this location is simply phenomenal and if you’re a history buff and in Rome you have to visit these museums which kept us entertained and informed for a good three hours.

I recommend pre-booking tickets to save on entry queues. We breezed through to the entry doors to the museum having pre-booked with GetYourGuide while the official Vatican tour advisers were warning guests of a 90 minute queue. GetYourGuide also offer an audio guide which was excellent for a self-guided tour which gave us the freedom we wanted.

Entry is not at St Peter’s Basilica but about a 15 min walk to the right (north east) around the Vatican walls so make sure you give sufficient time if you Google Maps to ‘The Vatican’, and be aware that the rooms can be packed and slow moving. We were able to take our time and found a few rooms with either aircon or open windows to cool down away from the crowds when we needed to.

October was a great time to visit as the temperature was in the low 20s (low 70s) but I’d be wary of visiting mid-summer when it is a lot hotter and probably busier. If you’re not a fan of crowded locations and heat then self-guided tours are probably a better option than a guided tour.

Overall, a fantastic visit which I heartily recommend.

title: The museums are worth your time beyond just the Sistine Chapel
text:
The museums in the Vatican are huge and it's easily a full day (or multiple days) to see everything. The exit out of the Sistine Chapel into the Basilica actually limits how much you can see of the actual Vatican Museums because there are a lot of things to see after you exit the Sistine Chapel. Don't try to cram everything into one visit and just explore the entirety of the Vatican Museums. 

A highlight for us was the early Christian exhibit art, sculptures, and artifacts in a huge wing that nearly no one was in. The museums also included an ancient Egyptian collection, modern art (even a Dali), and even a museum dedicated to the South Pacific. 

The Raphael Rooms are another highlight and far better than I expected.

title: Vatican employees are rude
text:
Buying the ticket months in advance was an ordeal since the official website never allowed me the option of buying a simple ticket without a guide, which was what I was looking for. So I bought the closest thing, which is the entry option with breakfast included without a guide. A scam breakfast! They promote it as a VIP breakfast with a view, the photo is of a beautiful terrace and the place is horrible. A roof in the patio with those transparent plastic walls that you can't see anything. There wasn't much to see anyway. They made us wait 20 minutes to enter even though the tables were empty. All the employees have a very bad face and treat people badly. Horrible food, service too. They bring you a couple of horrible, hard cold buns and there's a little bottle of water on the table. Then nothing for a while. So it's time to drink water and nibble on those hard buns. After a while they bring a plate with a little bit of scrambled eggs, the greasiest I've ever eaten, some pieces of hot dog and bacon. Everything horrible. Meanwhile the coffee or juice does not arrive. Everything is with a bad face. There is a man who makes pancakes that you have to get up to look for who also treats you badly. He reluctantly puts your pancakes on a small plate and drizzles them with honey without asking if that's what you want or not. At the end they serve you a coffee and a glass of boxed juice. It cannot be repeated. They rush you to clear the table even though there is no one waiting to come in. All this for 18 euros. A horror.
Of course the artists' works are wonderful but throughout the museum(s) the staff is very unfriendly. They treat people badly. An employee ended up yelling at me in Portuguese (obviously her native language) because I couldn't find a staircase she pointed out to me. I speak English and Italian but the lady's instructions were not good. He thought I wouldn't understand and yelled at me in Portuguese, but I do speak Portuguese. They treat people horrible. title: St. Peter’s Basilica: A Divine Masterpiece
text:
Visiting St. Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City was an experience that transcended the boundaries of mere tourism; it was a spiritual and architectural revelation. From the moment I laid eyes on its magnificent facade, I was spellbound by the grandeur and grace of this sacred monument.

Stepping inside, I was immediately enveloped in an aura of tranquility and reverence. The vastness of the interior, adorned with intricate frescoes, awe-inspiring sculptures, and the soft glow of natural light filtering through stained glass, left me breathless. The architecture, a seamless blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, was a testament to human creativity and devotion. Every corner seemed to tell a story, each artwork a masterpiece, creating an atmosphere that was both sublime and humbling.

The centerpiece, Michelangelo’s incomparable Pieta, was a sight to behold. The delicacy with which the sculptor chiseled marble into a representation of profound sorrow and divine serenity was nothing short of miraculous. It was a moment of profound contemplation, reminding me of the boundless depths of human emotion and artistic brilliance.

title: Half-forgotten pages of the Eternal City!
text:
The beginning. St. Peter's Square is separated from the rest of Rome by a white line drawn along the paving stones. They usually cross it without even noticing it, and for a moment this is the state border.☝️Next begins🇻🇦Vatican. Climax. When we saw St. Peter's Cathedral (we did this in winter and spring) with our own eyes, the main and only question arose - not who built it, but how such an unrealistic project in scale could be born in someone's head. From the outside, the grandeur of the building is not striking, as it is “absorbed” by the colonnade and the immensity of the square. Even climbing the dome does not allow you to fully understand the scale of the structure - attention is distracted by the views and dulled by physical fatigue. There are two ways to get there - use the elevator (to the right of the entrance to the cathedral), and then climb another 320 steps, or go all the way on foot, in which case there will already be 551 steps.👍 The stronger the shock when you get inside the cathedral and see the gray with gold, a shining space receding into the distance, in which people are completely lost. What was once a huge crowd at the entrance turns into barely visible figures, as if drawn to demonstrate scale. Together with the portico, the cathedral is 211 m long, without it - 186, more than any other temple in the world, the dimensions of some of them are marked on the floor of the basilica so that no one will doubt. part 3. Stunned by the scale, we switched to the details of the interior decoration. And these are cathedral doors. There are only 5 doors, the one on the far right is always locked - it opens once every 25 years, when the Catholic Church proclaims absolution. The central door (usually with a lock) was moved from the old basilica and is notable mainly for the views of Rome forged on its doors by master Philaret in the 15th century. From the entrance, the perspective abuts a 29-meter bronze canopy on columns twisted in an oriental style. In order to build a foundation for this heavy structure, it was necessary to break into the floor, disturb the relics and ashes of the dead - to commit incredible sacrilege. But Pope Urban VIII, who ordered this project, went for it. He not only ordered to dig up everything that was necessary, but also ordered the removal of bronze from the portico of the Pantheon (for which he deserved praise).
the proverbial “Quod non fecerunt barbari, fecerunt Barberini” -
“What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.”☝️Decoupling is certainly and obligatory, at any time of the year, morning, afternoon and evening!

title: Worth it
text: Ok. You’re going to have to stand in line, there is not a skip the line option and even private tours require you to stand in the big line, BUT it is totally worth it. There is no entry cost (there is a cost to rent audio guides if you want one),  but St Peter’s Basilica is stunning. There is floor to ceiling artwork, relics from the church including pieces of the cross, and every 5-10 steps is a completely new scene to take in. The pulpit in the middle is so much larger in real life than you can depict from pictures and just amazing to view it up close. There are prayer rooms you can sit in, and there was even a live service while we were there. I highly recommend getting up early to get in line and touring the facility before the later rush.

title: Worth the climb
text:
Stunningly beautiful.  It's just gorgeous inside,  and you can take an underground tour to view the popes resting places. Expect to queue to get in here, and wear appropriate clothes.. nothing revealing, it is, after all, a place of worship. The pop is in town on Wednesdays, so check if you can go in before turning up.
We also climbed the Cupola (dome) 
We took the lift part way and walked the rest... its about 330 steps plus the lift up (or 500 odd if you don't take the lift...) it's brutal in the heat. Its also narrow in places. Expect a stone staircase. We did it at the end of the day.. I'd fully recovered this as it meant we weren't being rushed up the stairs..
I'm reasonably fit.. but this is hard going. 
If you're asthmatic, don't forget your pumps!!

title: Church built on the fisherman's humble tomb
text:
Church built over the humble tomb of the fisherman from Galilee, the Basilica was built at the behest of Emperor Constantine around 320 AD.
It is located on the Vatican hill, not far from Nero's circus, the place where the first apostle Peter suffered martyrdom.
Today's Basilica, built over Constantine's, is an expression of the will of the Renaissance popes who used the work of great artists such as Bramante, Michelangelo, Bernini and Maderno.
Through a path of art, faith and spirituality, you can admire the magnificence of the building, walk the corridors, visit the chapels and appreciate the beauty of the many works of art, including La Pietà di Michelangelo.
You cannot miss visiting the tombs of the Popes located in the Vatican Grottoes.

title: Wonders to visit at least once in your life.
text: Two of us took the skip-the-line ticket without a guide and went straight in without any problems. I don't give my best just because on principle I don't accept that the only way to skip the queue is to give money to the touts since getting tickets on the official website is a utopia. It is a huge museum but if you read up a little and start with a clear idea of the route you want to take and what you want to see, it can easily be done even without a guide. Compared to many negative reviews I read, we were lucky enough to be able to see the Sistine Chapel calmly and to have found helpful staff who gave us directions. The chapel is at the end of a long corridor and before entering it remember to turn left to admire Raphael's wonderful rooms (the directions are clear). There are also works by Van Gogh, Morandi, Rodin, Matisse etc. along the obligatory route. which, given the amount of things you see, risk being overshadowed, but with a bit of luck you can admire them while sitting down to recover your energy before visiting the chapel.

title: Be prepared with these tips! Plan the earliest possible entry and pay to skip the line without a guide
text: Visiting this museum takes planning, courage, and patience. 1) Go very early before the museum is so full that you can barely move. 2) Once you go through an area you must continue in the same direction. There is a constant flow of people. 3) Buy the skip the line ticket without a guide so you have freedom to spend time on your interests. 4) Use the bathroom and eat before you arrive. title: Talking walking shoes, water and wee before you go in!
text:
We booked a tour with Italy Pass tour office (would not recommend). We got there about 5pm in October. The tour was good in that it meant we didn’t have to queue in the hot sun but lots of waiting around. But the Vatican itself… 

Book weeks in advance! Take decent walking shoes, wee before you go in and take plenty of water with you! Make sure you see what you want, you cannot go backwards. I regret not going round the gardens. 

So much to see, you could spend a day there! great if you love Art, but for us the novelty so wore off as you went through gallery after gallery after gallery. I’d say do you research, pick what you want to see and enjoy the experience. 

We’re animal lovers so we enjoyed the animal sculpture gallery. 

No photo in the chapel itself are allowed. 

Great views of the city through the window at sunset if your a photographer. 

Open until late when we were there.

title: The MOST obligatory stop in ROME
text:
Rome is the Colosseum, Pantheon, Trevi Fountain... but above all this, a visit to Rome has a mandatory stop in the small city of the clergy to visit the largest basilica in Christendom (193 m long, 44.5 m high, and covers an area of 2.3 hectares). The height means that its dome can be seen from any elevated area of Rome. It is considered one of the most important pilgrimage sites of Catholicism, although you do not need to be Catholic to appreciate the magnitude and beauty of this basilica.

Free admission, although this price does not include entry to the Vatican Museums.

A MUST STOP to see some of the most important sculptures, altarpieces and in general works of art of humanity such as the Pietà, by Michelangelo, the Holy Door of Vico Consorti, the tombs of all the Popes, the impressive Baldachin of San Pedro de Bernini or the incredible dome that rises to a total height of 136.57 m from the ground to the top of the external cross, being the tallest dome in the world.

title: Necessary visit.
text:
Without a doubt this is a beautiful, truly amazing and of course historical must see place in Rome.
Couple of added pieces, entrance is free. You don't have to buy tickets (unless you want to go up in the dome which we did and were very glad we did so), you don't need to be part of a tour unless you want to have more of the historical detail which can also be nice.
We paid approximately $130 total through "headout" which is a third party purchase to be assigned to a tour and in my opinion a total scam. 
Our guide , thru VOX (?) was wonderful and we were glad to have the information but not necessary. Also "headout" indicates the tour is 1 hour which is also untrue, many folks in our group had to leave because of schedule conflicts, we fortunately were able to catch the entire tour.
In closing, gorgeous, spiritual, holy place without question worth visiting. Just be aware of scammers trying to sell you things you don't need.

title: Сикстинская капелла и музеи Ватикана: первый вход утром
text:
Наконец, у нас будет достаточно дней в Риме, чтобы выделить день для этого места. Историй наслушались много. И о длинных очередях, и о столпотворении, когда желающих набивается так много, что даже, стоя, повернуться сложно, не то, чтобы присесть. Для себя я уже давно определилась с вариантами покупки  электронных билетов, на онлайн-сервисе, который даёт гарантию, что мы с мужем попадём на мероприятие или экскурсию в нужное время без нервотрёпки и очередей. В этот же раз, предложение, превзошло все наши ожидания. Вход в Сикстинскую капеллу за 30 минут до прибытия других групп или посетителей (!). С неограниченной возможностью во времени, когда можно провести целый день в музеях Ватикана и осмотреть одну из величайших в мире коллекций произведений искусства. Да, это то, что нам нужно. 
Время встречи: 07:05. На организационные моменты: перекличку, краткое знакомство, выдачу карт, наушников, ожидание опаздывающих, ушло минут 40. Нашу группу из 17 человек англоговорящий сопровождающий провёл ко входу в музеи Ватикана напрямую, минуя длинную живую очередь к кассам. Постояв в холле минуты две, пока сопровождающий получила билеты в кассе, нас повели к эскалатору. Отмечу, что таких групп, как наша, было ещё 2-3. Да, действительно, вход для основной очереди был ещё закрыт, начало открытия 9:00. Мы вошли на территорию музеев Ватикана на 1 час раньше. Но наверху нас рассадили на скамейки и стали вкратце рассказывать о Сикстинской капелле, на это ушло ещё минут 20-30. Учитывая, что в самой капелле нельзя разговаривать, вернее не желательно, и категорически нельзя фотографировать, а также в нашу экскурсию не входило разговорное сопровождение, а только проведение до места, то эти 30 минут были посвящены краткому описанию основных сюжетов на стенах и потолке Капеллы. И вот, наконец, пройдя галереи музеев Ватикана, напрямую, нигде не задерживаясь больше 30 секунд, но потратив какое-то время на Галерею географических карт Ватикана, мы вошли в Капеллу за 30 минут до запуска общего потока туристов в кассы, и минимум за 1-1,5 до посетителей в самой Капелле. Мы оказались не первыми, но это были посетители таких же групп, как мы. Всех вместе нас было очень мало. Места было предостаточно. Мы спокойно ходили по Капелле, сидели на всех четырёх сторонах, что позволило рассмотреть досконально, без суеты, каждый фрагмент потолка и стен. Это относительно небольшое помещение с максимально сконцентрированным количеством шедевров, вызывало противоречивые чувства. Восхищение и восторг от значимости и величия этих рукотворных шедевров и какое-то щемящее разочарование, что вот то, о чем ты знала всю свою сознательную жизнь, о чем мечтала в каждый приезд в Рим, и ждала последние несколько дней, свершилось! Было ощущение, что отсчёт времени, на какой-то момент остановился. Эти шедевры, как-будто, притягивают, вы попадаете в их ауру и оказываетесь в невесомости. Наверно, это и есть, тот самый отголосок синдрома Стендаля. А потом вы опускаетесь на землю и четко осознаёте, что всё, пора, это не может длиться вечно и надо уходить.

title: Overcrowded, geared towards tours, and without a care for the visitor experience
text:
The problems with visiting the Vatican Museums start days before you even go, because like several popular sites in Rome its business model prioritises tour companies. For anyone who hasn't booked a 'skip the line' ticket well in advance, the choices are presented as either cough up for the middle men, or stand in line forever. I opted for the smallest tour group I could afford, accepting it would at least get me in and hoping there would still be some independence.

No slight on the guide, who was incredibly knowledgeable, but once past the initial gardens it wouldn't have mattered if this was a tour group of 80: hundreds upon hundreds are guided into the corridors and pushed along, radios in ears, with little chance of pausing and zero opportunity to cross a room or go back. The tours miss out chunks of rooms - its disheartening to read after returning home of things you could have seen if you went by yourself - because their obvious destination is the Sistine Chapel. It is, quite frankly, mass tourism taken to its logical end, in which people are shovelled through an exhibition space, have no time to engage their own thoughts, but get to say 'I went there'.

The chapel is both the grand finale, and the confirmation you are on a conveyor belt. Guards constantly shout 'keep moving!' and 'no photos', and if one did 'keep moving' you would be out the door immediately. However, those who do wish to pause must stand in the middle, huddled like sheep in a show pen. Your thoughts on this master work of art are to be formed in this mass, beside a stream of prodded tourists, listening to people loudly telling you to collectively get going. 

St Peter's is far more civil and sensible. 

Leaving the Vatican Museum, I hated that I paid good money for a small group that simply jumped into the blob of people. I hated that I felt I had needed to forego controlling my own time and choice of rooms because tours are sold as the primary way to get through the door. I hated that I had become part of the problem in this horror show, just another person taking photos whilst being pushed through. These are not the thoughts that should come immediately after seeing a great art museum. 

Whilst it is undoubtedly making good coin out of the current situation, safety or decency ought to prompt the Vatican Museums to find a way to control visitor numbers and entry methods (e.g. cut the Sistine Chapel into a separate visit). Presently there are too many people and tour companies are crushing the experience as they feast. It is dreadful.

title: Book your own tour at Musei Vaticani for Cheap
text:
It is so easy to jump onto a tour website and select one which will "hold your hand" and provide a guided tour. However, you can book your own tour at Musei Vaticani for 35 Euros per person and still get a guided tour - provided by the Vatican Museum staff in may languages.

It is so easy to do. Go to the official "Musei Vaticani" ("Vatican Museum" in Italian) website, and choose your date and time. Do this well in advance, if you can, so it can be most convenient to you.

Without a pre-arranged ticket, the line-up runs down the entire street. 

With a ticket on your phone (or printed), walk right up to the front door, 20 minutes before your appointed time, and the attendant will direct you to the correct counter; they will go through some brief check-in paperwork and direct you to the meeting point with your Musei Vaticani guide. He was professional and spoke excellent English.

The official tour seemed to be almost identical to the other (externally provided) tours. In fact, most of the visitors seemed to be part of one guided tour or another, and everyone stopped in the same rooms to discuss the same artwork. 

There was one difference between the official tour and the private ones. The official tour ended at the modern gallery, and did not cover the modern period or the Sistine Chapel - you need to do these unescorted. Our Musei Vaticani guide did provide us extensive background about the Sistine Chapel in advance, but he could not accompany us. 

The signage in the modern section was comprehensive, and we were able to enjoy the religious works donated by Matisse, Rodin, Van Gogh, and other famous artists. Frankly, we watched various private groups speed through this section. 

As for the Sistine Chapel, one is not permitted to speak or take pictures. Although tour guides of small private tours seemed to keep talking in whispers, all of the other tours were silent. The security/attendants kept reminding people to be silent, so this was enforced. A benefit to not being part of the private tour was that we did not need to separate ourselves from the tour to use one of the seats on the side of the room.

Do this yourself - you can enjoy an official tour for much less that a private one.

title: Amazing chapel
text: A beautiful place, a chapel is one great work of art.  It is a rectangular room 40.93 m long, 13.41 m wide and 20.70 m high. It is covered by a barrel vault with telescopes. They are divided by an openwork balustrade made by Mino da Fiesole. The Sistine Chapel was famous for its excellent male choir, in which men with high countertenors also sang . From the beginning, the Sistine Chapel was intended for major church ceremonies. In the past, masses were often celebrated there. A conclave  takes place here. The chapel walls and vault are decorated with frescoes. The oldest are placed on longitudinal walls. They were made in the years 1481–1483 by artists from Tuscany and Umbria. Pope Julius II commissioned work on decorating the vault to Michelangelo. The paintings decorating the vault tell the story of humanity from the creation of the world, through original sin, to the biblical flood. On the wall in front of the entrance, Michelangelo painted the "Last Judgment" fresco. Pope Paul IV demanded the destruction of the work, considering it indecent. After persuasion, he agreed to paint intimate fragments.  In 1981–1994 Italian specialists carried out conservation works financed by the Japanese Television. The frescoes were cleaned, some of the curtains placed on the hips of the ''Last Judgment'' were removed.  The huge number of tourists means that the crowds admire the paintings. It is breathtaking, just  beautiful.  Although it is very  crowded,   I still recommend seeing the Sistine Chapel with your own eyes.

title: One of the most incredible places in the world
text:
Led through hall after hall filled with masterpiece after masterpiece, we finally made it to the Sistine Chapel. Every square inch was overflowing with detail....and no photographs were allowed. It was extraordinary beyond description, and even as I dealt with the RIDICULOUSLY crowded room, inhaling the BO and flatulence of the masses, getting repeatedly (yet softly) elbowed in the ribs, having my feet ground into dust by the bovine-esque crowds who were quite literally corralled through one of history’s greatest masterpieces, I was still awestruck by the sheer - I’m sorry but no other word will do - majesty of it all.

Michelangelo was apparently an ugly man. Seriously, it’s surprising how often I come across that reference in some of the more minor articles I’ve read regarding history’s greatest sculptor. Foul-tempered and aware (as we all should be) of the final curtain call that awaits us all, he nevertheless maintained an undeniably wicked sense of humor and was never afraid of giving a middle finger when one was due. Example: one contemporary cardinal who always complained of the nudity contained in the maestro’s works had, as revenge, his likeness painted onto the face of a judge who was burning and writhing in hell. The insult didn’t end there; the judge was caught within the muscular constrictions of a large, coiled serpent, and even the casual onlooker could see the scaly beast sinking its fangs deep within the cardinal judge’s testicles.

The Sistine Chapel has the same dimensions as the Temple of Solomon, and the last sight I caught as we left the beloved chamber was that of the hand of god reaching out towards the hand of Adam. They weren’t quite touching, but Francesca told us how the reddish aura surrounding the almighty resembled that of a brain. Google it yourself! Michelangelo actually did human dissections to better aid in his stone recreations, and though nothing but conjecture, it’s believed by many that the image of god upon the ceiling of the Chapel is entirely contained within a frescoed representation of the mind of man. We were constantly told by Francesca to come to our own conclusions, so read into THAT what you will.........

You won't be able to spend long in here as your tourguide pretty much rushes your through in about 10 - 15 minutes, and you won't have enough time to look at everything, but feel fortunate to be here. It's an amazingly beautiful place.

(Recommended length of visit is more than 3 hours, but ALLOWABLE length is 10 - 15 minutes, so........)

title: Fantastico
text:
Siamo stati a Roma per 3 giorni (22-23-24/08) e devo dire che è stato tutto fantastico quello che abbiamo visto. Il primo giorno abbiamo visitato il Colosseo e i fori romani prendendo il biglietto online qualche giorno prima per evitare code. Un’ottima soluzione perché in un pomeriggio abbiamo girato sia il Colosseo (bellissimo) che i fori che sono stupendi. È un bel giretto che vi impegnerà 3 ore circa però ne vale la pena e comunque puoi riposarti ogni tanto all interno dei fori. Nel biglietto c era anche il museo ma non si poteva visitare tutto perché una parte era in restauro. 
Consiglio comunque il biglietto che costa 24€ così vedi Colosseo e fori e ha la validità di 2 giorni.

title: 🇮🇹✨ Stairmaster Workout with a Heavenly View! 🏰🔝
text:
Who needs a gym membership when you can have a stair-climbing adventure like this at Basilica di San Pietro in Rome?! 🏋️‍♂️💦 Let me tell you, folks, this was the ultimate glute workout with an epic reward at the end! 🍑🏆

I visited the magnificent Basilica on a toasty July day, and boy, was it a hot one! 🔥 But that didn't stop me from embracing this heavenly experience. As I approached the grand entrance, I felt like a modern-day explorer ready to conquer the architectural marvel. 🕵️‍♀️🗺️

The moment I stepped inside, I was in awe of the sheer grandeur and beauty surrounding me. The Basilica's interior is nothing short of breathtaking, and I may have said "wow" a few dozen times. 😲🤩 Every corner seemed to reveal a new artistic masterpiece, and I couldn't resist snapping pictures like a shutterbug on steroids! 📸🦋

But then, my adventurous spirit kicked in, and I thought, "Why settle for an amazing view from the ground when you can climb your way to the top like a champ?" So, I decided to tackle the 300+ steps leading up to the dome. Challenge accepted! 💪🏰

Now, let me warn you, those steps weren't for the faint of heart. But as I huffed and puffed my way up, I couldn't help but imagine I was in a race with Usain Bolt – stair-climbing style! 🏃‍♀️🏆 I'm pretty sure my face turned as red as a tomato, but it was all worth it when I finally reached the top.

The view from the dome was mind-blowing! 🤯🔝 I felt like I could see the whole of Rome from up there! The Eternal City stretched out before me like a beautiful painting, and I was on cloud nine – or should I say, dome nine? 😉⛅️

As I caught my breath and marveled at the panorama, I couldn't help but feel a sense of accomplishment. Climbing all those steps was like winning an Olympic gold medal in cardio! 🏅🥇

If you're visiting Rome, the Basilica di San Pietro is an absolute must-see. Embrace the adventure, climb to the top like a stairmaster pro, and bask in the glory of the most breathtaking view in the city. 🏛️🌆 Trust me; your glutes will thank you later! 😉

#StairwayToHeavenlyViews #BasilicaBliss #RomeInJuly #GlutesOfSteel

title: Most Amazing Church In Christendom
text: This review is a long time coming. I don't know how I forgot this one. This was a  must do on our list as we are Catholic and we tried to get tickets to Mass ahead of time but we never got a response. Our hotel concierge tried as well with no luck. I had heard that once you see St. Peter's Basilica no other church compares. I didn't know that I believed that as we have been to Westminster Abbey and York Minster and were very impressed. The Basilica is overwhelming, but in a good way. There is so much to take in, there is no space left unadorned.  From Pope John Paul II's tomb to other various Popes to the Pieta. The Basilica is simply breathtaking and enormous. We didn't climb the stairs to the top of the dome as there are about 300 but you can spend a couple of hours here. There are altars for prayer and candles to light. You simply cannot convey the marvel that is the Basilica from outside in the square as well when you arrive.

title: The Glory of Vatican City
text:
St. Peter's Basilica is one of the crowning glories of Rome and the Catholic faith.  This spectacular building dominates the landscape with its imposing architecture, and inside the vast space still invokes mystery and devotion.

Well, we took a tour this time that led us through the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel, both of which are wonderful and impressive, but shoulder-to-shoulder crowded with other visitors.  When we entered the Basilica we were awe struck that even though it was full of people, we could still move easily and see all the sights.  

Of course Michelangelo's  Pieta is a must-see, but the dome, the altar, the sculptures and decor also capture and hold one's attention.  We did not climb to the top on this visit, but the view up there is  amazing.  

The last time we were in Rome Tripadvisor did not exist yet, so I have decided to add this review as memories of Rome are eternal, and no matter how many times one visits, the experience is always magnificent.

title: Must See and Take your Time
text:
St. Peter's Basilica is humongous,   But wherever you wander, the views are inspiring and beautiful.

Be respectful in your attire and keep your voices low.  Pictures are ok without flash.  

I would encourage you to start on the right as you enter and proceed down the right side, cross to the left side near the altar.  There is almost always a mass being performed and the seating upfront is roped off for those wishing to attend the mass and then reverse direction on the left side.  Review a guide book before visiting to get an idea of the additional areas to visit.

This is a religious site but be cautious- we were told of pick pockets in the basilica and one area of concern is to secure your wallet or purse while taking photos.

title: Got Closer To Heaven.
text:
St. Peter's Basilica in one of the most acclaimed churches in the world and as a Catholic, I always wanted to visit its headquarters. I was fortunate to catch a glimpse of the Pope during his audience in St. Peters Square that sits in front of St. Peter's Basilica.

Inside the breathtaking art and architecture was stunning and spiritually inspiring, like the bronze canopy over the High Alter in turn built over the tomb of St. Peter, or the cupola designed by Michelangelo as one of  the largest domes in the world........and La Pieta ...... another Michelangelo masterpiece in the form of a carved statue.

Their is a seemingly endless litany of relics and artifacts in the Basilica and their are no superlatives strong enough to reflect the magnitude of their presence.

I left the Basilica feeling a little closer to heaven and reinvigorating a semblance of religion in me.

title: Impressive Basilica
text:
This was my third visit to Rome but my first time inside the Basilica. You can enter the Basilica for free but the queues can be very long. I had visited the Vatican Museum and Sistine Chapel, and when you leave the Chapel, you join the Basilica queue near the entrance and I was inside within 5 minutes.
Nothing prepares you for the immense scale and beauty of this incredible building, and you don't have to be devoutly religious to appreciate it.
It was very busy inside so I'd imagine an early out late visit would escape the crowds.
When I left the Basilica I noticed there was an option to go inside the dome by elevator for 10 Euros, which I queued for about 30 minutes. It was well worth the wait as you see the dome from both inside and then views of Rome on the outside. Please note there are still may steps to climb despite using the elevator, which are very narrow. The slope of the dome also confuses the brain, similar to the leaning Tower of Pisa. I thoroughly recommend the Basilica.

title: Peterskirken
text:
Vi tog Metroen til Ottaviano ( 5 min. fra Vatikanstaten) og ankom til kirken ca kl 9 og skulle max vente 20 minutter på at komme ind i kirken. Der var kø, men det gik stærkt da, man blot skal igennem et sikkerhedstjek. Vi valgte den gratis udgave, uden tourguide, og hvis man blot er interesseret i at se den fantastiske smukke og helt overvældende kirke, er det nok den bedste model. Vi havde dog læst lidt op på kirkens historie inden vi kom.
Vi var også oppe i kuplen (Dome), som koster 10 € med elevator og 8€ hvis du bruger trapperne.. Vi købte adgang til elevator, men fortrød da vi så køen. Da vi har raske ben, spurgte vi om vi måtte tage trapperne i stedet. Det var Ok og vi kunne gå direkte til trapperne uden kø. Hvis man er klar til at bestige mange mange trapper og nogle stedet gå ad smalle og stejle passager, så er det faktisk en ret spændende tur. Ca halvvejs oppe kan man gå ind og se kirkerummet oppefra, men man kan også gå helt op og nyde udsigten udover Vatikanstaten og Rom. Alt i alt er det yderst spændende både historisk og kulturelt at besøge Peterskirken..  og en kæmpe oplevelse at se alle detaljer i og omkring kirken.

Bemærk gratis adgang til Peterskirken ikke giver adgang til Vatikanmuseum og det Sixtinske kapel.
Alle skal have dækket skuldre (f.eks. T-shirt) og shorts/kjole der mindst går til knæene.

placeInfo.name: Vatican Museums
placeInfo.address: Viale Vaticano, 00120 Vatican City Italy

title: Gorgeous but a terrible experience
text:
The works of art and the collections of antiquities are fabulous. I can’t fault that. However the experience of being in the museum was horrendous. There are so many pushy tour groups, and spaces become dangerously overcrowded. The museum flows through a number of narrow hallways and rooms with very little ventilation and at times it feels severely claustrophobic. By the time you reach the Sistine Chapel (which is equally rammed) you feel completely fed up and ready to leave. Which is just as well as the stewards rush people through the chapel to try and combat the overcrowding.  

In my mind, unless something is down to ease the dangerous overcrowding I would not attend again. Would caution anybody with health conditions or fears of small enclosed spaces or crowds to avoid completely.

title: Overcrowded

Would not recommend the museum despite the world class art collection. There are so many better things to see in Rome that are not this crowded. placeInfo.name: Vatican Museums
